To run Coverage Directed Solver in a three-step (or UUM) flow, use the following
commands:
• % vlogan [vlogan_options] file_list
• % vcs -vso ccex [elab_options] [libname].design_unit
• % simv -vso ccex <run_options>
The <vlogan_options>, <elab_options>, and <run_options> represent files
and options that are not related to Coverage Directed Solver.
Compile Commands
The first step in Coverage Directed Solver is to identify the connections between
covergroups and random variables. Identification of a connection at compile time is
referred to as compile-time connectivity generation.
To generate Coverage Directed Solver compile-time connectivity report, use the following
command:
%vcs -vso ccex -ccex_opts connect_report <compile_options>
• -vso ccex : Enables Coverage Directed Solver in compile-time connectivity mode if
connected covergroups are detected.
-ccex_opts connect_report : Generates the compile-time connectivity report of
Coverage Directed Solver.
User can specify path for connectivity report by specifying an additional argument to the
connect_report option as follows:
-ccex_opts connect_report=<report_path>
To visualize the connections between the coverpoint and crosses in covergroups to
random variables generated by Coverage Directed Solver at compile time, a covergroup-
level summary report of connectivity is available in ccex_summary.json under the same
directory where the compilation is done. This connectivity information is also annotated in
the URG report.

Runtime Commands
By default, Coverage Directed Solver biases the constraint solutions in the direction of
coverage inside a single simulation. This is referred to as intra-simulation biasing.
To enable Coverage Directed Solver with intra-simulation biasing, use the following
command:
% simv -vso ccex <other runtime_options>
To enable Coverage Directed Solver to bias the constraint solutions across multiple
parallel simulation jobs running on the simulations, each Coverage Directed Solver-
enabled simulation needs to know the merged coverage state of the simulations which
have completed.
To enable Coverage Directed Solver with inter-simulation learning by reading from the
previous VDB, use the following command:
% simv -vso ccex -ccex_opts auto_merge_dir=<inter-sim shared directory>
The <inter-sim shared directory> is the commonly accessible path by all
simulation jobs and has a different path than the one specified with -cm_dir.
The command above performs automated distributed merging of covergroup metrics and
deposits the merged coverage results into the specified directory. Coverage Directed
Solver uses the merged directory as an input to identify covered targets and therefore,
focus efforts on targeting and diversifying over uncovered or rarely covered coverage bins.
Alternatively, if you already have an external method to merge the VDB directories
continuously, this external and continuously-merged VDB directly may be provided to the
Coverage Directed Solver-enabled VCS simulation using the following option:
% simv -vso ccex -ccex_opts vdb_dir=<VDB dir path>
Runtime Commands to Replay a Simulation
If the auto_merge_dir option is used at runtime, then the simulation run can be replayed
using the replay option. Replay run uses the identical set of options as used in the
original run along with the replay option.

Root Cause Analysis
Following are the replay options:
• If cm_dir and cm_name name was not specified in the original run:
% simv <original_options> -vso ccex -ccex_opts replay
• If cm_dir and cm_name was provided in the original run, then specify cm_dir and
cm_name name of the original run using the following command:
% simv <original_options> -vso ccex -ccex_opts
replay_cm_dir=<orig_cm_dir> -ccex_opts replay_cm_name=<orig_cm_name>
• If only cm_dir was provided in the original run, then specify cm_dir name of the
original run using the following command:
% simv <original_options> -vso ccex -ccex_opts
replay_cm_dir=<orig_cm_dir>
• If only cm_name name was provided in the original run, then specify cm_name name of
the original run using the following command:
% simv <original_options> -vso ccex -ccex_opts
replay_cm_name=<orig_cm_name>
Root Cause Analysis
Root Cause Analysis (RCA) provides information on the constraints that block certain
coverage bins from being covered. The RCA capability can be enabled in simulation.
Along with the appropriate URG report commands described in Generating Reports, this
provides the ability to view the RCA of the covergroups in the URG report. The report
provides information on blocking constraints, if identified. It is important to note that the
RCA is a best-effort technology and may not be successful if the connectivity between the
constrained random variables and covergroups could not be successfully established.
Static RCA
Static RCA refers to first level Root Cause of holes in functional coverage. To enable the
first level RCA to be dumped during simulation, use the following command at runtime:
% simv -vso ccex -ccex_opts rca <other_runtime_options>
Note that basic coverage RCA depends on the connectivity between the random variables
and the coverage to exist. The annotated results of Static RCA are available in the URG
report using the URG options as described in Generating Reports.
Two types of Static RCA shown in the RCA column on the detailed page of coverpoints in
the URG report.

Generating Reports
• UNSAT: When some constraint might block the bin from being hit.
• UNSAT FOR STATE VAR: When the Coverpoint is connected to a state variable, which
cannot be changed.
• NOT SAMPLED: When the coverage group is not triggered.
Generating Reports
Coverage Directed Solver reporting brings together the information from the existing
constraint and the coverage reports or information into a URG report, which contains the
linked coverage to the connected constraints and random variables.

Coverage Directed Solver reporting brings together the information from the existing
constraint and the coverage reports or information into a URG report, which contains the
linked coverage to the connected constraints and random variables.
To generate the URG report for Coverage Directed Solver, use the following command:
% urg -ccex -dir simv.vdb <URG options>

Generating Reports
With the -ccex option, the URG report generates a new page named CCEX that provides
information on randomization. The following figure depicts the CCEX page, which is
generated in the URG report in the HTML format:

Generating Reports
The CCEX page provides the following information:
• Total Summary : Lists basic statistics on randomizations and covergroup.
• Targeted Summary : Lists information on the Targets.
• Connected Summary : Lists information on the coverpoints/crosses connectivity.
• Bin Summary : Lists information on the bins of coverpoints/crosses.
The URG report also has an indication that a covergroup has been targeted in the groups
page of the report.
The three new columns named CCEX CONNECTED, CCEX TARGETED, and RCA(s)
and two icons are added to the groups table showing CCEX information, as depicted in the
following figure:
•

CONNECTED column.
•

TARGETED column.
• RCAs column shows the percentage of bins for which Coverage Directed Solver can
provide root-cause analysis as UNSAT type.
Click on a specific group name to view the detailed page of the covergroup. The CCEX
PERCENT column is added to show the estimated targeting by Coverage Directed Solver
of coverpoints and crosses. It shows the covered space with denominator being the
number of coverage bins targeted by Coverage Directed Solver.

Generating Reports
Three extra columns namely RANDOMIZE COUNT, SAMPLE(s), and RAND VAR
LOCATION are added to the coverpoint table. The RANDOMIZE COUNT, SAMPLE(s)
show the times of randomization and sample separately. You can click the hyperlink in
RAND VAR LOCATION to open the corresponding source file.
In the bins table, for each bin CCEX provides the following two additional columns:
1. ILLEGAL COUNT: It displays the count of the number of bins found illegal in that
bin row. Note that the illegal decision is based on the tests that are run for Coverage
Directed Solver. For example,
◦ For a non triggered cover point, all bins are marked as illegal.
◦ An unsatisfiable connected bin is marked as illegal.
◦ A non-connected coverpoint is not be marked as illegal.
2. RCA: This column provides more hints about the uncovered point. For a connected
sample, it can provide information on the unsatisfiable constraint. For a cross, it can
provide information on which sample bins are unsatisfiable.
While the illegal bin identification is enabled by default, the root cause analysis (RCA)
requires that the simulation be run with a runtime option as follows:
% simv -vso ccex -ccex_opts rca <runtime options>
For details, see the Root Cause Analysis chapter.
If the RCA capability is enabled in simulation, the URG report provides information on
root cause of a coverage hole, in a best effort manner. This means that it attempts to
be conservative to avoid false-positives in the over-constraint identification. To see RCA
information in the URG report if RCA has been enabled, click the bin name of the RCA

Exclusion Support in CCEX
Exclusion Support in CCEX
Exclusion supports excluding cover item objects from Coverage Directed Solver targeting
at runtime.
For dumping exclusions, use the following command:
urg -dir simv.vdb -ccex -dump full_exclusions ccex_illegal
The new files are dumped in the directory where you are running. These files contain
excluded objects for the group coverage in the commented form. You can copy this file
to a new file, uncomment the objects you want to exclude and pass the new file as an
argument with the Coverage Directed Solver exclusion option -elfile in runtime.
For example,
Dumping the full exclusion file
You can dump the full exclusion file using the following commands:
vcs -sverilog -full64 test.v
./simv
urg -dir simv.vdb -ccex -dump full_exclusions ccex_illegal
This dumps the following files in the directory:
fullexclude.tb_def
fullexclude.tb_inst
Reading the exclusion file
You can read the exclusion file in the following way:
vcs -sverilog -full64 test.v -vso ccex
./simv -vso ccex -ccex_opts elfile=exclusion_file.el
urg -dir simv.vdb -format both -ccex

Exclusion Support in CCEX
Excluding Explorer Inferred Illegal Bins
You can generate the explorer-specific exclusion file containing a list of statically inferred
illegal cover point and cross bins.
For dumping exclusion, use the following command:
urg -dir simv.vdb -dump full_exclusions ccex_illegal -ccex
The new files are dumped in the directory where the above command was run. This file
contains all the illegal uncovered cover point and cross bins inferred from CCEX run.
Dumping the CCEX Exclusion File
You can dump the CCEX exclusion file using the following commands:
vcs -vso ccex <compile_options>
simv -vso ccex -ccex_opts rca <run_options>
urg -dir simv.vdb -dump full_exclusions ccex_illegal -ccex
This dumps the ccexIllegalBin.el and ccexNonSampledBin.el files in the working
directory.
The ccexIllegalBin.el file contains illegal bins and the ccexNonSampledBin.el file
contains unsampled bins. The exclusion files in the ccex mode would be dumped by
default in strict exclude mode (ExclMode). The ExclMode for both ccexIllegalBin.el
and ccexNonSampledBin.el files is set to strict by default.
Applying the Exclusion File With URG
You can apply the exclusion file to see the coverage score without illegal bins, using the
following command:
urg -dir simv.vdb -ccex -elfile ccexIllegalBin.el
You can also apply more than one exclusion file according to their ExclMode, using the
following command:
urg -dir simv.vdb -ccex -elfile ccexIllegalBin.el -elfile
ccexNonSampledBin.el -elfile abc.el
The exclusion file with ExclMode set to strict would be applied in strict mode and
other exclusion files in default mode.
The ExclMode is specified in the exclusion file header as follows:
//================================================== -> Header
// This file contains the Excluded objects
// Generated By User: user1
// Format Version: 2
// Date: Fri Apr 19 11:42:48 2024

Exclusion Support in CCEX
// ExclMode: strict/default/assert -> depicts the exclude mode of el
file
//==================================================

Enabling Bucketization
Enabling Bucketization
Each simulation distributes the cross or coverpoint space into fixed size buckets. The
bucket selection to target happens randomly to achieve the maximum coverage gain in a
regression environment.
Use the following options at runtime to enable the bucketization:
-ccex_opts enable_bucketize_target -ccex_opts seq_id=<id>
Limitations of VSO.ai
The Coverage Directed Solver flow is not supported for the following cases:
• VHDL
• Mixed Language (MX)

text:
Change-Based Verification
Change-Based Verification (CBV) is a key component of the VSO.ai smart stress phase,
leveraging its ability to identify changes in the design and its associated Cone of Influence
(COI). CBV optimizes test selection with the goal of catching all the unique failure
signatures around identified area of code changes.
When global ICO phase configuration is used, the recommended tests for
failure recall are impacted.
Installation and Setup
Separate installation or license is not required to enable CBV flow in VSO.ai.
The following are the minimum VCS version requirements to enable this functionality:
• VCS 2023.12-SP2-9
• VCS 2024.09-SP2-3
• VCS 2025.06
• VCS 2026.03
CBV Workflow
The CBV functionality is seamlessly woven into various stages of the VSO.ai workflow.
After design changes are identified, they are mapped to the coverage targets that exist in
the VSO.ai ML model.
Initialization Stage
To use the CBV flow, it is mandatory to enable the line or tgl portonly metric during
the Day0 run of generating the VSO.ai ML model. This is essential because identified
design changes are mapped back to line or tgl portonly coverage targets, allowing
you to stress coverage around those mapped targets in the VSO.ai stress phase.

CBV Workflow
1. Compile Step:
The CBV flow is tightly integrated with VCS compile. Enabling VSO.ai options is
mandatory during the compile step to allow the CBV flow to identify design changes
during the VSO.ai init step.
$VCS_HOME/bin/vcs \
-vso cso \
-vso_opts buildname=<buildname> \
-vso_opts workdir=<workdir> \
[other VCS options]
If multiple builds are used in the project, ensure that a buildname is
associated with each compile, as the CBV flow identifies design changes on
a per-build basis.
2. Init Step:
In the init step, the CBV flow identifies design changes and applies them to the
VSO.ai ML model. This left-shifts coverage closure for code changes and targets
unique failures around the modified areas during the Smart Stress phase. By default,
VSO.ai enables all the following three phases:
◦ Smart Stress
◦ Acceleration
◦ Exploration
If you need to target only the design changes and exit, you can specify --phase
stress[:<N>]. Where, N is an optional value used to specify the number of times the
identified design changes are to be stressed around coverage. By default the value of N
is 1.
On Day0, there are no design changes; therefore, the init step tags only the design-
level information to the vso_workdir.
You must specify the simv location to tag the design information generated during VCS
compile to vso_workdir.
The simv path can be specified to the init step using the simv_location variable for
each build in the configuration file. Alternatively, the simv path can also be specified
using one of the following options:
◦ simv_paths: Comma-separated paths to all the build simvs being targeted by the
regression run.
◦ simv_path_list: File containing simv paths to all the build simvs to be targeted by
regression run.

CBV Workflow
$VSO_HOME/bin/driver \
--init \
--phase stress[:<N>] \
--dbdir <dbdir> \
--workdir <workdir> \
--regr_config <config_file> \
--simv_paths <path_to_build_simvs> \
[other VSO init options]
Run Stage
During the ask step, VSO.ai intelligently recommends tests that can best exercise the
changes in the design based on its past learnings of coverage and failures of available
tests. The PHASE in the following ask output is marked as stress for such tests.
CSO_RESULT:TEST=<TEST_NAME> BUILD=<BUILD_NAME> RUN_ID=<RUN_ID>
SEED=<SEED_VALUE> SEED_TYPE=<SEED_TYPE> PHASE=stress
The Failure Recording feature in CBV enables the association of failures with
design changes. This helps identify more bugs in modified code areas during
future regressions.
Recording Failures
VSO.ai captures test failures in its database for offline estimation. There are two methods
for recording these failures in the model:
Individually
Performed during the Tell step for a given run using the following command:
$VSO_HOME/bin/driver \
--tell \
--workdir <path_to_workdir>\
[--failed [signature]]
Where:
--failed: Specified if the test run failed.
signature: Optional. A comma-separated list of signatures associated with the test
failure.
The signature can be any user-defined string. VSO.ai uses these signatures to target
unique failure signatures during the Stress phase of subsequent regression runs.
Additionally, this allows VSO.ai to track which signatures have been covered in the current
run, enabling it to prioritize its efforts on remaining uncovered signatures.

CBV Workflow
Batch Mode
In batch mode, use the following command:
$VSO_HOME/bin/driver \
--update_fails <fails.csv> \
--workdir <path_to_workdir>
Where:
• --update_fails: Records all failures specified in the input CSV file.
• CSV Format: Each row is a comma-separated list containing cm_name, buildname,
status (pass/fail) , and failure_signature.
• Optional Fields: The status and signature are optional. If no status is provided, it
defaults to fail.
• Signatures: Failure signatures can be either strings or numbers.
The following is a sample fails.csv file:
1.spi_host_csr_mem_rw_with_rand_reset_8627,bld1,fail,ERR1
1.spe_host_mem_partial_access_19400,bld1,Fail,
2.spi_host_speed_3036,bld1,, 1.spi_host_sw_rest_3196,bld2,,"ERR 2"
If the status and failure signatures for all failing tests are specified during the
Tell step of the Run stage, the --update_fails option is not required.
Finalization Stage
In this stage, the CBV flow generates learnings for the identified changes and associated
failures, merging them into the central dbdir. No additional options are required for CBV-
specific handling during the finalize and merge steps.
Additionally, CBV flow also offers the capability to generate exclusion file for all unchanged
targets identified for current regression run. The generated .el file (exclusion file, typically

text:
V-
specific handling during the finalize and merge steps.
Additionally, CBV flow also offers the capability to generate exclusion file for all unchanged
targets identified for current regression run. The generated .el file (exclusion file, typically
with .el extension) can then be used to create an urgReport for the modified portions of
the design, ensuring only the original changed targets are unexcluded. The .el file can
also be consumed by Verdi for interactive exclusion analysis.
$VSO_HOME/bin/driver \
--dump_exclusions_for_changes
--workdir <workdir> \
--vdbdir <vdb_path> \
--target_metric <metrics> \
--elfile_outdir <outdir> \

Analytics and Reporting
where,
• --dump_exclusions_for_changes is a Boolean option that enables the generation of
an exclusion file for unchanged design targets.
• --vdbdir specifies an input vdb to generate an exclusion file compatible with that vdb.
The vdb can be as follows:
◦ vdb for any single build and test
◦ Merged vdb across all tests of a particular build
◦ Merged vdb across all builds
◦ Merged vdb with different flex_merge options
The VDBs generated with flex_merge modules or using –
merge_across_libs as an input may not contain the complete information
on the changes identified.
• --target_metric: If specified, allows to selectively dump the exclusions for the
required metric.
• If specified, --elfile_outdir defines the output directory for generated .el files. If
not specified, these files are generated within the workdir by default. The resulting file
is named excl_for_changes.el.
Analytics and Reporting
For information related to CBV analytics for Smart Stress phase, refer to Visualization in
VSO.ai chapter in the VSO.ai User Guide.
The CBV flow dumps the detailed change report, change_detail_report.txt, for each
build during the init step. This report includes detailed information about the identified
changed elements in the design. The detailed report is saved under workdir/online/
info/builds/<buildname>/change_detail_report.txt.

Limitations

report:

The CBV flow generates a change_summary.csv file for each build that provides a
summary of all detected changes. This file is generated under workdir/online/info/
builds/<buildname>/change_summary.csv. The following figure shows the example of
the module diff summary report:
Figure 4 Module Diff Summary
Limitations
The following are the limitations of the CBV feature:
• Identification of design changes is supported only for Verilog, SystemVerilog, and
VHDL portions of the RTL.
• CBV support for testbench and VHDL is currently a beta feature, which requires
additional options to be specified during the initialization phase of VSO.ai. For more
information, refer to the VSO.ai Beta Features Guide.

Preface
The Verification Space Optimization (VSO.ai) tool is a comprehensive solution designed
to improve the efficiency of verification regressions. It uses machine learning and artificial
intelligence to optimally manage regression processes to meet the key verification goals,
including finding bugs, securing coverage, and exploring RTL functionality. This manual
describes how to use VSO.ai to simulate your designs and optimize regressions while
achieving these goals.
The preface includes the following sections:
• Customer Support
• Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.
Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and answers to
frequently asked questions about Synopsys tools. The SolvNetPlus site also gives you
access to a wide range of Synopsys online services including software downloads,
documentation, and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
If prompted, enter your user name and password. If you do not have a Synopsys user
name and password, follow the instructions to sign up for an account.
If you need help using the SolvNetPlus site, click REGISTRATION HELP in the top-right
menu bar.
Contacting Customer Support
To contact Customer Support, go to https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary

language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also
includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working
environment, including terms that are embedded in our software and IPs. At the same
time, we are working to ensure that our web content and software applications are usable
to people of varying abilities. You may still find examples of non-inclusive language in our
software or documentation as our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are
currently under review to remove exclusionary language.

Introduction to VSO.ai
VSO.ai is a comprehensive solution designed to increase the efficiency of verification
by leveraging machine learning and artificial intelligence. VSO.ai optimally manages
regression processes to achieve the key verification goals of finding bugs, securing
coverage, and exploring the RTL (Register Transfer Level) functionality.
VSO.ai offers the ability to calibrate compute resource usage. This computation can be
done by aligning regression efforts with the available compute budget and ensuring that
optimizations align with verification goals. The tool adapts to various regression types and
design abstraction levels. It is customizable for various verification project life cycles.
The improvements manifest as the following:
• Enhanced QoR (Quality of Results) with higher verification accuracy and coverage.
• Reduced TTR (Time to Results) owing to accelerated regression cycles and debugging
processes.
• Optimized CoR (Cost of Results) because of minimized compute resource usage and
associated costs.
• Customizable Workflows that adapt to various verification project life cycles and design
abstraction levels.
The improvements can be validated by using Comparative Analytics in compare mode for
a VSO.ai-run regression and a baseline regression that does not use VSO.ai.

Installation and Setup of VSO.ai
VSO.ai is packaged as part of the VCS product installation starting with VCS 2022.06-1.
To obtain the evaluation license and download the instructions for the latest version of
VSO.ai, contact your Synopsys Verification Applications Engineer (AE). To install and set
up VSO.ai, use the following commands:
setenv SNPSLMD_LICENSE_FILE <license file>
setenv VCS_HOME <VCS installation path>
setenv VSO_HOME $VCS_HOME/cso
set path = ($VCS_HOME/bin $VSO_HOME/bin $path)
Note: The CSO_HOME environment variable is changed to VSO_HOME. However, older
versions of VCS still support only CSO_HOME. Therefore, both CSO_HOME and VSO_HOME
environment variables must be set until VCS patch versions after June 30th 2025 are used
everywhere.
setenv CSO_HOME $VCS_HOME/cso
set path = ($VCS_HOME/bin $CSO_HOME/bin $path)

title: Version Y-2026.03-SP1, June 2026
text:
VSO.ai Workflow
The VSO.ai workflow for a regression run is categorized into the following three stages:
• Initialization Stage in the VSO.ai Workflow
• Run Stage in the VSO.ai Workflow
• Finalization Stage in the VSO.ai Workflow
Each stage is further subdivided into multiple steps:
Figure 1 Workflow Stages and Steps
The purpose of the initialization stage is to build a customized VSO.ai model for a new
regression run. Customization options are specified in this stage by using a configuration
(or config) file and passing options to VSO.ai. The configuration file enables you to specify

the default regression composition, which typically is a combination of builds (compiles)
and the tests associated with these builds. This regression composition is described in a
proprietary configuration file, that is, EMC, in the YAML format. For more details on the
configuration file, see Appendix D: Configuration File.
The following are the common terms used in this document:
Table 1 Common Terms Used in the Document
Term Description
buildname A unique compile configuration and binary executable file, that is,
simv.
testname A set of tests that can be uniquely labeled as a test template. Each
test template can be run with one or more different random seeds to
probabilistically cover what this set of tests can cover. Quite often,
the testname is different than what a UVM_TESTNAME or cm_name
would specify. Not labeling tests correctly could result in the loss of
accuracy of a VSO.ai model.
dbdir A common directory used by VSO.ai to merge the learning across
multiple regressions runs. The directory can be shared by multiple
users and projects.
workdir A working directory used by VSO.ai for a single regression run.
When users do not merge all their results into a central dbdir, it is
highly recommended to use a single workdir per project or user.
Doing so enables VSO.ai to maintain learnings for a single user in
the workdir across multiple regression runs.
The Initialization stage comprises the following steps:
• Configure Step
• Compile Step
• Init Step
Configure Step
The configure step is the first step in the Initialization stage of the VSO.ai workflow. This
step is to identify the builds and tests that VSO.ai should target for a regression run. A
configuration file is used to specify the builds to be targeted and within them, newly added
or deleted tests, if any. VSO.ai considers all tests in the configuration file as available for
targeting. The configuration file is mandatory for performing a VSO.ai regression, including
the first learning or Day0 regression. The file must also specify the number of times each
test should be run. This is done using the count option that should match the number of
runs of each test in the non-VSO.ai (default) regression run.

title: Version Y-2026.03-SP1, June 2026
text:
Figure 2 Example of the Configuration File in the VSO.ai Configure Step
The following is an example of a minimalist yaml configuration file:
config_name: ubus
- name: cfg1
- name: cfg2
- name: test_r8_w8_r4_w4
build: cfg1
count: 100
- name: test_2m_4s
build: cfg2
The YAM configuration file follows this hierarchical structure:
Refer to the Appendix D: Configuration File section on how to create this configuration file.
This configuration file is supposed to be a live file that reflects the current
state of the regression. Any changes to the user regression configuration

title: Version Y-2026.03-SP1, June 2026
text:
(builds, tests, counts) should always reflect in this file before the start of each
regression so that VSO.ai can adapt to these changes. The recommended use
model is to use the pre_init option in the init step to automatically generate
the VSO.ai configuration file from the regression configuration file of the user
using a pre-generated script.
Compile Step
VSO.ai is tightly integrated with VCS, both during compile/elaboration and simulation
steps. Enabling the VSO.ai options during the compile step of the Initialization stage
allows VSO.ai to adjust its ML model to account for any changes in the RTL and testbench
code during the init step. You must add the VSO.ai specific options to the command line of
a VCS build participating in a regression as follows:
$VCS_HOME/bin/vcs \
-vso_opts buildname=<BUILD_NAME> \
[other VCS options]
• BUILD_NAME is the unique name identifying the compile configuration.
• Other VCS options can be used to turn on the code and functional coverage dumping
for Day0 or for relearn runs.
Enabling the VSO.ai options at compile time is not expected to have any significant
performance overheads, except in the case of the learn mode, which is expected to
introduce a 5-10% performance impact.
Init Step
After the compiles of all the builds have completed, the init step in the Initialization stage
of the workflow builds a custom VSO.ai model for a regression run accounting for any RTL
and testbench changes using the init command as follows:
--init \
--regr_config <config_file> \
--target_metric <metric_list> \
--simv_paths <path_to_build_simvs> \
[--dump_total_targets]
[--pre_init <pre_init_script script_options>] \
[VSO grid options] \
[other VSO init options]

title: Version Y-2026.03-SP1, June 2026
text:
• --init prepares the workdir for the regression run from the learning stores in the
reference dbdir VSO.ai model directory.
• --dbdir is the reference VSO.ai model directory where the learning across regression
runs is stored. If the current regression run is the first run (also referred to as the Day0
run), either an empty directory dbdir must be created beforehand or the --dbdir
option should not be specified.
The dbdir cannot be ported across release streams, that is dbdir created
using one release cannot be used with another release.
• --workdir specifies the VSO.ai directory to use for this regression run.
• pre_init_script script_options specify the script (shell, python, perl) and its
input options that VSO.ai invokes at the beginning of the init step. Typically, the
input options are the path to the input user configuration file and the path to the output
VSO.ai configuration file used by VSO.ai as part of the regr_config option.
• config_file specifies the configuration file in the VSO.ai format.
• path_to_build_simvs specifies a comma separated list of paths to all the build
simv files targeted in the regression run. This list can also be specified using the --
simv_path_list input file. Additionally, the paths to each of the builds can be specified
in the VSO.ai configuration file. Refer to Appendix D: Configuration File for more
details.
• --dump_total_targets displays the total count of targets for each of the metrics
enabled in the current regression with each tell/update. You can view the progress of
the current regression without generating the URG report or VSO.ai report at frequent
intervals. You can view the total number of targets for each metric in the tell log files.
If test templates or builds are not recommended by the tool, the total target
count is not displayed completely. For group metric, the number of targets
can also change with different simulation runs of the same test template.
As the tool finds the total targets only once for each test template, it cannot
include the unique uncovered bins from other simulation runs of same test
template.
• VSO grid options enable using a grid to speed up the VSO.ai steps. It is highly
recommended to do so if there are multiple builds in the regression and multiple
targeted coverage metrics. Refer to the Grid and Parallel Job Options in the Appendix
A: Options for the list of supported grid options.

Additional Configuration Options
Additional init options can be classified into the following groups:
• Filtering Options
• Targeting Options
Filtering Options
VSO.ai provides the ability to limit the targeting for an individual regression run to specific
builds, tests, coverage metrics, and individual coverage bins by using the combination of a
configuration file and VSO.ai options.
• Builds are filtered using the configuration file. VSO.ai targets only the builds specified in
the configuration file.
• Tests can be filtered using the configuration file by setting max_count: 0 . In addition,
tests can be ignored using the following init command line option:
--ignore_testlist FILENAME
◦ FILENAME is a file containing the list of tests to be ignored. Each test in the file is
specified as testname@@buildname.
• Coverage metrics can be filtered by using the following option:
--target_metric <metric_list>
◦ metric_list is a comma separated list of supported metrics to target from (all,
assert, cond, fsm, group, line, tgl).
For a metric to be targeted by VSO.ai in a regression run, it must be enabled during
the VCS compile step. Also, the ML model for the metric must exist.
Only the metric type can be selected. Selecting the metric type automatically
enables targeting for both def and inst for the metric.
Additionally, VSO.ai targets only those coverage metrics for optimization that are
enabled in the current build and for which it has been able to build a reference ML
model. Any user specified metrics that do not meet this condition are ignored with
a warning during the Targeting phase. If the metric is enabled but has no reference
ML model, VSO.ai collects the data for the metric to build an ML model for the
subsequent regression runs.
Additionally, the fsm metrics can be filtered by using the following options:
--fsm {state, transition}

title: Version Y-2026.03-SP1, June 2026
text:
Toggle metrics can be filtered by using the following option:
--tgl {portsonly, all}
Individual coverage bins can be filtered by using the following options:
• --elfile FILENAME
• --elfilelist FILENAME
• --plan FILENAME
Refer to Filtering Target Bins for more details.
Targeting Options
VSO.ai targeting options are categorized into the following conditions.
• Phase Selection
• Exit Conditions
Phase Selection
VSO.ai operates in the following three distinct phases:
• Smart Stress Phase: for verifying design changes and catching related failures.
• Acceleration Phase: for achieving the expected coverage quickly.
• Intelligent Exploration Phase: for uncovering rare coverage and stimulus scenarios to
find bugs and increase functional and code coverage.
Smart Stress Phase
In the Smart Stress phase, VSO.ai does the following to verify design challenges and
catch failures:
• Prioritizes stress testing on the recent code changes and associated high-risk areas.
This testing reduces the time to detect failures and enables faster identification of
issues and turnaround time.
• Enables the stimulus diversification functionality. There is a focus on bug finding and
ensuring the diversity of random scenarios to increase the chances of potential defects.
• Selects regression tests efficiently. These tests focus on high-risk areas and early
failure detection. This enhances user efficiency and speeds up the verification process.
The risk mitigation achieved is >100% of the Unique Failure (Signature) Count
compared to baseline regression.

• Includes key metrics to confirm the effectiveness of this phase. These metrics comprise
the unique failure count, time to unique failures in regression, and increased event
counts for the recently modified code and associated high risk areas. VSO.ai analytics
shows a left shift in the unique failure detection rate.
The stress count is specified using the following option:
--phase stress[={N, count:N, runs:R, cpu[:C[X]]}]
• count:N: Stops the stress phase after the changes have been statistically covered N
times (This is the recommended method of specifying stress count).
• N: Stops the stress phase after the changes have been statistically covered N times.
• runs:R : Stops the stress phase after R test runs in the stress phase.
• cpu[:C[X]]: Stops the stress phase after the sum of the projected run times of all
the test runs in the stress phase exceeds the estimated total time taken by the default
regression.
◦ If C is used, it stops after the sum of the projected run times of all the test runs in the
stress phase exceeds C hours.
◦ If CX is used, then it stops after the sum of the projected run times of all the test runs
in the stress phase exceeds C times the estimated total time taken by the default
regression.
Acceleration Phase
Coverage efficiency is the coverage achieved per unit of the CPU time. It provides insights
into the speed of coverage accumulation during the accelerated coverage phase. The
coverage targets tracked by VSO.ai are an approximate proxy of the exact coverage
metrics. In this phase, VSO.ai focuses on the following to achieve optimal coverage
quickly:
• Recaptures high levels of coverage rapidly. This is done by optimally selecting tests
that have the highest efficiency in providing the volume coverage.
• Focuses on maximizing the code and functional coverage swiftly to increase
confidence in verification. It optimizes rapid coverage gains with the available compute
budget.
• Includes the rate and absolute level of specified functional and code coverage metrics
as the key metrics.
• Uses detailed URG reports and Verdi coverage views to obtain accurate values.

The acceleration phase is enabled by using the following option:
--phase acceleration[={runs:R, cpu[:C[X]], bin:B[X]}]
• The first two options runs:R and cpu[:C[X]] are described in Smart Stress Phase.
bins:B[X]: When specified the ask returns the test that covers around 'B'x of the
reference bins and then exits from acceleration, for example, 0.9x returns tests that
covers 90% of reference bins.
Intelligent Exploration Phase
In this phase, VSO.ai uncovers rare coverage and stimulus scenarios:
• Targets the seldom-tested areas of the RTL design using diverse test stimuli. It aims to
uncover hard-to-find bugs and ensures higher verification quality by exploring corner
cases and uncommon coverage situations.
• Includes the coverage of new and seldom-tested coverage areas, new failure
signatures and increased coverage, and stimulus diversity metrics in the presence of
constrained random verification as the key metrics. The hit counts of the new coverage
targets hit per unit of CPU time demonstrate the effectiveness of intelligent exploration
in discovering new coverage areas.
• Analyzes the progress in rare coverage targets (through the histogram of deciles
ordered by rarity of coverage event), providing insights into the depth of coverage
achieved during the Intelligent Exploration phase.
The exploration phase is enabled by using the following option:
--phase exploration
By default, VSO.ai enables all three phases, and therefore, yields a more efficient
regression. The phases can be changed by using the following option:
--phase {stress[:N], acceleration, exploration}
One or more phases can be selected by either repeating the --phase option or specifying
a comma separated list of phases. The order of targeting is always fixed: the Stress phase
followed by the Acceleration phase, and finally the Exploration phase. Additionally, if any of
these phases need to be configured with multiple sub options, each of the phases must be
specified using a separate --phase option.
The Stress phase also supports a user configurable parameter N that specifies the
number of times the changes should be stressed. By default, VSO.ai determines an
appropriate value of N that depends on the type of changes and amount of historical data
available.

title: Version Y-2026.03-SP1, June 2026
text:
se also supports a user configurable parameter N that specifies the
number of times the changes should be stressed. By default, VSO.ai determines an
appropriate value of N that depends on the type of changes and amount of historical data
available.

For example, to enable the Stress phase with a count and runs limit, use the following
--phase stress:count:N,runs:R
To enable the Acceleration phase with the percent and run limits, use the following
--phase acceleration:percent:P,runs:R
By default, each regression run targets all three phases. This exercises all the recent RTL
code changes and again targets all the bins that were covered in the previous runs.
To accumulate coverage across multiple regression runs while continuing to stress the
code changes, use the following phase option:
--phase stress,exploration
This option skips the Acceleration phase and focuses on stressing the code changes
instead. This helps to increase the coverage score and uncover hard to find bugs.
VSO.ai must make these phase switching determinations before knowing the
result of all the simulation runs. Therefore, it uses a combination of the following
to make these decisions:
• The result of completed simulations
• A statistical model for the result of the ongoing simulations
Exit Conditions
By default, the exit condition depends on the phases selected. If the Exploration phase is
not selected, VSO.ai stops returning tests after it has achieved its goals of the stress and
accelerated coverage.
VSO.ai stops the Stress phase after it has provided enough tests to cover the goal of
stressing the code changes and catch all unique failure signatures related to the code
changes. This can be controlled by the user by using the stress:N option. Depending on
the code changes, it is possible that the total time taken in the Stress phase can exceed
the total time of the default regression.
The goal of the Acceleration phase is to get to the same number of covered bins as what
the default (non-VSO.ai) regression would be able to probabilistically cover using the latest
RTL and TB code within the budget of a single regression run.
If Exploration is selected as a phase, VSO.ai continues to target rare coverage and
stimulus scenarios to increase coverage and find new bugs after completing the Stress
and accelerated coverage phases. By default, VSO.ai limits the test selections in the
Exploration phase such that the estimated runtime of these tests is within the remaining

regression budget. This is the time remaining after subtracting the estimated time of the
Stress and Acceleration phase from the estimated time of the default regression.
The exit condition can be overridden by using the following option:
{fails:F, runs:R, cpu:C[X], :MX}
fails:F --exit stops returning tests if F test runs have failed.
runs:R returns a maximum of R tests.
cpu[:C[X]] stops returning tests when the projected run times of all tests selected so
far exceeds the total time taken by the default regression. If C is used, it stops after the
projected run times of all tests selected so far exceeds C hours. If CX is used, it stops after
the projected run times of all tests selected so far exceeds C times the total time taken by
the default regression run.
<metric>:MX limits the target for each individual metric to a percentage of the number of
bins in the reference for that metric. For example, line:0.99X would stop targeting line
coverage after it hits 99% of the number of bins in the reference.
VSO.ai relies on the YAML configuration file to determine the constitution of the
default regression run. If the configuration file is not specified during the current
initstep, it relies on the last version that was seen and saved in the dbdir.
VSO.ai uses historical data to determine the average run time for each of the
tests. The actual run times for the tests in the current regression run can vary
depending on multiple factors such as code changes, random seed, machine
configuration and load.
Multiple exit conditions can be specified by either using a comma separated list or
repeating the –-exit option. If multiple conditions are specified, VSO.ai stops as soon as
any one of the conditions is reached.
VSO.ai must make these exit determinations before knowing the result of all the
simulation runs. Therefore, it uses a combination of the following to make these
decisions:
• The result of completed simulations
• A statistical model for the result of the ongoing simulations
This is necessary to ensure that VSO.ai does not end up returning a much
larger number of tests to be run than what is required to reach the specified
goals.

Run Stage in the VSO.ai Workflow
Run Stage in the VSO.ai Workflow
The purpose of the run stage in the VSO.ai workflow is to run the VSO.ai selected tests
and record the results. The run stage comprises the following three steps:
• Ask Step
• Execute Step
• Tell Step
Ask Step
VSO.ai intelligently selects a set of tests by using the ask command in the Run stage of
the VSO.ai workflow. Each selected test run is associated with a unique run_id and some
additional run arguments that VSO.ai returns. The command is as follows:
--ask [{N, all, runs:N, runs:all, cpu[:C[X]]}] \
[--out <filename>] \
[--fmt {csv, json, shell}] \
[--simstats]
• If –-ask N or –-ask runs:N is specified, VSO.ai returns a list of the next N tests that
should be run, with each entry having all the earlier fields.
• If –-ask all or –-ask runs:all is specified, VSO.ai returns a list of all the tests that
should be run to meet the target criteria with each entry having all the earlier fields
from. Note that this is an estimated list and the final coverage might not actually meet
the targeted goal because of constrained random tests and changes to the RTL and
testbench.
Additionally, unless a --exit cpu[:C[X]] or –-exit runs:R option is specified
during the init step. The -–exit fails:F option is ignored with --ask all .
If cpu[:C[X]] is specified, VSO.ai returns a list of tests where the projected run times
of this list of tests is closest to the total time taken by the default regression.
◦ If C is used, VSO.ai returns a list of tests where the projected run times of this list of
tests is closest to C hours.
◦ If CX is used, VSO.ai returns a list of tests where the projected run times of this list
of tests is closest to C times the total time takes by the default regression run.
• --workdir <workdir> specifies the working directory.

Run Stage in the VSO.ai Workflow
• --out FILENAME , if specified, the output is written to FILENAME. If not, the output is
written to the standard out.
• --fmt, if specified, the output format matches the requested format. .csv is the default
format.
The following is the output from the ask step in the CSV format (single line):
CSO_RESULT:TEST=<TEST_NAME> BUILD=<BUILD_NAME> RUN_ID=<RUN_ID>
SEED=<SEED_VALUE> SEED_TYPE=<SEED_TYPE> PHASE=<PHASE_NAME>
PEAK_MEMORY=<PEAK_MEMORY>
◦ TEST_NAME is the name of the test template selected to run, such as testname.
◦ BUILD_NAME is the name of the build selected to run, such as buildname.
◦ RUN_ID is the VSO.ai-specific run_id for this ask to be passed to the simulation job.
◦ SEED_TYPE is a type of the seed value, for example, “failure” or “golden”.
◦ SEED_VALUE is a possible random seed to be used for this test run. If SEED_TYPE is
failure or golden, VSO.ai expects that seed to be used for this run. If it is blank,
you can either use the suggested seed or disregard it and supply your own random
seed.
◦ PHASE_NAME is the name of the VSO.ai phase that this run was selected for, that is
Stress, Acceleration, or Exploration.
◦ PEAK_MEMORY represents the peak projected memory for this test if the –-simstats
option is passed to the ask step.
This is an estimate based on a combination of historical evidence and
accounting for any RTL changes made to the current design. This can be
used to select the appropriate scheduler queue for the job.
• If –-fmt json is specified, the output is a dictionary in the JSON format, with each
tuple from above converted into a key value pair.
If –-fmt shell is specified, the output is of the form <key>=<value> that can be used
in a shell script.
• --simstats, if specified, the output of this step also contains the estimated peak
memory for the test.

Run Stage in the VSO.ai Workflow
VSO.ai relies on the YAML configuration file to determine the constitution of the
default regression run. If the configuration file is not specified during the current
init step, it relies on the last version that was seen and saved in the dbdir.
VSO.ai uses historical data to determine the average run time for each of the
tests. The actual run times for the tests in the current regression run can vary
depending on multiple factors such as code changes, random seed, machine
configuration and load.
Execute Step
In the execute step of the Run stage in the VSO.ai workflow, the user is responsible for
running the simulation job corresponding to the VSO.ai selected build/test by passing it the
VSO.ai suggested parameters. The command is as follows:
<simv> \
-vso_opts workdir=<workdir> \
-vso_opts run_id=<RUN_ID> \
+ntb_random_seed=<SEED_VALUE> \
<other simv options>
• other simv options specifies the simv options required to turn on the code and
functional coverage dumping for Day0 or Relearn runs.
If the returned SEED_TYPE is not failure or golden and you want to discard the VSO.ai
returned SEED_VALUE, the following option can be used to generate a different random
seed for this run instead of the +ntb_random_seed option:
+ntb_random_seed_automatic
Tell Step
When the simulation run has completed, VSO.ai needs to know the result of the simulation
to determine the current state of failures and coverage for the regression run. By default,
VSO.ai includes the coverage from a failing test in its targeting and reporting. If this is not
required, the –-ignore_failed option can be used during the init step. The result of
the simulation run is given to VSO.ai in the Tell step of the Run stage using the following
--tell <RUN_ID> \
[--failed [signature]]

Finalization Stage in the VSO.ai Workflow

• --failed is specified if the test run failed.
• signature is a comma-separated list of signatures the test failed with. The signature
can be any user-defined string and is used by VSO.ai to target all unique failure
signatures during the Stress phase in the subsequent regression runs. It also notifies
VSO.ai that a particular failure signature has been covered in the current regression
run so that it can focus its effort on other failure signatures.

VSO.ai that a particular failure signature has been covered in the current regression
run so that it can focus its effort on other failure signatures.
VSO.ai uses an approximate proxy for coverage. Additionally, VSO.ai reports a
coverage percentage based on the total number of covered bins from the last
regression run that was merged in dbdir. Therefore, the coverage percentages
reported by VSO.ai in the tell output may not match the actual URG coverage
score.
Finalization Stage in the VSO.ai Workflow
The purpose of the finalization stage in the VSO.ai workflow is to notify VSO.ai that the
regression is complete. VSO.ai then proceeds to generate the results of the regression run
and create the learning from this regression run so that it could be merged into the central
dbdir.
The VSO.ai report uses an approximate proxy for coverage. Therefore, the
coverage percentages reported by VSO.ai are not exactly the same as what
URG reports. You should always use URG even for a VSO.ai regression to
determine the exact coverage score.
The Finalization stage comprises the following steps:
• Finalize Step
• Report Step
• Merge Step
Finalize Step
The finalize step of the Finalization stage in the VSO.ai workflow uses the following
command to notify VSO.ai that the regression run has completed:
--finalize \

Finalization Stage in the VSO.ai Workflow
--workdir <workdir>
The finalize step aggregates all the warnings and error messages from each of the log
files into a single file. And any log files (except from the main online.log and tell.log
files) that do not have any errors or warnings are deleted.
The –-analytics option to get an updated status of the regression.
Report Step
The report step in the Finalization stage of the VSO.ai workflow is optional. By default,
the finalize step automatically generates a report for the regression run. Reports can,
however, be used to generate an intermediate report while the regression run is still
ongoing. This can be done by using the following command:
--report \
[--reportdir REPORTDIR]
The report is available in the workdir/report directory by default, unless --reportdir
is used. When --reportdir is specified, the report is available in REPORTDIR. The
generated report is currently a statically generated HTML page that can be opened in a
browser. To view this report, run the following command:
firefox <vso_workdir>/report/index.html
This is scheduled to change in the next release to be a server hosted report.
Merge Step
VSO.ai uses transfer learning to retain the information about the covered coverage targets
and failures to merge them in the next run. Transfer learning is the ability to capture the
knowledge from the previous regressions to enhance results in the future runs.
If a regression run is successful and has meaningful data, it is recommended that the
merge step should be invoked in the Finalization stage of the workflow so that VSO.ai can
leverage the learning from the current regression runs in future regression runs. This is
done by invoking the following command:
--merge \
--dbdir <dbdir > \
[--out <outdir>]

Simplified Use Model of VSO.ai
This step merges the learnings of this regression run from the workdir into the dbdir if
the --out option is not specified.
Figure 3 Merge Step
This figure is a pictorial representation of the different steps.
Configure, Compile and Init are part of the Initialization stage.
Ask, Execute and Tell are part of the Run stage.
And Finalize and Merge are part of the Finalize stage. Ask, Execute, and Tell are in a
loop depending on the number of Ask steps invoked.
dbdir is the reference VSO.ai model directory where the learning across regression runs
is stored. workdir specifies the directory to use for this regression run and is accessed by
every step in the flow, both for reading and writing.
Simplified Use Model of VSO.ai
The VSO.ai Ask-Tell interface has multiple benefits:
• Tell gives VSO.ai an accurate picture of the current state of regression, which VSO.ai
uses to update its ML model online. It allows VSO.ai to leverage reinforcement
learning. VSO.ai can dynamically adapt its test recommendations to achieve the
remaining goals based on what is achieved thus far in a regression.

text:
Simplified Use Model of VSO.ai
However, it is possible to trade-off QoR for ease of use to make it easy to deploy VSO.ai in
the regression environment. VSO.ai supports a three-step flow that involves the following
steps:
1. Configure VSO.ai and compile each build by using the following VCS compile
$VCS_HOME/bin/vcs \
-vso_opts buildname=<buildname> \
[other VCS options]
2. Get a test list of all tests to be run and run each of the suggested tests. This is done by
chaining the init and ask steps using the following command:
--init \
--ask all \
--pre_init “<pre_init_script script_options>” \
--regr_config <config_file> \
--target_metric <metric_list> \
[VSO grid options] \
[other VSO init options] \
[other VSO ask options]
Run all the predicted simulation jobs, passing all the relevant options as described in
the execute step:
<simv> \
-vso_opts workdir=<workdir> \
-vso_opts run_id=<RUN_ID> \
+ntb_random_seed=<SEED_VALUE> \
<other simv options>
3. Finalize the result after the regression has completed. This is done by chaining the
finalize and merge steps and providing the failures in bulk by using the following
--finalize \
--merge \
[--update_fails <csv file> ]
--update_fails records all the failures in the <csv file> in bulk.

Wrapper Interface in VSO.ai
Refer to Recording Failures for more information.
Wrapper Interface in VSO.ai
In the Run Stage, the three steps in the workflow, that is, ask, execute, and tell through
the Ask-Tell interface provide maximum flexibility and controllability. However, it does
require additional efforts to integrate with the existing regression environments. VSO.ai
provides a Wrapper Use Model to simplify the integration of VSO.ai for simple regression
environments. In this case, VSO.ai performs all the steps of the regression, including the
execute phase where it launches the simulation jobs on the grid. The Wrapper Use Model
has limitations as VSO.ai is the one initiating the simulation. For example, it is possible
that a configuration or test chosen by VSO.ai requires prerequisites to be established
before running. Therefore, it is primarily recommended for proof-of-concept trials. The
advantage is its ease of integration with the existing regression scripts.
Using the Wrapper Use Model requires the test execution options to be added to the
VSO.ai configuration file using the arguments keyword. For a single build, if the execution
options for all tests of the single build are the same, the execution command line can be
specified as an argument to --online. The arguments line in the configuration file is not
required. In this case, the --online option should be the last option passed to the driver
command since VSO.ai considers all options after --online to be the simv execution
command.
config_name: ubus

- name: cfg1
simv_location: "/path/to/cfg1/simv"
comp_vdb_path: "/path/to/cfg1/compile vdb"

- name: cfg2
simv_location: "/path/to/cfg2/simv"
comp_vdb_path: "/path/to/cfg2/compile vdb"

- name: test_r8_w8_r4_w4
build: cfg1
count: 100
arguments: -vso cso -lca -vso_opts testname=test_r8_w8_r4_w4 -cm_name
test_r8_w8_r4_w4_$${EMAN_RANDOM} +UVM_TESTNAME=test_r8_w8_r4_w4
+ntb_random_seed=$${EMAN_RANDOM} ${common_opts}

- name: test_2m_4s
build: cfg2
count: 100
arguments: -vso cso -lca -vso_opts testname=test_2m_4s
-cm_name test_2m_4s _$${EMAN_RANDOM} +UVM_TESTNAME=test_2m_4s
+ntb_random_seed=$${EMAN_RANDOM} ${common_opts}

Wrapper Interface in VSO.ai
For more information on how to create configuration file with the complete
information for the Wrapper interface instead of the Ask-Tell interface, refer to
Appendix D: Configuration File.
The command to enable the Wrapper User Model is as follows:
--regr_config <config_file> \
--target_metric <metric_list> \
[VSO grid options] \
[other VSO options] \
--online <path_to_build_simv> <simv options>

Visualization in VSO.ai
The purpose of dashboards in VSO.ai is to visualize, analyze, and track the key metrics
related to software testing and coverage. The Analytics Dashboard provides insights
into coverage metrics, progress tracking, and trend analysis across the three regression
phases of VSO.ai.
Use Model to Access the Analytics Dashboard
After the init step is completed, users can access the analytics dashboard in VSO.ai by
using the following command:
$driver --analytics --workdir <vso workdir> --port <port>
The driver --analytics command starts a server in the specified port (8001 by default)
enabling users to view the analytics dashboard in a web browser such as, Firefox.
The same use model applies to the compare flow as well.
The following sections describe the various regression phases, the available dashboards
in VSO.ai, and the data these dashboards provide across the various phases of
regression:
Regression Phases in VSO.ai
As we learned in prior sections that VSO.ai enables Smart Stress, Accelerated Coverage,
and Intelligent Exploration phases under the same compute budget as the default
regression, thus yielding a more efficient regression. Various metrics are available to
measure the effectiveness of a VSO.ai regression. An example of a metric for gauging
cost-effectiveness is the cumulative CPU time used to fulfill or surpass the stress,
failure, and coverage metrics of the default regression. The Analytics view provides a
dashboard with a high-level set of comparative metrics is provided to support the claim
of more efficient regressions within the provided compute budget. It helps to measure the
effectiveness of each phase and provides comparisons with the default user regression
(if enabled in compare mode) to build trust in the system. Through these metrics, VSO.ai
aims to provide a comprehensive view of regression effectiveness in comparison with an
unoptimized regression. This comparison allows users to make informed decisions about

title: Version Y-2026.03-SP1, June 2026
text:
their verification processes. Raw data is also made available to users to build customized
dashboards.
The high-level metrics are approximations and detailed drill down of coverage
and RTL change information are available in Verdi or URG reports for more
granular insights.
The Analytics dashboard can be invoked at any point after the init step. You have on-
demand access to the live views of analytics. These views enable you to monitor and
analyze the VSO.ai runs during execution, without having to wait for completion.
The following is the summary dashboard for a VSO.ai regression run:
Figure 4 Summary Dashboard for VSO.ai vs Default Regression
Key Terms in the VSO Analytics Dashboard
VSO: All data shown for VSO represents an optimized regression run.

DEF: Represents the default regression run. All data shown for DEF is statistically
estimated unless the compare mode is enabled. In that case, it reflects the actual default
regression metrics.
UI Elements for Coverage Metrics
Figure 5 UI Elements for Coverage Metrics
The following are the UI elements for coverage metrics:
• Instance and Definition selectors show the types of coverage metrics available.
• Code Coverage: Line, Toggle, and FSM coverage. These are enabled only if the
metrics are available in the regression.
• Assertion Coverage: Only enabled if the assertion coverage is available and turned on
in the regression.
• Group Coverage: Enabled if the functional coverage is available.
Graph Controls
• Zoom: Functionality to increase or decrease the viewing scale of the graph for detailed
analysis.
• Reset: Button to revert any user-added changes to the default graph settings.
• Refresh: Button provided on each page shows the current status of the working
directory at that point in time.
Compare Mode – Default vs VSO.ai
The OPT and DEF buttons enable you to compare the standard metrics from the default
regression with optimized metrics generated by VSO.ai. The compare flow must be
enabled for an accurate calculation of the default metrics. Alternatively, a statistical
estimate of regression is shown instead if not in compare mode, providing an approximate
reference.
When activated, this mode overlays the VSO-optimized metrics onto the existing metrics.
This provides a comparison between traditional metrics and AI-enhanced insights.
Opt and Def Buttons

• Default Metrics: Default regression metrics
• VSO Metrics: VSO regression metrics
Progress Chart
The Progress Chart is a line chart that displays the progress over time based on the
various coverage metrics. The metric selector changes the coverage metric displayed.
Figure 6 Total coverage and failure progression

• Tabs:
◦ Zoom and reset options are available for this graph.
◦ The Details button shows the chart data in tabular format for easier analysis.
Figure 7 Tabular View of the Progress Chart

• Columns:
◦ X-Axis: Represents the CPU time or the number of runs selected by the toggle
button.
◦ Y-Axis: Represents the coverage percentage (only approximate to URG coverage)
(0% - 100%), for example, "80%".
• Lines:
◦ VSO: Represents progress in the VSO run.
◦ DEF: Represents the estimated progress (actual progress if in compare mode) for
the default run.
◦
Markers on lines: Represent the failure status of the run and shows the number of
failure signatures for the corresponding run.
By default, up to 100 points are plotted on the line. These are adjustable
through --max_markers to ensure a balanced representation without
excessive computation in the estimated flow. For example, if there are 1000
runs, the progress data is generated for every 10th run. A higher marker
count can affect the dashboard generation time as the progress plot must be
computed for each additional marker.

The VSO.ai Analytics dashboard provides a tabular representation of the current metrics.
It compares the VSO and default values. It also shows a gain if the compare mode flow is

Covered CBV Targets

The cards in the dashboard are grouped based on their respective categories—Smart

The Smart Stress cards shows failure detection in the stress phase, It displays the

VSO.ai Diagnostics and Advanced Views
The diagnostic capabilities of the VSO.ai Analytics dashboard provide visibility into the
VSO runs, test optimization, coverage tracking, and failure analysis.
In the following sections, this custom document describes the advanced views and
provides the steps to access them:
• Accessing Diagnostics and Advanced Views
• Bin Distributions and Patterns
• Tests Summary and Distribution
• Failure Signatures and Patterns
• Test Runs and Execution Details

To access Diagnostics & Advanced Views, click the Diags button on the navigation bar.

• Prob Distribution

Prob Distribution
The Prob Distribution view is an interactive histogram visualization of probability
distribution. It shows the probability distribution of bins by deciles.
Select a coverage metric to view its probability distribution. You can choose metrics for
group, line, toggle, assertion, or FSM coverage.

Refer to the following screenshot for an example that shows probability distribution for

Figure 16 Probability Distribution Histogram - group.def

The Unhit Bins view provides a summary of unhit bins for each coverage metric. You can

Refer to the following example:

coverage metric.

The details include the following:

Offline Estimation in VSO.ai
VSO.ai provides the capability to generate a very rough estimate of the expected
VSO.ai gains without having to integrate the VSO.ai steps into the existing regression
environment. Gain estimates are not provided for all VSO.ai value points currently.
Generating an offline estimate with a VDB generated from default regressions
requires a special license that can be obtained by contacting Synopsys
Verification Application Engineers.
Generating an offline estimate requires a complete set of test vdbs from a full regression
run. The following steps are involved in generating the offline estimate.
• Mapping a Test vdb to a Build Name and Test Name
• Building a VSO.ai Model
• Recording Failures
• Estimating Gain
Mapping a Test vdb to a Build Name and Test Name
During the extraction of data from a VDB during the offline estimation step, VSO.ai extracts
all available test paths based on -cm_name and -cm_dir. These paths are extracted
from the VDB directory name or VDB directories list provided using the --vdbdir or --
vdbdirlist option. For example, test paths identified for an example VDB (simv.vdb) are
as follows:
HOST_BASELINE_RH1x1/ts_rnd_tp9_9896
HOST_BASELINE_RH1x2/ts_rnd_tp9_1175
HOST_BASELINE_RH1x2/ts_rnd_tp8_1175
HOST_BASELINE_RH2x1/ts_rnd_tp8_1078
HOST_BASELINE_RH2x1/ts_rnd_tp7_1078
HOST_BASELINE_RH2x2/ts_rnd_tp6_1296
HOST_BASELINE_RH2x2/ts_rnd_tp6_2036
Determining a Build Name
Using --build_regex 'BASELINE_(.*)\/ts' , VSO.ai identifies 4 unique builds, RH1x1,
RH1x2, RH2x1, and RH2x2.

Chapter 5: Offline Estimation in VSO.ai
Building a VSO.ai Model
Determining the Test Template Name
A regular expression containing a group can be provided to VSO.ai using the --
cmname_regex<regex> option. This regular expression is used to match and identify the
test template substring from the cm_name and cm_dir string. Using --cmname_regex
'(ts.*?)_\d+', VSO.ai identifies 4 unique test templates, ts_rnd_tp6,ts_rnd_tp7,
ts_rnd_tp8, and ts_rnd_tp9. --cmname_regex is a regular expression that can be used
to extract the test template name from a test vdb. Alternatively, the --namemap_file
option can be used.
The --namemap file is a tab-separated file, which can either be written by you or
automatically generated using the --test_regex option of VSO.ai to assist in verifying
or adding specific mappings. When the --test_regex option is used, the namemap file is
created in <vso_workdir>/csv/tests_namemap.csv with the following rules:
• All unmatched tests precede the matched tests.
• For all unmatched tests, the test name and build name is NONE. You must review
these and ensure that they are properly filled.
You can use the --test_regex option independently or along with the existing --
cmname_regex/--build_regex option. The mappings specified in the namemap file take
precedence over the mappings derived from the command line --cmname_regex/--
build_regex options.
Building a VSO.ai Model
This stage builds a VSO.ai ML model for offline estimation by using all the test vdbs from
a complete regression run. In addition, VSO.ai needs to be able to map each test vdb to a
corresponding buildname and testname.
To build a model, run the following command:
--vdb2hm \
--vdbdir <path_to_vdb> \
--build_regex <build_regex> \
--cmname_regex <test_regex> \
[grid options] \
[other options]
• --vdb2hm builds the VSO.ai model.
• --vdbdir <input_path_to_vdb> is the path to an input VDB directory. If there are
more than one VDBs, specify the list of VDBs in a text file and pass the file using the
–-vdbdirlist <path_to_file_listing_VDBs> option.

title: Version Y-2026.03-SP1, June 2026
text:
Chapter 5: Offline Estimation in VSO.ai
Recording Failures
• --workdir<workdir> creates the VSO.ai database under <workdir>.
• --build_regex is a regular expression that can be used to extract the build name
from a test vdb. This is not required if there is a single build. Alternatively, the --
namemap_file option can be used.
• --cmname_regex is a regular expression that can be used to extract the test template
name from a test vdb. Alternatively, the --namemap_file option can be used.
• grid_options is a step that is recommended to be run on the grid using the VSO.ai
grid options if there are a large number of test vdbs.
Recording Failures
VSO.ai records the information regarding failing tests (failures) to its database as part
of offline estimation. The test information can be updated in bulk by using the following
--update_fails <csv file> [—update_fails_fmt {cm_name, run_id, batch}] \
--workdir <workdir>
• --update_fails: records all failures specified in <csv file> .
The format of the input CSV file varies based on the --update_fails_fmt option:
◦ cm_name: cm_name, build, PASS/FAIL, signature
◦ run_id: run_id, build, PASS/FAIL, signature
◦ batch: testname, build, nfails, nruns
For the cm_name and run_id formats, the status and signature fields are optional. If
no status is specified, it defaults to fail. The failure signatures are either strings or
numbers.
The following is a sample CSV file using the cm_name format:
1.spi_host_csr_mem_rw_with_rand_reset_8627,bld1,fail,ERR1
1.spe_host_mem_partial_access_19400,bld1,Fail,
2.spi_host_speed_3036,bld1,, 1.spi_host_sw_rest_3196,bld2,,"ERR 2"
• cm_name: is default for coverage-enabled flow (ensuring backward compatibility).
• run_id: is used to update failures in a coverage-enabled flow when the appropriate
option is specified.

Chapter 5: Offline Estimation in VSO.ai
Estimating Gain
It is recommended to use run_id as the fmt for both coverage and no
coverage flow going forward.
• batch: This option replaces the deprecated —update_fails_batch option.
The --update_fails option is not required if the status and failure signatures
for all failing tests are provided during the tell step in the Run stage.
Estimating Gain
VSO.ai estimates the number of runs required on an average to get the same coverage
as the original regression by using the --train option on the model built in the Building
a VSO.ai Model stage. This estimate is not guaranteed but gives an idea of the average
number of test runs needed in a subsequent regression.
To get the estimates of the required runs, execute the following command:
--train \
[other options]
The estimation results are available on stdout as well as in the following VSO.ai work
directory:
<vso_workdir>/train/train.log.

Filtering Target Bins in VSO.ai
VSO.ai supports two mechanisms for filtering the target bins:
• Filtering With Exclusion
• Filtering With HVP
Exclusion is used to specify a hierarchy of bins to be excluded while an Hierarchical
Verification Plan (HVP) plan is used to specify a hierarchy of bins to be included (while the
rest is excluded).
For more details on URG, see the URG section in the VCS User Guide.
Traditionally, the exclusion and HVP plan files can only be applied after the
regression has completed and all the coverage results are available. This is
because functional coverage is of a dynamic nature and the set of all functional
coverage bins cannot be determined until all the runs have been completed.
Therefore, when they are used for filtering in VSO.ai, the target numbers
reported by VSO.ai initially are not going to fully account for all possible
exclusions specified by the exclusion file or HVP plan.
Filtering With Exclusion
The following command can be used to generate an exclusion file from a merged vdb:
urg-dir simv.vdb -dump full_exclusions
The new files are dumped in the directory where you are running. These files contain
excluded objects for the coverage metrics in the commented form. You can copy this file to
a new file, uncomment the objects you want to exclude, and pass the new file to the init
step using the following option:
--elfile <exclusion_file>
Additionally, if multiple exclusion files are to be used, the following option can be passed to
the init step instead of the --elfile option:
--elfilelist <exclusion_file_list>

Chapter 6: Filtering Target Bins in VSO.ai
Filtering With HVP
exclusion_file_list: is the file containing a list of exclusion file paths, one per line.
• In addition to providing the exclusion file option, you must specify the path for all the
build simv files either by specifying the simv_location in the configuration file or by
using -–simv_paths/--simv_path_list command line option. Alternately, you can
also specify comp_vdb_path in the configuration file to specify the compile VDB path
for each of the builds.
• The -–simv_paths/--simv_path_list option or comp_vdb_path field is not required
if only functional coverage is being used and required if any code coverage metric is
being used as part of the targeted metrics.
The above two methods apply for both --elfile/--elfilelist and --plan options.
For more information, refer to section Appendix D: Configuration File.
Filtering With HVP
Bin filtering can also be done using an HVP plan. VSO.ai supports both a plan file and a
server based HVP plan. As in exclusions, you need to specify the paths for all the build
simv files if any code coverage metric is being used.
The HVP plan file can be specified at the init step using the following option:
--plan <hvp_plan_file>
Additionally, the server plan can be specified using the following options:
--hvp_server <HVP_SERVER> \
--hvp_proj <HVP_PROJ> \
--plan <PLAN_NAME>
--mod <MODIFIER_FILE>

When comparing the count from the online report with the score from a URG report, the
following considerations should be noted:
• Scores matches for assert and FSM.
• For Tgl, scores matches when URG report is generated with -portsonly.
• Line and Group numbers differs.

Line coverage (line/block coverage) in VCS measures: Whether each executable line
or statement block in the RTL/code is executed at least once during simulation.
A block is essentially:
◦ A group of statements treated as one execution unit
◦ Typically corresponds to:
▪ begin end
▪ procedural blocks (always, initial)
▪ single-line statements
For example,
always @(posedge clk) begin
if (en) begin
y <= a + b;
end
end
Coverage breakdown:
◦ always block → 1 block
◦ if (en) condition → condition coverage (separate metric)
◦ y <= a + b; → a line/block to be executed
