Preface
The Siloti Replay Simulation User Guide provides detailed description of every command
and option of Siloti Replay Simulation.

Audience
The audience for this manual includes engineers who are familiar with languages and
tools used in design and verification.
They are frequently required to complete Engineering Change Orders (ECOs) on gatelevel netlists.
This document assumes that you have a basic knowledge of the platform on which your
version of the Verdi platform runs: UNIX or Linux.
It also assumes that you are knowledgeable in Verilog or VHDL, simulation software, and
digital logic design.

Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and FAQs about
Synopsys tools.
It also provides access to online services such as software downloads, documentation,
and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
If prompted, enter your user name and password.
If you do not have a Synopsys user name and password, follow the instructions to sign up
for an account.
If you need help using the SolvNetPlus site, click REGISTRATION HELP in the top-right
menu bar.

Contacting Customer Support
To contact Customer Support, go to https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com.

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed.
We are reviewing and removing exclusionary language from our products and supporting
customer-facing collateral.
Our effort also includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering
and working environment. This includes terms embedded in our software and IPs.
At the same time, we are working to ensure that our web content and software
applications are usable to people of varying abilities.
You might still find examples of non-inclusive language in our software or documentation.
Our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are currently under review to
remove exclusionary language.

Introduction
In this chapter:
* Overview
* Verdi Power Analysis Acceleration Overview

Overview
Siloti Replay Simulation is a technology that allows you to use simulation results from
other abstractions as the input data to the rerun full or partial simulation. Siloti Replay
Simulation allows you to select the time range or scopes as the target and use the input
from other simulation runs to feed into the simulator and generates simulation results of
the current target scope or time range.

Verdi Power Analysis Acceleration Overview
Verdi Power Analysis Acceleration uses Siloti Correlation and Siloti Replay Simulation
technologies to help user run the gate level simulation and dump necessary signals
waveform for power analysis tools to calculate the power consumption.
To obtain the most accurate power analysis results, you must generally use the later
design stage of simulation result as the switching activity data for the power analysis.
However, due to the runtime of gate level simulation that takes long time, users face the
challenges to obtain the gate level simulation for the power analysis. With Siloti Correlation
technology, users can use the RTL simulation result to correlate to the gate level design.
Siloti Replay Simulation takes the input from the RTL simulation and run the gate level
simulation to obtain the gate level simulation result for the power analysis.
You can also refer to the PowerReplay User Guide. The PowerReplay product allows early
and accurate power estimation and also leverages multiple technologies including Siloti
Replay.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Generate Target FSDB From Source FSDB With
Replay Simulation
The Verdi Automated Debug Platform provides a methodology that automatically
generates the target waveform from the original environment.
The target scope can be either RTL or gate-level design.
The most frequent application is generating a gate-level waveform for a chip design from
the RTL design environment.
You do not need to bring up the gate-level environment.
The waveform generation methodology also reduces the effort to perform gate-level power
analysis from weeks to hours.
It uses established EDA technology and power analysis flow.
This major reduction in effort and increase in productivity enables earlier power analysis in
the design flow.
Earlier analysis is not practically possible using traditional gate-level analysis.
Moreover, the methodology produces waveforms identical or nearly identical to those from
gate-level simulation.
Consequently, the design can be analyzed and optimized iteratively throughout the postsynthesis design flow.
This enables much earlier detection and easier resolution of power issues.
The Replay methodology provides the following features:
* Generates accurate gate-level waveforms automatically.
* Enables you to correlate and analyze results in the RTL environment without bringing
up the entire gate-level environment.
* Eliminates the necessity to simulate from time zero for every power analysis run.
* Imposes no changes on the established power analysis methodology and tool flow.
The methodology employs the main tool feature "replay simulation".

It reruns gate-level simulation with RTL simulation waveforms as input stimuli.
It can also rerun RTL simulation with gate-level simulation waveforms as input stimuli.
Replay simulation provides a direct mapping flow to map signals from RTL to gate-level
and vice versa.
For power analysis, this technology maps RTL signal waveforms to gate-level signals to
drive simulation again.
Supported Platforms and Simulator
The supported platforms are LINUX32/64 and SUSE32/64. The supported simulators are
Synopsys VCS and Cadence IUS.
This chapter also covers the following topics:
* Direct-Mapping Flow
* Practice
* Known Problems and Limitations

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
In a complex SOC design, replay simulation enables you to obtain gate-level or RTL
simulation results of a specific block, say ASIC 1 block in the figure below. The following
sections explain how to use replay simulation through the wisim utility to focus on direct
mapping to the ASIC 1 block.

Figure 1

SoC Design

The wisim utility provides a simple way to simulate a target design, either RTL or gatelevel design, using a source FSDB file. The wisim utility maps the signals from the RTL
to the gate-level design or from the gate-level design to the RTL where the mapping file
contains both flip-flop mapping and input mapping. Then, the wisim utility automatically
generates stimuli that can be given as input to the target design simulation. This means
you can use the RTL testbench to directly generate a gate-level FSDB file without
modifying the testbench by the correlation flow.
The following figure shows the complete replay simulation. Consider that you already
have the gate-level design and an FSDB file for the RTL design. You might generate a
new FSDB file that shows the gate-level waveform and a SAIF file to estimate the power
consumption for the ASIC 1 block. The gate-level design and RTL-FSDB files can be used
with the wisim utility to generate the new testbench for the specified scope. Then, the
simulator is invoked to run this partial simulation to generate the on-demand FSDB file and
SAIF file.

Figure 2

Replay Simulation Correlation Flow

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Usage
To start running the wisim utility, you must prepare the input and output files.
Figure 3

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text: Input and Output Files of Direct Mapping for Replay Simulation Correlation

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Required Data
As shown in the figure, the required data for the direct mapping flow includes the following:
* Design Files: Design files that are imported to the Replay Simulation.
Note:
It is recommended to replace the symbol library with a simulation model.
* Source FSDB File: Contains signal values required by the source signals in the
mapping file.
* Mapping File: Contains the signal list of target signals mapped to the source signals
(See the Text Mapping File section for text mapping file details).
* Configuration File: Contains the specifications of the target scope, time range, units,
and scripts (See the Configuration File section for details).
* SDF file: The Standard Delay Format (SDF) file stores the timing data that includes the
delay information. This file is optional for the direct mapping flow.
Note:
The wisim utility forces all target signals in the mapping file if their mapped
source signals are found in the source FSDB file. The wisim utility
generates value changes in order according to the input source FSDB file
that contains the event sequence information when two mapping signals
have value changes at the same time.

Normal Flow
The direct mapping flow of replay simulation includes three phases: extraction,
compilation, and simulation. Each phase has a corresponding option to be executed with
the wisim utility.

Phase 1: Extraction
This phase extracts the design and generates the new testbench using the
-replay_extract option on the wisim command line. Also, to import a file to set the
configurations, use the -config option as follows:
%> wisim -top "work.system" -config config_file -replay_extract

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
For more details on the -config option, see the Configuration File section.
By default, all files generated by the wisim utility are collected in whatIf/ directory. You
can modify the directory name by using the -target <target_dir_name> option for the
wisim utility.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Optionally, you can use the -saif option in the extraction phase to enable the SAIF file
dumping in the simulation phase. The wi.saif file in the replay simulation directory is
generated after completing the flow. Currently, only the VCS simulator is supported to
generate the SAIF file. For example:
%> wisim -top "work.system" -config config_file -replay_extract -saif

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
In addition, you can set the WISIM_DUMP_MAP environment variable to 1 before the
extraction phase to dump the wi_dump_map.txt file of the parsed mapping table. You can
check the mapping results after executing the wisim utility.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Phase 2: Compilation
This phase compiles the extracted design and testbench using the -replay_compile and
-config options specified on the wisim command line. The syntax is:
%> wisim -config config_file -replay_compile

Phase 3: Simulation
This phase runs the simulation using the -replay_sim and -config options specified on
the wisim command line. The syntax is:
%> wisim -config config_file -replay_sim

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
To convert all mapping signals containing unknown values to `0' or `1' set the constant
value -x_to_const option with value `0' or `1' in the simulation phase and then pass
the value to the target design. For example, to convert the unknown value to 0 using the
following command:
%> wisim -config config_file -replay_sim -x_to_const 0

The wisim utility also provides the following dumping option settings in the simulation
phase for users to customize the simulation without recompiling:
* +WI_NO_DUMP: Disables FSDB file dumping during the whole simulation.
* +WI_NO_SDF:Does not perform SDF annotation.
* +WI_NO_SAIF: Does not generate the SAIF file.
* +WI_DUMP_VCD: Enables the VCD file dumping.

Sanity Check
You can perform sanity check before extraction phase to measure the quality of input files
in advance. For example:
%>wisim -top "work.system" -config config_file -sanity_check

The main function of sanity check is to validate the accuracy of the mapping file. The
following is the checklist for sanity check:
1. All left side signals in the mapping file should be in the imported design.
2. All right-hand-side signals in the mapping file should be in the FSDB.
3. All boundary input/in out signals for the target scope must be in the mapping file.
(By default, the checked scope is the target scope in configuration file. If you want to
change the checked scope, use set Boundary_Check_Scope = NewScopeName in the
configuration).
4. The compilation/simulation script conforms to the requirement of Replay Simulation
(This is not turned on by default. You need to add the following line to configuration file
set Checking_Rule= +script to turn it on).
After sanity check, the output log is collected in whatIf.check/, which contains the
following files:
* wi_check.log: Specifies the log file for sanity check.
* wi_newmap.txt: If there are any incorrect signal pairs in the mapping file, they are
collected in the file.
* wi_unmap.log: If there are any dropped signal pairs during sanity check, they are
collected in this file.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Remap Flow
The direct mapping flow also provides an efficient method to apply remapping
requirements.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
When updates exist in the mapping file and no updates exist in the design files or the
FSDB file, you might run the original correlation flow again from the extraction phase to
the simulation phase. The wisim utility provides an alternate and simple way to remap
the mapping file without spending time to extract the extracted design and generate the
generated testbench again.
Note:
The normal direct mapping flow needs to be executed at least once to extract
the target design and generate the testbench for the first time.
To notify replay simulation analysis for using the remap flow that does not extract the
design again and execute the simulation phase, use the -remap option in the extraction
phase. For example:
%> wisim -top "work.system" -config config_file -replay_extract
-remap
%> wisim -config config_file -replay_sim

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Configuration File
The configuration file format for the direct mapping flow is shown in the following example:
set
set
set
set
set
set
set

FSDB = ./rtl.fsdb
Scope = system.i_cpu.i_ALUB
Map = ./map.file
Begin_Time = 1000
End_Time = 3000
Time_Unit = ns
Simulation_Compile_Script = ./ius_wi_compile.rc

set
set
set
set
set
set

Simulation_Run_Script = ./ius_wi_run.rc
delay = ./delay.map
SDF = "../Design/CPU_max.sdf" "system.i_cpu"
Design = ./system_load.command
Exclude_Module_File = ./exc_mod.txt
FSDB_HIER_MAP = RTL_Hierarchy_in_Mapping_file

RTL_Hierarchy_in_FSDB

The required inputs are highlighted in red and the optional inputs are highlighted in
green. The following table shows the configurations for the direct mapping flow of replay
simulation:
Configuration

Description and Example for the Configuration

FSDB

The dumped FSDB file of the source design. Example:
set FSDB = ./rtl.fsdb

Scope

The target scope of the entire design hierarchy. Example:
set Scope = system.i_cpu.i_ALUB

Map

List the target signals and map to source signals (see the Text
Mapping File section for details).
set Map = ./map.file

Begin_Time

The begin time for replay simulation.
NOTE:
If the begin time is not specified, the minimum time of the input
FSDB file is used as the begin time automatically. Example:
set Begin_Time = 1000

End_Time

The end time for replay simulation. NOTE: If the end time is not
specified, the maximum time of the input FSDB file is used as
the end time automatically.
set End_Time = 3000

Time_Unit

The time unit for Begin_Time and End_time. NOTE: If either
the begin time or the end time is specified, the time unit must
be specified in the replay simulation configuration file.
set Time_Unit = ns

Simulation_Compile_Script The simulator compilation script (see the Simulation Compile
Script Examples section for an example).
set Simulation_Compile_Script = ./vcs_wi_compile.rc

Simulation_Run_Script

The simulator simulation script (see the Simulation Run Script
Examples section for an example).
set Simulation_Run_Script = vcs_wi_sim.rc

delay

Optional. The configuration specifies the extra delay time for
the mapping signals as needed. The parsed mapping table
contains delay as well. The format is:
<full path of target signal> #<delay value>

The delay value following the "#" operator can be a positive or
a negative integer. Following is an example for the delay file:
top.clk #-10
top.rst #10

By default, the time unit in the delay file is identical to the time
unit of the input FSDB. If you want to use different time unit in
the delay file, they can specify it in the first line of the delay file
as follows:
// time_unit <s|ms|us|ns|ps|fs>

Following is an example of the delay file with the time unit:
// time_unit ns
top.clk #-0.01
top.rst #0.01

NOTE: Even if a delay file has its own time unit, the delay value
is finally converted to an integer according to the time unit of
the input FSDB.
The configuration is only used for replay simulation.
set delay = ./delay.map

SDF

Optional. The SDF file is annotated when running the
simulation if this data is specified. The format is as follows:
set SDF = "<SDF_file_path>"
"<corresponding_instance>" "" "<SDF_log_file>"
"<mtm_spec>"

Even if the SDF file is included in the original testbench, it is not
extracted by the wisim utility automatically. You have to specify
the SDF file in the configuration file manually. The default MTM
for the SDF file is typical. It needs to be specified if the MTM of
SDF file is not typical. Multiple SDF files can be specified in the
configuration file.
set SDF = "../Design/CPU_max.sdf" "system.i_cpu" ""
"SDF_log1.txt" "MAXIMUM" ""
set SDF = "./CPU_max2.sdf" "system.i_cpu_02" "" ""
"MINIMUM"

Design

Optional. The configuration loads the target design with the Tcl
command file. Alternatively, specify design importing options on
the wisim command line. For example,
%> wisim -sv -f run.f -config config_file
-replay_extract

set Design = ./system_load.command

Exclude_Module_File

Optional. The configuration specifies a list of module names to
exclude into a file. During the extraction phase, those modules
are empty modules with module ports and signals only. If
the specified modules are not found, a warning message is
displayed. If a top module is specified in the file list of excluded
modules, the top module is not excluded. The following is an
example for the file of excluded modules:
MODULE1
MODULE2
MODULE3
NOTE: The signals of the excluded modules should not be
mapped in the mapping file.
set Exclude_Module_File = ./exc_mod.txt

FSDB_HIER_MAP

Optional. Use this configuration option, if the mapping file's
RHS hierarchy is different from RTL FSDB.
set FSDB_HIER_MAP = dut.usub.my_register
tb.udut.usub.my_register

In the current mapping flow, you must set the scope (in the "set Scope" configuration)
carefully according to the mapping file. The wisim utility extracts the design only under the
specified scope so the signals that are not included in the scope are ignored.
Note:
All configuration keywords in the configuration file are not case-sensitive.

Text Mapping File
The format of the text mapping file (used by the "set Map" configuration) is shown below:
<target signal with full hierarchical name> => <source signal with full
hierarchical name>

Or
<target signal with full hierarchical name> => <constant>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The "=>" operator can be replaced by the "~>" operator for inverse-mapping. The
mapped value is inversed if the"~>" operator is used in the mapping file. The following is
an example of the mapping file:
target_top.u1.u2.u3.t_sig1 => source_top.u1.u2.u3.s_sig1
target _top.u1.u2.u3.t_sig2 ~> source_top.u1.u2.u3.s_sig2
target _top.u1.u2.u3.g_sig3 => 1'b1

The following rules must be considered when creating the mapping file:
* The prefix ("1'b" in above example) must be added for a constant value.
* The scope delimiter is fixed to `.'.
* By default, the wisim utility forms the bus-to-bus mapping. See the Form Bus Flow
section for the form bus flow details.
* All target signals must be inside the target scope.

Form Bus Flow
If a bit selection of a bus exists in the mapping file, the wisim utility forms the bus-to-bus
mapping if it is possible. All bits of a gate-level bus must be mapped to the same RTL bus
if any bit is mapped to a bit of an RTL bus. Equivalently, all bits of a target bus must be
mapped to a constant if any bit is mapped to a constant. Assuming T is a 2-bit bus, the
bus can be mapped as follows:
T[0] => C[0]
T[1] => C[1]

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
When a bus-to-bus mapping fails, the following is the flow for forming a bus in replay
simulation:
1. If it fails to form a bus, the wisim utility keeps the bit-level mapping. The following are
possible reasons that cause the wisim utility to fail to form the bus:
a. The mapping for a bus is not completely described:
T[0] => B[0] // T[1] is not specified in the mapping file

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
b. The mapping for a bus cannot be a bus in the waveform part:
T[0] => B[0]
T[1] => C[0]

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
c. The mapping for a bus contains both inverted and non-inverted mappings:
T[0] => B[0]
T[1] ~> B[1]

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
d. The mapping for a bus contains both constant and non-constant mappings:
T[0] => B[0]
T[1] => 1'b1

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
2. To drop the bus signals that cannot be formed as the bus-to-bus mapping, set the
WISIM_DROP_BUS_BIT environment variable to 1:
setenv WISIM_DROP_BUS_BIT = 1

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Then, the signals that meet failure cases in the flow are dropped and not forced.
3. To skip the flow to form a bus, set the WISIM_SKIP_FORM_BUS environment variable to
1:
setenv WISIM_SKIP_FORM_BUS = 1

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Then, replay simulation does not form a bus. But, it still keeps the valid mapping
description in the mapping flies.

Simulation Compile Script Examples
You need to create and specify the Simulation Compile script by the "set
Simulation_Compile_Script" configuration in the configuration file. The following is an
example of the Simulation Compile script for VCS:
#!/bin/csh -f
setenv VCS_HOME <VCS_INSTALL_PATH>
setenv PATH $VCS_HOME/bin:$PATH
setenv PLATFORM LINUX64
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH
${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/VCS/${PLATFORM}:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
setenv TAB ${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/VCS/${PLATFORM}/novas.tab
setenv PLI ${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/VCS/${PLATFORM}/pli.a
### COMMAND ###
vcs -full64 -sverilog -f wi_run.f -P $TAB $PLI +cli+4 -debug_pp
### debug_access flow ###
#setenv NOVAS_HOME $VERDI_HOME
#vcs -sverilog -f wi_run.f -debug_access+f+w+cbk+fwn
-debug_region=cell+lib

The wi_run.f file in the replay simulation directory is generated by the wisim utility for the
required design scope and new testbenches.
The following is an example of the Simulation Compile script for IUS:
#!/bin/csh -f
## ncsim flow ##
setenv CDS_INST_DIR <IUS_INSTALL_PATH>

${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM}/boot:${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/I

The top module WI_TB_TOP (highlighted in red) is a fixed name and has to be placed
before the original design top (designTop in this example).

text:
Practice
This practice section demonstrates how to use the crdb and wisim utilities to conduct a
gate-level (GTL) simulation from the RTL FSDB file.
* Input:
RTL design (for crdb)
RTL FSDB (for wisim)
GTL design (for both crdb and wisim)
* Output:
GTL simulation result (performing crdb for G2R mapping and wisim for replay simulation)

Step1: Generate Mapping File
1. Change the directory to DEMO/CORR/.
2. Prepare two designs:
Compile RTL design to rtl.lib++: vericom -f run_rtl.f -lib rtl
Compile GTL design to gate.lib++: vericom -f run_gate.f -lib gate

3. Generate the mapping file with the crdb utility by using the following commands:
crdb -RTL "-lib rtl -top system" -GATE "-lib gate -top system" -crdb
g2r.crdb -expMap g2r.map.gz -allreg -top_inport -target_scope system
-expGateUncor -impSVF design.svf

Practice

The following are descriptions of these commands:
-expMap: Output the mapping file in the gzip format.
-allreg: Map all registers.
-top_inport: Map all input and inout signals of the target scope.
-target_scope: Specify the target scope.
-impSVF: Specify the .svf file.
-expGateUncor: Export uncorrelated signals.
4. Check the following files to review the correlation results:
crdbLog/crdb.log file shows the correlation ratio similar to:

g2r.map.gz file is the mapping results in the gzip format.

Step2: Replay Simulation
1. Change the directory to DEMO/VCS/
2. Check the configuration file, wi_config.

Known Problems and Limitations

3. Modify VCS_HOME in the vcs_wi_compile.rc file to the VCS install path.
4. Set the correct VERDI_HOME to VERDI install path.
5. Perform the replay extraction using the following command:
%>wisim -lib gate -config wi_config -replay_extract

All required data for wisim is generated under whatIf/.
6. Perform replay compilation:
%>wisim -config wi_config -replay_compile

An executable for simulation is generated as whatIf/simv.
7. Perform replay simulation:
%>wisim -config wi_config -replay_sim

The simulation result (wi_result.fsdb) is generated under whatIf/.

Known Problems and Limitations
The following are the known problems and limitations:
* The signals in the mapping file cannot be a part/bit selection of a packed structure.
* The following data types are not supported in the left-hand side of the mapping file for
IUS simulation:
Integer types:
1. shortint
2. int
3. longint
4. byte
5. integer
6. time
enum
real
SVTB signals
* For IUS simulator, FSDB dumping might be incorrect in IUS10.2 and IUS11.1 versions.

Known Problems and Limitations

It is recommended to use other IUS simulator versions, such as IUS12.1 for replay
simulation FSDB dumping.
Alternatively, the FSDB_IUS_NO_OPTIM environment variable is provided for IUS10.2
and IUS11.1 versions to avoid this issue:
setenv FSDB_IUS_NO_OPTIM 1

* For protected code, replay simulation analysis does not support the target scope.
It also does not support sub-scopes that include protected code.

This book is designed to allow you to quickly become proficient with the Siloti system. The

Audience
The audience for this manual includes design, verification, and silicon validation engineers
who require enhanced visibility into their full-chip simulation, emulation, or hardware
acceleration results.
This document assumes that you have a basic knowledge of the platform on which your
version of the Siloti system runs, UNIX or Linux, and that you are knowledgeable in Verilog
or VHDL and digital logic design and verification.
Also, depending on the application, familiarity with the Verdi platform, softwarebased
simulation, emulation, or hardware acceleration concepts is helpful.

Introduction
The SilotiTM Visibility Automation System speeds up simulation by eliminating the
overhead associated with recording signal values and by enabling full visibility of design
activity based on a relatively small amount of signal data captured during full-chip
simulation, regression simulation, and hardware emulation/acceleration. The Siloti system,
(R)
which is integrated with the Verdi Automated Debug System, makes verification more
efficient by enabling comprehension of complex IC and system-on-chip (SoC) behavior
in conjunction with simulation and hardware-based verification applications. Using this
capability, you can perform the following:
* Achieve full visibility into the functional operation of designs with limited affect on
verification performance
* Enable analysis and debug of gate-level verification results on the RTL design
* Reduce the overall cost of verification
The Siloti system mitigates the expense of obtaining enough signal value information to
debug complex problems found during emulation, acceleration, and full-chip simulation.
Since the Siloti system automatically analyzes a design to determine the essential signals
(signals whose values must be captured during verification), infers values for signals not
captured, and maps gate-level signal data back to the RTL; design comprehension and
debug is greatly enhanced and simulation time is dramatically reduced.
The complementary Verdi platform is an advanced solution for debugging digital designs
that increases design productivity with complex System-on-Chip (SoC), ASIC, and FPGA
designs. The powerful technology provided in the Verdi platform helps you comprehend
complex and unfamiliar design behavior, automate difficult and tedious debug processes,
and unify diverse and complicated design environments. The Verdi platform and the
additional nAnalyzer and nECO modules enable engineers to locate, isolate, understand,
and resolve bugs in a fraction of the time of traditional solutions.
This chapter includes the following topics:
* Technology Overview
* Application Overview

Chapter 1: Introduction
Technology Overview

Technology Overview
The following figure illustrates the overview of Siloti visibility enhancement products:
Figure 1

Siloti Visibility Enhancement Products Overview

The Siloti system provides the following engines and modules:
* Visibility Analysis Engine
* Data Expansion Engine
* Abstraction Correlation Module

Visibility Analysis Engine
The Visibility Analysis engine analyses your RTL or gate-level netlist. It identifies the
minimum signals required for complete visibility in a selected design area. These are
known as essential signals. The Data Expansion engine uses the data from these signals
for its tasks. By capturing only essential signals, you can improve simulation speed and
efficiency.
To determine the essential signals, the Visibility Analysis engine relies on a complete set of
logic equations inferred from the HDL description. For each functional block, it recursively
traverses the inferred logic, extracts the primary inputs, register outputs, memory outputs,
and the outputs of non-synthesizable blocks, The tool then writes these signals into a file

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
m the HDL description. For each functional block, it recursively
traverses the inferred logic, extracts the primary inputs, register outputs, memory outputs,
and the outputs of non-synthesizable blocks, The tool then writes these signals into a file
that can be used to control dumping by simulators or other verification tools.

Data Expansion Engine
It is hard to understand abnormal device behavior when you have only limited data. The
Data Expansion engine is applied to compute missing signal values `on-demand' using
knowledge of the design function. After these values are calculated, you can use time-

Chapter 1: Introduction
Application Overview

based debugging to trace the cause of problems. Using the Data Expansion engine
together with the Visibility Analysis engine gives you the most complete view of the design
during debug.
The Data Expansion engine starts with register values and main inputs. It sorts the
combinational logic between registers using a linear algorithm and calculates signal values
with a cycle-based engine, without considering logic or wire delays. These computed
values are sent to the application window where you view the design.
The Data Expansion engine computes signal values only when you need them for
debugging or display. To show this, a new value called "NC" (Not Computed) is used in
the FSDB file and display windows. If a signal's value is not captured or expanded, NC is
displayed. After expansion, the computed signal values are shown in a different color to
help you tell them apart from values captured during verification.

Abstraction Correlation Module
A gate-level netlist is typically hard to understand when generated by synthesis tools.
To easily understand the meaning of gate-level logic, it is important to have an ability
to correlate gate-level verification results back to the RTL design descriptions. The
Abstraction Correlation module can be applied in the background to map gate-level signal
data to the RTL design for easier debug and understanding.
The Abstraction Correlation module interoperates seamlessly with the Data Expansion
engine to automatically enable analysis and debug of the gate-level results with full
visibility on the RTL design.

Application Overview
The Siloti system supports the following applications:
* Full Chip Simulation
* Emulation and Hardware Acceleration

Running full-chip simulations means you must balance simulation speed and debugging
ability. If you dump a lot of signal data, you can debug faster and understand the design
better. But dumping too much data makes the simulation run slowly. Many teams avoid
dumping signals at first and only do so after an error is found. This can cause many extra
simulation runs and make it hard to keep the project on schedule.
To improve this, you can use a method that dumps only a small number of key signals.
This method gives you enough visibility for debugging while keeping simulation

Chapter 1: Introduction
Application Overview

performance high. The Visibility Analysis engine helps you pick the right signals to dump,
so you can see the important parts of your design.
Set up your simulator to dump only the selected essential signals before you start
the simulation. After the simulation finishes, process the dumped data with the Data
Expansion engine. This engine computes the values of signals that were not dumped,
using cycle-accurate calculations without timing delays. With the Siloti system, you can
analyze the expanded data and use advanced debug features, just as if you had dumped
all signals during simulation.

Emulation and Hardware Acceleration
Debugging emulation and hardware acceleration systems can be difficult. These systems
often show only a few internal signals and use gate-level views that are unfamiliar.
Because they are hardware-based, teams must repeat synthesis and compilation steps to
add debug logic, like internal logic analyzers, and then run tests again.
When you set up emulation to dump registers, it can affect speed and turnaround time.
While dumping registers or using logic analyzers lets you see some signals, it may not
include the signals needed to fix a specific issue. This can lead to many rounds of setup
and testing, and you still might not see all signals at the RTL (Register Transfer Level)
level.
The Data Expansion engine and Abstraction Correlation module work together to
automate debug. They use limited signal data to help you trace problems in the RTL
design. The Abstraction Correlation module maps gate-level signal data from registers
to the RTL registers. The Data Expansion engine then processes this data to show RTL
combinational values.
Together, these tools provide RTL-based debug with high visibility of most internal signals
in the emulated design. To make emulation faster, you can use the Visibility Analysis
engine to lower the number of registers dumped in each run. If your emulator allows, you
can control this step during setup.

This chapter summarizes the various methods for starting the Siloti system, loading the
design, and loading the simulation results stored in the Fast Signal Database (FSDB).

Reference Source Files on the Command Line
This method loads the design directly from the source files. It can only be used for singlelanguage designs.
1. Use the following command to reference the source files on the command line:
% Verdi -f <source_file_name>
HDL

where source_file_name is a file that lists all of the HDL source files.
2. Then use the File -> Open Waveform File command to load the FSDB.

Reference Design and FSDB on the Command Line

1. Use the following command to reference both the source files and the FSDB on the
command line:
% Verdi -f <source_file_name> -ssf <fsdb_file_name>

where source_file_name is the source file name and fsdb_file_name is the name of
the FSDB file.
2. Use the following command to reference both the compiled library and the FSDB on
the command line:
% Verdi -lib <libName> -top <TopBlock>
-ssf <fsdb_file_name>

where libName is the compiled library and TopBlock is the highest-level block you
want to see and fsdb_file_name is the name of the FSDB file.
If the specified FSDB file is an Essential Signal FSDB, you are presented
with a Question dialog box related to Data Expansion. If you plan to use the
Siloti system, click Yes; otherwise, click No. Data Expansion can always be
started or the options changed by invoking the Tools -> Visibility -> Setup
Data Expansion command.

Perform Behavior Analysis on the Command Line

Perform Behavior Analysis on the Command Line
To perform Behavior Analysis on the command line, you would specify the -ba option.
1. Referencing the source files:
% Verdi -f <source_file_name> -ba -ba_mode <mode> -ssf
<fsdb_file_name>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
where source_file_name is the source file name and fsdb_file_name is the name of
the FSDB file.
2. Referencing the compiled library:
% Verdi -lib <libName> -top <TopBlock> -ba
-ba_mode <mode> -ssf <fsdb_file_name>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
where libName is the compiled library and TopBlock is the highest-level block you
want to see and fsdb_file_name is the name of the FSDB file.
The -ba option executes Behavior Analysis using the Behavior Analysis
settings from the novas.rcresource file unless you specifically include them
on the command line. Refer to the Verdi utility description in the Verdi and
Siloti Command Reference for a list of Behavior Analysis options.
The -ba_mode option specifies the default mode for Behavior Analysis.
The mode options are Working Scope Behavior Analysis (wsba) or Module
Based Behavior Analysis (mbba). The mode can also be specified by
environment variable, refer to the Behavior Analysis section of Appendix A
in the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference for details.

Perform Data Expansion on the Command Line
To perform Data Expansion on the command line, you would specify the -de or -DE option
in addition to loading the FSDB file and performing Behavior Analysis. The -de option
performs Data Expansion in auto time window mode. The -DE option performs Data
Expansion based on the specified options.
1. Referencing the source files:
% Verdi -f <source_file_name> -ba -ba_mode <mode> -de -ssf
<fsdb_file_name>

or

The -ba option is optional if either the -de or -DE option is specified.

Loading when Design and FSDB Hierarchies do not Match
Use the following command if you dumped the FSDB file for the entire design but you only
want to load a portion of the design for debug.
% Verdi -f <source_file_name> -ssf <fsdb_file_name> -vtop <map_file_name>

where source_file_name is the source file name, fsdb_file_name is the name of the
FSDB file and map_file_name is the name of the map file.

hierarchy

design

The map file is used to match the design hierarchy to the hierarchy in the FSDB file so that
the simulation results are correctly annotated on the source code and schematic views.
The Siloti system automatically generates a virtual hierarchy in the design according to the
definitions in the .map file. The syntax is as follows:
module_name = hierarchical_instance_path

Recommended Method for Performing Essential Signal Analysis

The map file matches the case sensitivity of the associated language. For
example, Verilog is case-sensitive so if the module definition is all capitalized,
the map file description needs to be as well (that is, cpu does not equal CPU).
VHDL is not case-sensitive (that is, cpu equals CPU).
If you incorrectly enter the module name in the map file, you might see an error similar to
the following in the compiler.log (File -> View Import Log):
*Error* view cpu is not defined for inst i_cpu
"virtual_top_autov_15123.gen:, 7:

This error needs to be eliminated. Check the module definition in the source code and
confirm that the map file matches it exactly.

Recommended Method for Performing Essential Signal Analysis
The recommended method for performing Essential Signal Analysis is to use the esa
utility.
1. Referencing the source files:
% esa -f <source_file_name> -db <ESDB_file_name> -bas <top_scope>

where source_file_name is the source file name, top_scope is the design top
scope for Behavior Analysis, and ESDB_file_name is the file name for the generated
essential signal database.
2. Referencing the compiled library:
% esa -lib <libName> -db <ESDB_file_name> -top <TopBlock> -bas
<top_scope>

where libName is the compiled library, TopBlock is the highest-level block you want to
see, top_scope is the design top scope for Behavior Analysis, and ESDB_file_name is the
file name for the generated essential signal database.
If -bas is not specified, the working scope is obtained from the novas.rc
resource file (if one exists); otherwise, the default is the top module of the
design.
If you are using a gate-level design, the -cellModel 0 option must also be
included to enable the symbol library.

Application Tutorials
This chapter introduces you to applications where you can use the Siloti system and
familiarizes you with its core concepts and use models.
This chapter consists of the following sections:
* Prerequisites
* Full Chip Simulation
* Emulation
* Debug Gate-Level Results on the RTL Design

Prerequisites
Before you begin the tutorials, you (or your system administrator) must install Verdi and
Siloti systems as described in the Installation and System Administration Guide. You must
also complete the following steps to set up the Siloti environment and the files required for
tutorials:
The optional Novas-2012??-demo.tar.gz package must be installed (where
2012 corresponds to the year and ?? corresponds to the month).
1. Add the Verdi application (binary) to the search path and specify the search path to the
license file.
For details, see the Setting Up the Environment and Running the Software section in
the Installation and System Administration Guide.
2. Create a working directory using the following command:
% mkdir <working_dir>

3. All of the tutorial data resides in the $VERDI_HOME/demo directory. Make a copy of
these demo files in your working directory using the following directory:
% cp -r <VERDI_INST_DIR>/demo <working_dir>

Many companies do not dump all data during full-chip simulations. It takes a lot of time to
save large amounts of simulation data.
Instead, teams often use a method where the verification environment finds problems first.
Examples include the testbench or assertions.
Then, they run a second simulation with data dumping enabled.
This process can add a full day to the project schedule each time an issue is found.
You must wait for the second simulation to finish before you can start debugging.
The Siloti system helps in two important ways:
1. Visibility Analysis - Determines the optimal set of signals to capture during simulation.
The set is minimal but sufficient to enable full visibility into design operation during
debug using the Data Expansion engine.
2. Data Expansion - Processes the limited data captured during simulation.
It calculates or expands values for combinational signals to enable full visibility into
design operation and efficient debug.
This technology improves the standard full-chip simulation process.
It gives you complete visibility into your design and lets you use automated debug tools.

list.

Determine Signals to Dump
The Visibility Analysis engine helps you find which signals you need to capture during a
full-chip simulation. This ensures you can see all important parts of your design. If you
want to debug a group of signals, a block, or the whole design, use Visibility Analysis to
identify the essential signals. You can pass this list of signals to the simulator for dumping
during simulation. If you only dump the minimal set of signals, you can still view the full
design operation later using the Data Expansion engine and VIA (Verdi Interoperability
Apps). You can create the essential signal list with a command line tool.
The Siloti version that generates the essential signal list and that expands the
essential signal FSDB file must be same.

Command Line
To perform Visibility Analysis, perform the following steps from the command line:
1. Change to the RTL directory using the following command:
% cd <working_dir>/demo/siloti/rtl

2. In a shell window, execute the following command to perform Essential Signal Analysis:
% esaesa -f run.f -db es -bas tb_CPUsystem

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
1) If -bas is not specified, the working scope is obtained from the novas.rc
resource file (if one exists). Otherwise, the default is the top module of the
design.
2) The -db option specifies the file name of the essential signal database. A
directory <ESDB_filename>.esdb++ is created for storing the essential signal
database.
3) If you are using a gate-level design, include the -cellModel 0 switch to
enable the symbol library.

For details on the esa utility, see the Utilities chapter of the Verdi and Siloti Command
Reference.
The essential signal database is saved in the es.esdb++ directory, that is used with the
+fsdb+esdb="ESDB_filename" command-line option during simulation. For details,
see FSDB Dumping Commands chapter of the Linking Novas Files with Simulators and
Enabling FSDB Dumping manual. You need to link the appropriate Novas object file for
FSDB dumping to your simulator. For details, see Linking Novas Files with Simulators to
Enable FSDB Dumping document.

Setup for Data Expansion
Assume that the RTL description provides the input for the Visibility Analysis engine,
which was used to generate the list of essential signals. This file was then used as input
to the fsdbDumpvarsToFile dump command during the full-chip simulation of the RTL
design to generate the FSDB file. For details on the dumping commands, see FSDB
Dumping Commands chapter of the Linking Novas Files with Simulators and Enabling
FSDB Dumping manual.
You can setup Data Expansion using the command line.
The Siloti version that generates the essential signal list and that expands the
essential signal FSDB file must be same.

the specified options. For a list of -DE options, see the Verdi utility description in
the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference.

Many companies today augment their verification strategy with low-cost commercial
emulation solutions - either for acceleration or firmware/software development purposes.
In many cases, these systems provide minimal observability of internal signal data. It is
often limited to some subset of registers in the design, which has a significant adverse
affect on understanding and debugging problems that occur during emulation. The Siloti
system can provide significant benefits in the following three specific areas:
1. Visibility Analysis - Determines the optimal (minimal but sufficient) set of signals that
the emulator must capture to guarantee full visibility into the critical portions of the
design and thus, efficient debug.
2. Data Expansion - Processes the limited data captured by the emulator and calculates
or expands the values for the combinational signals to enhance visibility into design
operation and to enable full and efficient debug.
3. Correlation - Maps the error location or emulation data back to the RTL design to
correlate it for efficient analysis and debug.

This chapter consists of the following sections:
* Input Requirements
* Determine Signals to Dump
* Setup for Data Expansion
* Debug With Data Expansion

Input Requirements
To use the Siloti system with emulation, you require the following items:
libraries

symbol

gate-level

RTL

* RTL design or gate-level design with symbol libraries to generate the essential signal
list.
VCD

* FSDB or VCD file with emulation results for the essential signals.

Determine Signals to Dump
Use the Visibility Analysis engine to determine which signals to dump. Visibility Analysis
answers the question: Which signals are captured by the emulation system to guarantee
full visibility into the critical portions of the design? Given a set of signals or a block for
which you must have full visibility after the fact, the goal is to determine the essential set
of signals that is captured by the emulator system for later processing using the Data
Expansion engine.
Some tools have their own way of choosing critical signals (for example,
registers). Therefore, it might be appropriate to start with that mechanism and
skip this step.
Assume you want to debug the entire chip after you run emulation and that the RTL
description generates the essential signal list and provides the input for the emulator. The
results for the essential signals are then captured during emulation and match the signal
names used in the RTL description.
If the results from emulation match the signal names used in the netlist but you
want to debug on the RTL design, see the Debug Gate-Level Results on the
RTL Design section.
You can generate the essential signal list using the command line.

The Siloti version that generates the essential signal list and that expands the
essential signal FSDB file must be the same.

Regular Expression Examples
Using the Regular Expression section on the Default Rules tab in the Perform CRDB
Correlationform, the following rules result in the described substitutions.
Figure 9

Regular Expression Examples

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
1. Matching string is "u1" and substitution string is "m2"
Gate Matching Exp field contains: u1
RTL Substitution String field contains: m2
Causes strings like "top.u1.s1" to become "top.m2.s1".
2. Match on the first %d and replace with @1
Rule:u%d => m@1
Causes "u1" to be mapped to "m1" and "u5" to be mapped to "m5".
3. Match on string combination, then replace and change order.
Rule: abc_([A-Z]+)_%d => cba_@2_@1
Causes strings like "abc_PQR_555" to be mapped to "cba_555_PQR".

Chapter 4: Appendix A: Name Mapping Rules
Predefined Rules Examples

4. If your gate-level design top does not match your RTL, you can use this rule to create a
`virtual top'.
Rule: ^top => tb.newTop
Causes strings like "top.u1.s1" to be mapped to "tb.newTop.u1.s1".
5. Delete the string by leaving the substitution string `empty'.
Rule: pre_ =>
Causes strings like "top.pre_u1.s1" to be mapped to "top.u1.s1".
Regular Expressions work on a single design name only; they do not
work for names crossing multiple hierarchies with delimiters. For example,
assuming a full name of u1.u2.\escaped_name.abc.dfg.q, the rule u2.%s.q
=> u2.q does not work since the left hand side crosses multiple hierarchies
but the rule abc.dfg => xyz works since the left hand side belongs to a single
name.

The Predefined Rules on the Default Rules tab of the Perform CRDB Correlation form
follows the regular expression name matching and substitution string syntax; however,
the data types are specially treated. The predefined rules support three gate-level to RTL
correlation types: hierarchical separator, tri-state devices and registers.
Perform CRDB Correlation Form - Predefined Rules

Separator

Hierarchical

1. Hierarchical Separator is the separator for flattened signal/instance. Only one
character is allowed.
Example 1:
RTL uses: top.u1.u2.sig[0]
Gate uses: top.\u1!u2!sig[0]
Specify the hierarchical separator as `!'.

Chapter 4: Appendix A: Name Mapping Rules
Applying Rules

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Example 2:
RTL uses: top.u1.u2.s1
Gate uses: top.u1#u2#s1
Specify the hierarchical separator as `#'.
Common hierarchy separators such as underscore `_' and dot `.' do not
need to be specified as they are handled internally.
Tri-state

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
2. Tri-state is the format for tri-state instance and tri-state output net. Example:
Gate uses: bus1_tri
Specify the rule as: %s_tri
Causes the gate "bus1_tri" signal to be mapped to "bus1" in the RTL.
Register

3. Register is the format for register instance and register output net only. The register
substitution consists of the register string and the register index format. Example:
Gate uses: ccu_fetch_reg_3_
Specify the rule as: %s_reg_%d_
Causes the gate "ccu_fetch_reg_3_" signal to be mapped to signal "ccu_fetch[3]" in the
RTL.
A rule in the Register or Tri-state field can only contain one '%s' and it must
be at the beginning of the rule. For example, the rule "%s_reg_%d" is valid
but the rule "\%s_reg_%d" is not.

expression and predefined rules are applied).

Example 3:
Assuming the Register field of the Predefined rules include:
%s_Z_%d
and a library cell for a register is defined as:
FF abc_Z_6(.CK(clk), .Q(n123), .QN(n124), .RN(reset));
This causes the library cell abc_Z_6 to be mapped to the RTL register signal abc[6].
If either the simulation library or the symbol library is available for the flip-flop (FF),
the register output nets, n123 and n124, are also mapped to abc[6] and its inversion
respectively. In addition, the clk and reset signals are mapped according to the attributes
of the CK and RN pins they are connected to and the syntax of the RTL code that defines
register abc[6].
It is very common for an RTL register net to be synthesized to a gate-level
flip-flop or latch library cell; therefore, the recommendation is to first correlate
a register library cell to its corresponding register net using the Regular
Expression and Predefined rules. Then the correlation algorithm correlates
the nets connected to the cell according to the pin attributes of the cell from
either the symbol library or the simulation library.

Appendix B: Design Extraction Messages
Overview
The design extraction engine, which is called CG2, checks target scope and exclude
module before code generation.
1. Target Scope Check
If target scope is not specified correctly, Add/Set scope failed messages are
reported. CG2 does not perform extraction. Review the target scope setting. For
example,
[CG2 Log]: Target scope is not specified. Set scope failed.
2. Exclude Module Check
If exclude module is not specified correctly, Failed to add exclude module
messages are reported. Review the exclude module setting. For example,
[CG2 Log]: Fail to add exclude module, module "test" not found.

After the checks, CG2 starts to collect viewing scope, traverse and process the design.
If there are VHDL scopes under the target scope, it is not supported currently. The
following message is reported.
[CG2 Log]: VHDL is not supported yet.

When traversing/processing the design, CG2 skips statements in the initial block and
protected module/interface/package with [CG2 Info] messages. If there are some
problems or unsupported constructs in the design, [CG2 Warning] and [CG2 Error]
messages are reported. Note that the View, File and Line information are also reported
to help users check their design. For example, the following message means that class
variable "packet_obj" is not supported, which can be found inside module "CPU" on line 26
in "test.v".
[CG2 Warning]: Class variable is not supported
Verbose: class variable is "packet_obj"

View: "CPU"
File: "test.v"

Overview
The Verdi(R) Automated Debug Platform provides a unique approach to analog mixedsignal (AMS) verification that enables engineers to debug complex AMS designs. AMS
debug features provide visibility into design hierarchy and source code for both analog
and digital designs. When digital and analog FSDB files are loaded, you can view and
debug analog signals through the annotated source code, schematic and waveform. This
document focuses on the VHDL/Verilog-SPICE Mixed-Signal design scope.

text:
Prerequisites
The following are the prerequisites to use the mixed-signal debug features in the Verdi
platform:
* Use the Verdi platform with version J-2014.12-2 and later.
* Generate the analog FSDB file by using the CustomSim simulator with version 2014.09SP3 in the VCS cosim flow.
* Generate the digital FSDB file by using VCS simulator with version J-2014.12-1 and
later in the VCS cosim flow.
* Compile your design using the vericom/vhdlcom and spicom utilities.
The following sections describe how you can generate the FSDB and KDB files.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Generating the Simulation Result

Generating the Simulation Result
Perform the following steps to run the simulation and generate the waveform of your
mixed-signal design into Verdi:
* Use the set_waveform_option -format FSDB option inside the CustomSim
command file to have CustomSim generate an FSDB output with analog signals .

* Add the -ad option in VCS command line to compile your AMS design . For example:
//Compile and analysis your design
%> vcs digital_design_file(s) -ad
[=mixed-signal_control_file] [vcs options]
//Execution the simulation
%> simv [vcs run-time options]

Executing the simulation command generates two FSDB files. One includes digital
hierarchy and signals, and another includes analog hierarchy and signals.

Loading the Design and Simulation Result into Verdi
The Import Design from Library feature is supported to load your mixed-signal design
into the Verdi platform. Compile your design into the Verdi KDB with both digital and
analog hierarchy/signals. Use the spicom utility to compile the SPICE/Spectre/Eldo or any
other analog models into the netlist model.
The following sections describe how to compile your design with compilers, and how to
load KDB and FSDB files into the Verdi platform in detail.

Compiling a Mixed-Signal Design
The following sections describe how to compile your design with spicom and how to load
KDB into Verdi.
* Compiling and Importing a SPICE Design
* Compiling With the SPICE Unified Front-End Flow
* Support Spectre Format Probes in Unify Dumping

1.
2.

For details on the configuration commands, see the CustomSim User Guide.
For details on the compilation and simulation options, see the Mixed-Signal Simulation User Guide.

Compiling a Mixed-Signal Design

Compiling and Importing a SPICE Design
When your mixed-signal design includes SPICE and Spectre format, use the spicom utility
to compile the analog modules of your design. If your design files include Verilog formats
(such as, Verilog-A), spicom automatically invokes vericom to compile these files. The
compile log files of spicom and vericom are separated.
To compile and load your design into Verdi, perform the following steps:
1. Use the vericom utility to compile Verilog modules in your design. Its syntax is as
follows:
%> vericom <your_verilog_design> [vericom_options]

2. Use the vhdlcom utility to compile VHDL modules in your design. Its syntax is as
follows:
%> vhdlcom <your_vhdl_design> [vhdlcom_options]

3. Use the spicom utility to compile analog modules in your design.
You need to add the following option to the spicom command line:
-ad: Loads the simulation setup file.
Additionally, the following options are optional:
-topname: Specifies a name for the top cell. The default value is topcell.
-lib: Specifies the library to save your design. The default value is work.
For example, to use the AD file as the input, use the following command:
% spicom -ad vcsAD.init

This command creates the netlist type data in the design created. The analysis
statement for simulation (for example, ALTER, PRINT, DATA, and so on) is not compiled.
4. Use the vhdlcom utility to compile VHDL modules in your design. For example:
% vhdlcom <your_vhdl_design> [vhdlcom_options]

5. Add the -msv option into the Verdi command line to enable mixed-signal debug
features. For example:
% verdi -top <your_design_top> -msv

6. To load the specified report file of interface elements, use the -msvDir option if you
have the report file of the interface elements. For example:
%> verdi -top <your_design_top> -msv -msvDir simv.msv

Loading FSDB Files

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text: Verdi supports loading only one report file when loading a design into Verdi.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Compiling With the SPICE Unified Front-End Flow
You can compile SPICE designs in Verdi by invoking vlogan, vhdlan, or vcs, and
specifying the -kdb option along with the AD file.
Add the -kdb option on the VCS command line as follows:
%>vcs -kdb -ad=vcsAD.init

VCS internally invokes spicom with this command line to analyze the vcsAD.init file, and
the KDB model of SPICE is generated.
When you specify the -kdb option, the $VERDI_HOME variable must be set.

Support Spectre Format Probes in Unify Dumping
Verdi unify dumping supports spectre format. Dump spectre format only when the user
specifies it. You get this information from the simulator. Then analog simulator provides
spectre format probes to dumper and dumper then selects dump corresponding probes
with the dumping option into FSDB.

Loading FSDB Files
To debug the mixed-signal design with the simulation result in Verdi, you need to load a
virtual file that includes digital and analog FSDB files into the nWave window.
To create the virtual file which includes digital and analog FSDB files, perform the following
steps:
1. Click the nWave

icon to invoke the nWave window.

2. Use the File -> Edit Virtual File option to invoke the Virtual File Editor form.
3. In the Virtual File Editor form, double-click the digital FSDB file as the first FSDB in the
virtual file. Then, double-click the analog FSDB file as the second FSDB file.

4. Specify the virtual file name in the Save as field and click OK.
5. Both digital and analog FSDB files are loaded into the nWave window through the
virtual file. The time-units of the digital and analog FSDB files are synchronized. The
master scope is the digital FSDB file.

You can set up the cosimulation debugging in the Verdi AMS using the GUI with the
following capabilities:
* Swap view for instances which have multiple views.
* Port mapping in case of port mismatches between views.
* Set up parameters for interface elements.
* Save the configuration in the AMS control file. (vcsAD.init as default)
All these features are discussed in detail in the following sections. To avail this capability,
set the environment variable VERDI_ENABLE_AMS_SETUP.

To edit the control file for a design, use the menu option AMS Configuration under the
Tools menu as shown in the following figure:
Figure 1

AMS Configuration Menu Item

You can also use the AMS toolbar item to access the configuration widget as shown in the
Figure 2

AMS Configuration Toolbar Item

Select the AMS Configuration to open the widget which is used to setup the control file to
perform AMS co-simulation in Verdi.
Two different configuration widgets are available: one for pure digital designs and another
for mixed digital and analog designs.

AMS Configuration Widget for Pure Digital Designs
If you have a pure digital design, Verdi displays an AMS Configuration widget containing
the following five tabs which appear as shown in the following figure.
For more information on each tab and its functionality, click the tab name in the following
list:
* The Choose Tab
* The A/D Tab
* The E/R Tab
* The Resistances Tab
* Extra Options
The following functions are common to all the five tabs in the configuration widget as
shown in the following figure:
* Cancel: Discards current settings and closes the widget.
* Save/Save As: Saves the current settings to a file after performing some error checks.
A warning message is displayed in the following scenarios:
Simulator field is empty
Analog Netlist File field is empty
Spice Top checked but the Top Name field is empty
Cell, port, and node fields are empty for the A/D interface element
Node field is empty for the E/R interface element
Node or r field is empty for node resistance override
Node or file field is empty for the resistance map file
* Preview: Shows the commands on the preview widget.

Figure 3

AMS Configuration Widget

The Choose Tab
The Choose tab enables you to setup the choose and spice_top options as shown in
figure The Choose Tab. The * symbol indicates the mandatory fields. Following are the
descriptions of each field in the tab:
* Simulator: Specifies analog simulator type.
* Analog Netlist File: Specifies analog netlist file.
* Command File: Specifies analog simulator command file.
* Spice Top: Specifies whether the top-level of a design is a SPICE design.
* Top Name: Specifies the SPICE top name, the default name is snps_sptop.

Figure 4

The Choose Tab

The A/D Tab
The A/D (Analog to Digital and Digital to Analog) tab enables you to set up a2d and d2a
commands.
The A/D tab contains two kinds of interface elements: a2d and d2a as shown in figure The
A/D Tab. The definition of each of these interface elements is as follows:
* Analog to Digital Interface Elements:
Node: Specifies hierarchical path of the instance.
Cell: Specifies the cell name.
Port: Specifies the port name.
Low Threshold: Specifies the low threshold values.
High Threshold: Specifies high threshold values.
High Impedance: Specifies the high impedance.
Vdd Net: Specifies the dynamic supply.

Minimum Voltage: Specifies minimum voltage for VDD.
Minimum Voltage Logic: Specifies the logic value passed to the digital engine
when the conversion is disabled.
Cap.Load: Specifies the load capacitance to be inserted at interface net.
* Digital to Analog Interface Elements:
Node: Specifies the hierarchical path of the instance.
Cell: Specifies the cell name.
Port: Specifies the port name.
Power Net: Specifies the PowerNet name.
Rise Fall Times: Specifies the rise and fall times.
Rise Time: Specifies the rise time.
Fall Time: Specifies the fall time.
Delay: Specifies the delay before the analog transition starts.
Logic-X: Specifies rules on how a logic X must be translated to a voltage level.
High Voltage: Specifies the high voltage.
Low Voltage: Specifies the low voltage.
Vdd: Specifies the dynamic supply.

Figure 5

The A/D Tab

The E/R Tab
The E/R (Electrical to Real and Real to Electrical) tab enables you to set up e2r and
r2e commands.

h Voltage: Specifies the high voltage.

The E/R Tab
The E/R (Electrical to Real and Real to Electrical) tab enables you to set up e2r and
r2e commands.
The E/R tab contains two kinds of interface elements: e2r and r2e as shown in figure The
E/R Tab. The definition of each of these interface elements is as follows:
* Electrical-to-Real Interface Elements (e2r):
Node: Specifies hierarchical path to the e2r interface.
Type: Specifies if e2r is converting voltage values to digital, or the current through a
resistor.
Fidelity: Specifies the absolute voltage/current threshold value for e2r events.
Min.Fidelity: Specifies the voltage difference between two e2r events.
Gain: Specifies multiplier when converted to digital.
Resistor: Specifies value or the resistor.
* Real to Electrical Interface Elements (r2e):
Node: Specifies hierarchical path to the e2r interface.
Type: Specifies if the e2r converting voltage values to digital, or the current through
a resistor.
Fidelity: Specifies the absolute voltage/current threshold value for e2r events.

Gain: Specifies multiplier when converted to digital.
RF Rate: Specifies value of the resistor.
Figure 6

The E/R Tab

The Resistances Tab
The Resistances tab enables you to set up rmap_file and map_by_node commands.
The following are the descriptions of each field in the tab:
* Default Resistance Map: Specifies the default resistance map.
* Resistance Map Files: Specifies the resistance map file.
File Name: Specifies resistance map file.
Node: Specifies node name.
Instance: Specifies instance name.
Subcircuit: Specifies subcircuit name.
Port: Specifies port name.
Node File: Specifies node file.
Instance File: Specifies instance file.
Subcircuit File: Specifies subcircuit file.
* Node Resistance Overrides: Specifies resistance value to the interface resistor.
Resistance: Specifies resistance map file.
Node: Specifies node name.

The following functions are common to all the three tabs in the configuration widget:
* Preview: Displays a preview of the updates you have made to the control file. The
updates are highlighted in blue and additions are highlighted in green and deletions are
highlighted in gray as shown in figure Figure 12.
* Add: Adds the command with the green font color as shown in figure Figure 12.
* Change: Comments the original command and adds the new command instead of the
original one.
* Delete: Comments the command with the gray font color as shown in figure Figure 12.
The command style may different from the original one. For example, the
original is use_spice -inst x -cell M, the new option is use_spice
-cell M -inst x.
* Save: Saves the current settings to a file.
* Apply: Applies the current setting and then reloads the file.
* OK: Applies the new settings and then closes the form.
* Cancel: Closes the form.
Figure 12

The Preview Tab

The Swap View Tab
The Swap View tab enables you to change the view of an instance. You can view SPICE,
Verilog, and VHDL views of an instance.

Figure 13

The Swap View Tab

The following are the descriptions of each field in the tab:
* Instance: Displays instances with swapped views. It supports the drag and drop
operation. If an instance is highlighted in green, that is, no port is mismatching. If it is
highlighted in red, that is a port has mismatches. You can also delete the instance. The
icon of an instance indicates the status of the current view.

Spice view to Verilog/VHDL View

Verilog view to Spice view

VHDL view to Spice View

* Hierarchical Name: Displays the hierarchical name of an instance in the list.
* Spice: Swaps to the Spice view of the selected item. The instance is selected if the
current item is already in the Spice view.
* Verilog: Swaps to the Verilog view of the selected item. The instance is selected if the
current item is already in the Verilog view. The instance is disabled if the instance does
not have the Verilog view.
* VHDL: Swaps to the VHDL view for the selected item. The instance is selected if
current item is already in the VHDL view. The instance is disabled if the instance does
not have the VHDL view.

* Port: Lists the ports of digital and analog views. It supports the drag and drop operation
inside the list. You can drag a port and drop it to the same column port to swap its
position.
* Position: Ports in the same row are mapped; other ports are opened.
* Name: Ports that have the same name are mapped; other ports are opened.

text:
Interactive Simulation Debugging of
Mixed-Signal Designs
Verdi provides an approach to perform Analog Mixed-Signal (AMS) Interactive Simulation
Debugging that enables you to debug complex AMS designs during the simulation.
To perform AMS debugging in the Interactive Simulation Debug mode, you must compile
mixed-signal designs with VCS and Verdi, configure the simulation setting, and then
enable the Interactive Simulation Debug mode.
The following sections describe how you can debug analog mixed-signal designs in Verdi:
* Performing Interactive Simulation Debug of Mixed-Signal Designs
* Dumping Analog Signals in FSDB File in VCS-CustomSim Co-simulation Flow
* Dumping Automatic Inserted Connect Modules (AICM) Signals in the Verilog-AMS Flow
* Enabling Through Net Dumping Information in FSDB File
* Debugging in Source Code Pane
* Interface Elements Enhancements
* Debugging in Waveform View
* Viewing Runtime Interface Elements in nWave
* Debugging in the Schematic View
* Debugging in WaveView
* Tracing Signals in the Temporal Flow View
* Filtering Signals Based on Signal Types in nTrace
* Mapping the Port Configuration
* Modifying the Analog Configuration During Runtime (Using ace reread)
* Tracing Results of Connect Modules in the AMS Designs
* IE_All_Only Option for MSV Common Dump

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
* Event-Based Real-Time View Swapping (RTVS)
* Enabling Hierarchy Checking for RTVS Qualification
* Donut Configuration Support in RTVS
* Managing AMS Profile Viewing in Verdi

After you compile mixed-signal designs in Verdi, you can interactively debug the design.
The AMS Interactive Debug mode for AMS designs supports the following features:
* Provides various methods to dump voltage of analog signals.
* Shows voltage values as annotations for analog signals in interactive debug mode.
* Shows analog signals in the interactive Watch tab.
* Forces/releases the voltage of nodes with a user-defined slope.
* Saves/restores the simulation session/state.
* The waveform allows you to save/restore a signal .rc file with analog signals in form of
v() being dumped and restored.
* Offers an interactive console to enter CustomSim interactive commands with ace
preceding and then loads a UCLI command file to execute it.
The following sections describe the supported interactive simulation debug features:
* Getting Started
* Setting the Simulator Type in Preference Page
* Using the Interactive Watch Tab
* Annotating Values
* Dumping Analog Signals
* Using Force/Release Node Voltage
* Saving or Restoring Simulation Session or State
* Using the Interactive Console
* CustomSim Signal Name Format

* Supporting Verilog-AMS in the Interactive Debug Mode
* Limitations

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Getting Started
Verdi supports AMS interactive debug mode with the following flow:
1. Prepare the AMS design.
2. Compile the AMS design with VCS and acquire the simv that has the debug capability.
For more information, refer to the document of VCS/CustomSim/PLI.
3. Use Verdi to load the AMS design with cosim option specified by as follows:
Specify -msv when importing the design from the command line.
In nTrace, select File -> Import Design -> From library -> Options, toggle on the
Cosim Debug command and load the AMS design.
4. Select Tools -> Run Simulation.
Verdi creates and opens a single FSDB to include the digital and analog signals dumped
by the FSDB dumper. The following figure provides an overview of the Verdi AMS
Interactive Mode.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Figure 14

Overview of Verdi AMS Interactive Mode

You can run AMS interactive debug with the AMS design. However, the simulation is
controlled by VCS and following are the limitations that exists in VCS/CUSTOMSIM when
running AMS interactive debug:
* Step or next for an analog design is not supported.
* Breakpoints cannot be added into analog design.
* Rewind is blocked for an AMS interactive debug mode.
These limitations cause some menu options and right-click menu options to be disabled.
For more information on the simulation and interactive debug commands, see the Verdi
and Siloti Command Reference Guide.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Setting the Simulator Type in Preference Page
You can specify the simulator in the Simulator field of the Simulation Preferences form
(invoked with Tools -> Preference -> Simulation -> Simulator option).
If you specify the -msv option in command line, the simulator type in preference is
changed to VCS-AMS.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Figure 15

New Simulator Type in Preference

* Previously, Verdi had -simType option to indicate the simulator type when invoking
Verdi. If you specify both the -msv and the -simType options, then Verdi issues a
warning message and honors the -msv option.
* Verdi issues a warning message when you invoke the simulation by different simulator
types when running AMS interactive debug. For example,
You can use the simulator type VCS and run interactive mode with AMS simv.
You can use the simulator type VCS-AMS and run interactive mode with digital only
simv.

Points to Note
* Verdi does not support runtime options for the dumper with the command
line. You must specify them using the $fsdbDumpvars() task; for example,
$fsdbDumpvars("+msv+v").
* The Verdi options that must be specified after the -verdi_opts option, for example:
./simv -do temp.do -verdi -verdi_opts "-ssf xx.fsdb"

* Specifying -ad_runopt=a2dopt+d2aopt or -ucli -ucli2Proc option is not required
in Interactive Debug mode.
* The following is an example command to invoke interactive mode for mixed signal cosimulation in Verdi:
verdi -simBin simv -i ./simv -verdi

Using the Interactive Watch Tab
The Interactive Watch tab displays analog signals, ports/nodes, and their voltage value
at the current simulation time. You can add analog signals, ports/nodes to the Watch tab
with the drag-and-drop or the Add to Watch right-click menu option, as illustrated in the
Figure 16

Signals Added to Interactive Watch Tab

You can also drag SPICE instance to the interactive Watch tab. All analog ports and
nodes that are defined in this SPICE instance are added to the Watch tab. For example,
jj.inst1 is a SPICE instance. You can drag it to the Watch tab. All its ports and nodes
are added to the Watch tab.
Figure 17

Ports and Nodes Added to Watch Tab

The Watch tab provides the following information for analog variables:
* Name: The variable name.
* Value: The voltage value of the current simulation time. For example, 3.30V.
* Type: Analog signal, port, or node.
* Scope: Full hierarchical scope.
You can summarize the effectiveness of each right-click options in the interactive Watch
tab in an analog design.
* The following options are disabled with analog signals:
Set the Breakpoint
Set Radix
Add Object to Watch Tab
Show Declaration, Show in Class Browser, View Object References
Dump Object to FSDB file, Dump, Add Object to Waveform
* Limitation:
The Watch tab displays the voltage value. The current value is not supported in the
Watch tab.

Annotating Values
Voltage values can be annotated to the analog signals in Source Code and nSchema
panes by using the Source Active Annotation toggle command (the corresponding
shortcut key is `x').
The voltage value is shown as 3.30V.
Figure 18

Voltage Value Annotation

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Limitation:
This feature has the following limitations:
* The Tools -> Preference -> Spice -> Annotation option does not work in interactive
debug mode.

signal is not dumped earlier. If it is dumped, you can change it from nWave.

Dumping Analog Signals
Verdi allows you to dump voltage and current of analog signals. Similar to interactive
debug mode with digital design, you can dump the voltage value of an analog signal in
AMS interactive debug mode in the following ways:
* Drag the specified analog signal from the Source Code window and drop it to nWave.
* In nTrace, right-click the signal and select the Add Signal(s) to Waveform option.
* In nTrace, right-click the signal/instance and select the Dump to FSDB File option.
In nTrace, right-click the signal/instance and select the Drag option. In nWave, right-click
the signal pane and select the Drag option. If you select analog signals, Verdi dumps the
voltage value of the selected analog signal. If you select analog instances, Verdi dumps
the voltage value of the analog signal under selected analog instance.
