Dump Menu Item

Figure 20

AMS Signal Dump Form

Limitation
This feature has the following limitation:
* If you dump analog signals using SPICE statements, CustomSim configuration
file, or CustomSim interactive dumping command in split mode, the analog signals
are not dumped into the Verdi interactive FSDB files including .print, probe,
probe_waveform_voltage, and iprobe_waveform_current.

Dumping Analog Scope
You can dump the analog scope by dragging and dropping the sub-circuit or device
from nTrace to nWave. For example, if you drag the jj.inst1.mn1 device from nTrace
to nWave, all voltage values of analog signals under jj.inst1 are dumped. The port of
jj.inst1.mn1 is added to nWave as before.

You can also dump the analog scope by dragging and dropping the instance from the
instant pane to nWave. For example, if you drag the jj.inst1 device from nTrace to
nWave, all voltage values of analog signals under jj.inst1 are dumped. The port of
jj.inst1 is added to nWave as before.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Dumping Batch Signals
You can dump batch signals with the nWave -> File -> Restore Signals option that is
same as interactive debug mode with the digital design.

Using Force/Release Node Voltage
Verdi provides the force value form for SPICE signals to force voltage values. Right-click
the specified signals to select the nTrace -> Force Signal Value -> Set Force menu
option. The force value form includes the following fields:
* Signal name: Specify the signal to force by entering the name of the specified signal to
this field.
If the force value form is invoked with the nTrace -> Force Signal Value ->
Set Force right-click menu option, the name of the signal is filled in this field
automatically.
* Value: Specify the forced voltage value in the field. The unit is Volt. The default is the
current value.
* slope value: When this option is turned on, specify the slope value for the analog
signal by entering the value to this field. The unit is second/volt. The default value is
1ps/volt. You can specify the time unit such as 1ms, 1us, or 1s. The default of the slope
value option is off.
If the time unit is not specified in this field, the time unit is in seconds.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Dumping Analog Signals in FSDB File in VCS-CustomSim
Co-simulation Flow
The UCLI dump command enables you to dump analog signals in the FSDB file in the
VCS-CustomSim co-simulation environment. The UCLI dump command supports dumping
of the hierarchy scope with mixed digital and analog modules, for an object specified in the
design.
This is described in detail in the following sections:
* Dumping of the Analog/Digital Signals into an FSDB File
* Performing Merge Dumping
* Limitation

Dumping of the Analog/Digital Signals into an FSDB File
This section describes how you can dump digital signals, analog signals, or both analog
and digital signals in the FSDB file. The following steps are prerequisites for FSDB
dumping:
1. Set the VERDI_HOME variable as follows:
% setenv VERDI_HOME <verdi_path>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
2. Compile the design with the -debug_access option, as follows:
% vcs -debug_access <file_name>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
You can now use one of the following ways to invoke Verdi dumper on analog signals:
ucli% dump -msv[=on|off]
ucli% dump -file analog_mixed_signal.fsdb -type fsdb

OR
ucli% dump -file analog_mixed_signal.fsdb -type fsdb -msv[=on|off]

You can use the -msv option to enable (on) or disable (off) dumping of analog signals
throughout the simulation. By default, this option is enabled if on or off is not specified.

Dumping Analog Signals in FSDB File in VCS-CustomSim Co-simulation Flow

The analog targets are ignored if the -msv option is not specified.
Once an analog scope is enabled with the dump -msv on command, it cannot be disabled
for dumping throughout the simulation using the dump -msv off command.
If -type is not specified, you can use the following command to set the default dump type
as FSDB:
% setenv SNPS_SIM_DEFAULT_GUI verdi

Use the dump -add UCLI command to dump analog signals, digital signals, or both analog
and digital signals in the FSDB file.
Example-1: dump -msv (on|off) is not specified.
The -msv option is enabled by default when on or off is not specified. Consider the
following example:
ucli% dump -msv -type fsdb -file analog_mixed_signal.fsdb
ucli% dump -add top.a -fid FSDB0

This example dumps all the analog and digital signals of the top.a scope.
You must specify the -fid argument if multiple dump files are open, if not VCS issues an
error message.
Example-2: dump -msv off is specified
ucli% dump -msv off -type fsdb -file analog_mixed_signal.fsdb
ucli% dump -add top.U0 -fid FSDB0

This example dumps all the digital signals of the top.U0 scope and all the hierarchies
under it, excluding all analog signals in the hierarchy.
For more information on the dump -add and dump -file UCLI commands, see Integrating
VCS with Verdi chapter in the VCS User Guide.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Usage Example
If the -msv option is set to on, the dump -add a.b.c -type command exhibits the
following behavior:
* If a.b.c is an analog net, dumps its voltage.
* If a.b.c is an analog sub-circuit, dumps all ports and internal nets of the sub-circuit.
* If a.b.c is digital net, dumps its digital value.
* If a.b.c is digital instance, dumps the signal inside this scope.
* If a.b.c is digital or analog instance where c contains mixed-signal hierarchies, then
both digital and analog signals of c and its hierarchies are dumped.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Dumping Analog Signals in FSDB File in VCS-CustomSim Co-simulation Flow

Dumping Current Probes Using the UCLI Command
You can dump current probes using the UCLI command or Verdi dump tasks by specifying
the corresponding command in CustomSim configuration file. If not, Verdi issues error
messages and signals are not dumped.
The following table lists UCLI and CustomSim Probe Commands that you can use to
dump the current probes:
UCLI Commands

CustomSim Probe Commands

dump -add top -i -fid FSDB0

iprobe_waveform_current -i top.* -limit 99

dump -add top -i2 -fid FSDB0 iprobe_waveform_current -i2 top.* -limit 99
dump -add top -iall -fid
FSDB0

iprobe_waveform_current -iall top.* -limit 99

dump -add top -isub -fid
FSDB0

iprobe_waveform_current -isub top.* -limit

The values in the table are examples only, the scope name and current option
can be changed as required.

Performing Merge Dumping
You can dump analog (spice) signals/scopes into the first opened FSDB file, that is, the
default FSDB file. You can also use fsdbDumpvars to dump digital signals into the same
FSDB.
Perform the following steps:
1. Specify the following command in the CustomSim configuration file (xa.cfg):
set_waveform_option -format fsdb -file merge

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
2. Set the VERDI_HOME variable as follows:
% setenv VERDI_HOME <verdi_path>

3. Compile the design with the -debug_access option, as follows:
% vcs -debug_access <file_name>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
4. The spice signal specified to be dumped in the configuration file is dumped to the first
FSDB file opened. If there is no FSDB file opened, the FSDB dumper creates an FSDB

Dumping Analog Signals in FSDB File in VCS-CustomSim Co-simulation Flow

with the default file name which is novas.fsdb, and dumps the spice signal into this
FSDB file.
5. If you do not want to use novas.fsdb as the default FSDB file, you can use the
following command to specify the default FSDB file name to xxx.fsdb. This file
becomes the default FSDB file. If this is not specified, then the default file name is
novas.fsdb.
simv +fsdb+default_filename+xxx.fsdb

or
setenv FSDB_DEFAULT_FILE_NAME xxx.fsdb

If any CustomSim probe command is invoked on a SPICE signal, its wave
is dumped in the target FSDB file. For more information on the CustomSim
configuration commands, refer to the CustomSim Command Reference User
Guide.

text:
Usage Example for Merge Dumping
The following example describes how the common dump flow and the single merged
FSDB file flow work together.
Consider that you have the following design:

Consider that the configuration file xa.cfg has the following settings:

The following CustomSim command dumps a signal's voltage under the scope

The VCS command (UCLI command) file has the following setting:

When you use -file merge in the configuration file, the configuration file provides the
target probes to the dumper and then the dumper dumps these probes in the FSDB file.
When you use the +msv option, the dumper queries the configuration file for the probes

Limitation
This feature has the following limitation:
If an instance or a signal name in a SPICE scope contains a SystemVerilog hierarchy
delimiter ".", for example, a signal is named as xx.bb, in merged single FSDB flow, the
signal may not be put into right hierarchy in the FSDB as expected.

Dumping Automatic Inserted Connect Modules (AICM) Signals in
the Verilog-AMS Flow
This feature enables you to dump the AICM (*_aicm) signals into the Fast Signal
Database (FSDB).
To enable the dumping, do the following:
1. Set the following environment variable:
setenv FSDB_MSV_D_AICM 1

2. Use explicit dump commands as follows:
dump -add <aicm_signal_name> -fid $digitalDumpFile

Enabling Through Net Dumping Information in FSDB File

Examples

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The following command dumps the snps_sptop.in2__aicm signal into the FSDB.

Enabling Through Net Dumping Information in FSDB File
The analog view of a2a through net in digital scope and the digital view of d2d through
net in analog scope can be dumped through dump command without extra environment
variable setting. The digital view of a2a through net is filtered to avoid the confusion
caused by the z value.
In the nWave window, for a2a, a2d, d2d, and d2d tags to appear, for example, v(clk)
(a2a), you need to import the design and interface element report file. Also, when multiple
interface element types are available for the signals at same time, the tags are separated
by "/" without duplication.

Use Model
In analog scope, to enable the digital view of d2d through net, use the following simulation
command:
* dump -add *
In digital scope, to enable a2a through net dumping of the current in the analog view, use
the following simulation commands:
* Dump analog current signals
For example, dump -add * -i
* Dump the total current flow
For example, dump -add * -isub
* Dump analog current signals
For example, dump -add * -vaI

Debugging in Source Code Pane

In digital scope, to enable a2a through net dumping of the voltage in the analog view, use
the following simulation commands:
* Dump analog voltage signals
For example, dump -add * -v
* Dump analog voltage signals
For example, dump -add * -vaV

The [upfList] column appears in the IE table only when the information in the table includes
the UPF report.
The [upfList] includes the following columns:
* UPF Supply Net Vdd (upfSupplyNet_vdd)
* UPF Supply Net Vss (upfSupplyNet_vss)
* Vdd Group ID (VddGropupId)
* Vss Group ID (VssGroupId)
* UPF Supply Source Vdd (upfSupplySource_vdd)
* UPF Supply Source Vss (upfSupplySource_vss)

IE Property Table Functions
The IE table enables you to perform the following functions:
Jump to the nTrace or nSchema Window
The columns in the IE table that support jump to nTrace and nSchema windows are: node,
vdd, vss, top_net, dig_drv, and ana_port.
Click the hyperlink in the column to jump to the nTrace source window or the nSchema
window. This function is available only when the source window or the nTrace window is
open.
If you click a hyperlink when both nTrace source window and nSchema window
are open, then nSchema window becomes the active window.
Figure 52

Hyperlink to nSchema Window

Jump to the UPF File View
Click the hyperlink in the upfSupplyNet_vdd and upfSupplyNet_vss columns, to jump to
the supply net defined in the UPF file.
Click the hyperlink in the upfSupplySource_vdd and upfSupplySource_vss columns to
jump to the supply source and find the first string that matches with the content in the cell.

Figure 53

Hyperlink to the Supply Source in the UPF File

The Supply Source window does not support jump to the TCL command in the
UPF file view. Use the Search option to find and select the first Isd/vdd18 that
appears in the UPF file view.
Add to the nWave Window
Right-click a cell and select Add to waveform.

Figure 54

Menu to Add Waveform

If the signal is a Spice or Verilog signal, find and add all its dumped signals to
the waveform.
Add to the nWave feature is available in the columns: node, vdd, vss, top_net,
dig_drv, ana_port, upfSupplyNet_vdd, upfSupplyNet_vss, upfSupplySource_vdd, and
upfSupplySource_vss only and the table cell cannot be empty.
Create New Schematic
Right-click a cell, select New Schematic, and then select schematic type from the
submenu .

Verilog-AMS signals can be categorized into the following:
* Nodes: The current node should be different according to their position and usage in
the Source Code pane.
* Branches: There are two types of branches in Verilog-AMS, unnamed branch and
named branch. Adding signals for a branch is easier than for a node, as branches do
not have position-related issues.

Dumping of nWave Signals
When you drag-and-drop or right-click to add Verilog-AMS signals to nWave, it triggers the
dumping of the corresponding signals. The signals to be dumped and be added should be
same as drag-and-drop in post-simulation.
If a Verilog-AMS instance is a leaf, the dumper cannot selectively dump a specific port
current. That is, all nodes, current branch is dumped if you dump port current of leaf
Verilog-AMS instance.
In the stand-alone nWave window, IEs and through nettypes are displayed through the
information that the simulator dumped in the FSDB file on analog signals. For a2a, these
tags appear on both analog and digital signals, while other tags are shown only on analog
signals. Thus, the IEs and through nettype tag only label on the analog side signal.
* The n2n is dumped as d2d with the previous scenario.
* When signals are aliased to through net or IE, they contain a tag, even if
they are not through net or IEs.
* When signals are not aliased as through net or IE they do not have a tag,
even if they are through net or IE.

Supporting Unknown (X) and Inactive (Z) States for WReal Objects
nWave supports predefined nettypes that mimic Verilog-AMS wreal behavior. This enables
the use of both a nettype-based and wreal-based flows.
Accordingly, nWave supports Unknown and Inactive states shown as an X and a Z in 1bit, 4-state logic. These states are represented with wreals using the predefined macros
wrealXState and wrealZState.
Similar to WrealX and WrealZ signals, nWave also supports real (realX and realZ)
signals and displays them as shown in the following figure. If wrealXState is assigned to
a real object, it is shown as an X in the waveform. Also, if a wrealXState is assigned to a
real variable, it is shown as an X in the waveform. Also, if wrealZState is assigned to a
real variable, it is shown as a Z in the waveform.

In some scenarios, a debug session starts by adding the base signal to nWave. To debug

It is therefore difficult to find the block that you might want to debug. You can use the menu

as shown in the following figure:
The Show Focus Connection option traces the connections (driving instance to loading
instances with connecting net) of the selected net, port, or instance pin and summarizes
the results in the Show Focus Connection form as shown in the following figure.
This option is available in full hierarchical and flattened schematic windows. It is
not available in partial hierarchical windows.

Focus Connection form is automatically updated to display the new connection results.

updated automatically and the option must be invoked again.

Mapping Symbols and Models in nSchema
Verdi AMS allows you to define a symbol library (config file) for SPICE designs that maps
symbols with models, in a .csv format. You can then import this config file along with your
design into nSchema to map the model in your design with a specific symbol. You can also
define a symbol for an empty model of your design.
The config file format must define one model per line, as follows:
[SYMBOL_TYPE],[MODEL_NAME],[PIN1;PIN2;PIN3]

Where,
* SYMBOL_TYPE: Defines the symbol type. If the symbol type is not specified,
nSchema uses macro symbols as the default symbol. The SYMBOL_TYPE can be any
one of the types defined in Table 3.
* MODEL_NAME: Specifies the model names that you select as the special symbol in
nSchema.
* PIN: Specifies the PIN names of the user model. The PIN names and the total number
of PINs must be equal to the model definition. The PIN number decides the kind of
symbol that is shown in nSchema.
The following are examples of the mapping file entries:
NMOS,nch_mac_psp,D;G;S;B
NMOS,n_elvt_dnw_psp,D;G;S;B;ISO;SUBST
PMOS,pch_lvt_mac,D;G;S;B
RESISTOR,rm1w,PLUS;MINUS
PNP,pnp1d6_mis,C;B;E

After you have created the config file, use the following command to import it into
nSchema:
%spicom [filename.lvs] -lib TOP
%verdi -msv -spicetbl [filename.csv] -f [designfile]

nSchema loads this config file and creates a table for the design. If a model in the design
source code has the same name as the one in the mapping table, the model symbol is
replaced with the specific symbol from the table. The SYMBOL_TYPE and PIN number
decides the kind of symbol that is shown.
Reloading the design reloads the mapping file. Use the Save/Restore Session
option to keep the config table settings.

Save/Restore session keeps/imports the mapping file. The segment of session
file in under [hb] and the key word as follows:
spiceTblFile = filename(absolute path)

The direction of the symbol pin uses the rules of the current SPICE model pin
direction, if there are no other suggestions provided. The default pin direction is
inout.

You can debug in Verdi using WaveView as it offers state-of-the-art analog debugging
capability, and it also helps in analyzing measurements and calculator debugging
functions.

Prerequisites
Before invoking WaveView, you must perform the following steps:
1. Set the setenv NOVAS_WAVEVIEW_BETAenvironment variable.
2. Import your design with the -msv option.
3. Set the WaveView install directory using either of the following options:
Set the setenv NOVAS_WAVEVIEW_DIR $WaveViewInstallDir environment
variable.
Specify the Custom WaveView Installation Directory in the Preferences form as
shown in the figure Preference Setting for WaveView.

Figure 100

Preference Setting for WaveView

Invoking WaveView
To invoke WaveView, choose Tools -> Custom WaveView in nTrace and nWave as
shown in the figures WaveView for nTrace and WaveView for nWave respectively.
If you invoke WaveView without executing the prerequisites, a warning
message is displayed.

Figure 101

WaveView for nTrace

Figure 102

WaveView for nWave

You can also select WaveView from the toolbar item as shown in the figure WaveView
Toolbar Item:
Figure 103

WaveView Toolbar Item

After you select Custom WaveView in the menu, the WaveView tab is automatically
added and sets the layout to stack layout.
Standalone nWave does not support this feature.

Adding Signals to WaveView
To add selected signals to WaveView, right-click and select Add Signals to WaveView
command in nWave as shown in the figure Right-click Option in nWave:
Figure 104

Right-click Option in nWave

These menu options are only visible when the prerequisites are all set (as
mentioned in section Prerequisites) and a FSDB file is loaded in Verdi.

Invoking WaveView and Loading FSDB File Automatically
The Add Signals to WaveView command does not request you to invoke WaveView
or load FSDB file in WaveView first. It invokes WaveView automatically if you have not
invoked from Verdi. It also loads the corresponding FSDB file to WaveView.
After you have invoked WaveView and opened an FSDB file, you can add signals to it.
To add signals into WaveView, perform the following steps:
1. Check if WaveView has opened the target FSDB file. If not, open the target FSDB file.
2. Retrieve signals from the target FSDB file.
3. Add signals into the current active WaveView tab.
A new panel is opened for each signal added to WaveView. As shown in figure Add
Signals from Verdi to WaveView, two signals are added to WaveView. Therefore
two panels are created for each signal.
The current active WaveView tab does not allow adding new signals. In this case,
another WaveView tab is opened automatically.
For example, WaveView does not allow adding the X-Y axis panel to a WaveView
tab as it is in stack layout with non X-Y axis panels.
Figure 105

Add Signals from Verdi to WaveView

WaveView Tab Layout Limitation
WaveView supports various layouts to display its panels and it is not mandatory to change
the layout to stack layout. Due to this, the following limitations are applicable:
* The signals to be added may be inserted to the upper right column of the current panel
as shown in figure WaveView Layout Limitation.
* The time range between each panel may be different. Therefore, all the panels are
synced to the first X-Y axis panel in the current WaveView tab. This is explained
in more detail in section Synchronizing Cursor and Viewing Range From nWave to
WaveView.
Figure 106

WaveView Layout Limitation

Synchronizing Cursor and Viewing Range From nWave to
WaveView
nWave provides the Window -> Sync Waveform View option to sync view range and
cursor to the other nWave windows. This option is also applicable to WaveView if it is
already invoked by Verdi as shown in figure Updating WaveView Waveform in Verdi
Interactive Mode. This command is enabled only in the following scenarios:
* If more than one nWave or WaveView windows are invoked by Verdi.
* Window -> Sync Waveform View is disabled.

Tracing Signals in the Temporal Flow View

* Unidirectional connection from nWave to WaveView is available.
Figure 107

Menu Command to Sync View Range and Cursor to WaveView

Updating WaveView Waveform in Verdi Interactive Mode
This capability is only supported in the Verdi Interactive Mode. After you invoke this mode,
Verdi checks if the file is updated and requests WaveView to update all WaveView tabs in
the following scenarios:
* When the simulation time changes.
* When new signals or scopes get dumped.

The following are the limitations for this feature:
* WaveView updates the waveform only when the session is increased in the FSDB.
Therefore, it is still possible that the WaveView window does not get updated even if
Verdi requests for the update.
* WaveView updates the signal list only when the file is regenerated. Therefore, new
dumped signals cannot be added to WaveView unless you manually select the file in
WaveView and reload it using the right-click option Reload WDF Signal List.

Tracing Signals in the Temporal Flow View
To debug a design, you need to understand the structure and the behavior of the design.
Visualizing the structure and behavior of the design is very useful and convenient to
become familiar with the design and then debug it.
Temporal Flow View (TFV) provides flow views that are unique temporal views and
analysis tools that allow the visualization and analysis of the design's behavior through
time. TFV identifies and displays causal control and data paths - the registers and signals

Tracing Signals in the Temporal Flow View

that actually caused the erroneous value to occur - through multilevel combinational logic
within one or more register-to-register transfer stages.
TFV provides the following capabilities for the analysis of analog and digital signals:
* Traces digital signals and analog signals on the tracing path using Trace This Value
(cycle based) / Trace Triggering Path (transition based).
* Displays Interface Elements (IEs) and Through Nets (TNs), as shown in the following
figure:
Figure 108

IE and TN Elements in TFV

* Uses function blocks with specific labels to represent analog blocks on TFV. TFV does
not trace into the analog blocks; TFV only traces through analog blocks and uses a
specific label as analog blocks, as shown in the following figure (the green symbol is an
analog block symbol):
Figure 109

Tracing Through Analog Blocks in TFV

* Syncs with nWave, nTrace, and nSchema thereby showing the waveform, Source
Code pane, and circuit detail of digital and analog signals.
* Allows you to drag and drop (D&D) signals to nWave, nTrace, and nSchema, showing
the waveform, source code, and circuit, respectively.
For more information on TFV, see Chapter Temporal Flow View Tutorial in the Verdi User
Guide and Tutorial and Chapter Flow Views in the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference
Manual.

Mapping the Port Configuration
In AMS support for leading trace, the following options are available These options help
ensure accurate pass-through between different design languages, such as Verilog,
VHDL, and Spice.
In AMS designs, each block in the design can have definitions in more than one view. For
example, a block can have both SPICE and Verilog definitions. To select a particular view
of a multiview cell, use the mixed-signal options use_spice or use_verilog.
By default, mixed-signal simulation assumes that a multiview cell (for example, a cell with
Verilog and SPICE views) has the same number of ports and port names in both views.
But, if the number of ports or the names of the ports differ between the two views then
compilation errors are issued.

Mapping the Port Configuration

To resolve the port inconsistency problem between different views the port_map option of
the use_spice, use_verilog, or use_vhdl options must be used.
Also, to handle discrepancy in the number of ports (for example, if one view has extra
ports), you can use the port_connect option.
The following table describes the mixed-signal commands and their descriptions:
Command

Description

use_spice

Used to explicitly instruct the tool to use the SPICEview
of a multiview cell for a child cell under a Verilog or
VHDL parent.

use_verilog

Used to explicitly instruct the tool to use the Verilog view
of a multiview cell for a child cell under a SPICE parent.

use_vhdl

Used to select the VHDL view of a multiview cell
instantiated in a SPICE block.

The following figure shows how the port_map option works for Verilog parent modules with
SPICE submodule.
Figure 111

Port Mapping Example

The following table describes the category and the details used in the figure:
Category

Details

SPICE

.subckt inv a_0 a_1 b_0 b_1

HDL

module inv(x, y);
input [1:0] x;
input [1:0] y;

Instantiated

inv i1_inv(i, j);

Modifying the Analog Configuration During Runtime (Using ace reread)

Port Map

use_spice -cell inv \
-inst top.i1_inv \
port_map (y -> { a_0, b_1}, x -> {b_0, a_1});

Following are the different ways in which port mapping can be specified:
* use_spice -cell inv1 -inst top.x1 port_map (a => y, b => x);
* use_spice -cell inv2 -inst top.x2 port_map (* =>snps_by_name);
* use_spice -cell inv3 -inst top.x3 port_map (* =>snps_by_position);
* use_spice -cell inv4 -inst top.x4 port_map (* =>snps_open);
* use_spice -cell inv5 -inst top.x5
For more information about different ways of mapping the port, see the Port Mapping
section in the Mixed-Signal Simulation User Guide.

This feature has the following limitations:
* In the spice domain, the contributor analysis is limited. For example, the ports of
primitive devices are in/out port. Therefore, all the inst-ports are listed as contributors.
* For analog signals with continuous waveform, it is not possible to conduct active driver
analysis as the correct value fluctuates and cannot be determined. In this situation, the
status of drivers must be the possible drivers.

Modifying the Analog Configuration During Runtime (Using ace
reread)
Generally, it is required to re-compile, re-elaborate, and re-simulate after you modify
or adjust parameters or settings of a design. This change can happen frequently and
the process of simulating the design takes longer time. To reduce the simulation time,
CustomSim supports the interactive ucli command "ace reread". This enables you to
change the parameter or simulation settings during runtime with a SPICE design and
helps reduce the simulation time.
You can run the ace reread command in the Verdi Interactive Console to make
modifications to the analog configurations, such as simulation accuracy, temperature, or
limited aspects of a netlist during runtime (that is, during the simulation of a design).
For more information about the using the ace reread command in CustomSim, see the
Mixed-Signal Simulation User Guide.

Modifying the Analog Configuration During Runtime (Using ace reread)

Prerequisite
Requires CustomSim Version L-2016.06-SP2 or later.

Use Model
After compiling, elaborating, and simulating the design, load the design in the Verdi
interactive mode. You can open nWave and dump signals using the drag and drop options
and run the ace reread option as needed (refer to Figure: Executing ace reread in the
Interactive Console).
For information on how to open FSDB and load the signals in nWave, see section
Debugging in Waveform View.
Figure 112

Executing ace reread in the Interactive Console

After executing the ace reread option in the Interactive Console, the hierarchy in FSDB
file might change. The following situations might occur after the execution of ace reread:
* For additional signals dumped, the signals are reflected in FSDB after running ace ace
reread.
* For signals that disappear in the design, the signals and their value before the time
point still exists. However, no value is dumped after that time point when running ace
reread.
* For the existing signals, changed value is later appended on the original signal.

Modifying the Analog Configuration During Runtime (Using ace reread)

Example
Consider the waveform shown in Figure: New Signal v(i) Added and Signals v(zn) and
v(zn1) are Removed and Added Back Later, which depicts the configuration change during
runtime. To make this configuration change, in the Interactive Console, perform the
following steps:
1. Run the simulation for time 1000 using the following command:
SimCMD> run 1000

2. Remove v(zn) and v(zn1) from the design and add a new net i that has a voltage value
v(i).
3. Run the ace reread option:
SimCMD>ace reread

4. Again, run the simulation for time 1000 to progress the simulation for time 2000.
SimCMD> run 1000

5. Add v(zn) and v(zn1) back at time 2000. As the signals are removed from design at
time 1,000, there are no value changes dumped for these signals after time 1000.
Later, add the signals back as the signals that existed once are appended with the
value change on them starting from 2,000.
6. Run the ace reread option:
SimCMD>ace reread

Figure 113
Back Later

New Signal v(i) Added and Signals v(zn) and v(zn1) are Removed and Added

Tracing Results of Connect Modules in the AMS Designs

This feature has the following limitations:
* Adding or removing a hierarchy with this feature is not supported as the same is not
supported with CustomSim.
* Verdi does not reload the design to show the latest source code if you change the
source code when you use ace ace reread. The changes in simulation are only
reflected in the waveform.

Tracing Results of Connect Modules in the AMS Designs
In AMS designs, the connect modules are automatically inserted to connect the
continuous and discrete disciplines (mixed nets) of the design hierarchy together.
In leading trace, the results are passed through the connect module instance and lists the
result as shown in the following figure:
Figure 114

Traced Results for Connect Module

The behavior of tracing driver for the instrumented signal top.analog_clk__aicm is the
same as the original signal top.analog_clk, and the connect module information is listed
as shown in the figure.
The tracing feature for the signal under connect module is not supported.

IE_All_Only Option for MSV Common Dump
The +IE_All_Only option dumps both the analog and digital signal of all types of IEs, that
is d2a, a2d, n2e, e2n, r2e, and e2r.

The mixed-signal simulation supports multiple views for a cell, which may include both
digital and analog perspectives. At compile time, you can choose a single view for the cell.
This is called cell-based partitioning. You can also select specific instances of the cell. This
is known as instance-based partitioning. The selected view determines the master of the
respective instances when the design is elaborated. This selection cannot be changed
during the simulation, which is the limitation of the existing mixed-signal solution.
The Real-Time View Swapping (RTVS) feature addresses this limitation and lets you
switch between digital and analog views during simulation. You can select the analog
view for specific time windows to improve simulation accuracy. For other time periods, the
digital view runs, which helps maintain good overall simulation performance.
Using event-based RTVS configurations, you can use a control signal in the design to
choose various configurations at different time windows at runtime.

Licensing Requirements
To use an event-based RTVS configuration, you must have the Verdi Elite (verdi -elite)
or Verdi Apex (verdi -apex) license.

Use Model of Event-Based RTVS Configurations
In an even-based RTVS, switching views is selected by a logic signal or an integer
variable defined in the Verilog code. The signal or integer variable is identified by the
following command:
rtvs_option -sel_sig <signal_name>;

Where signal_name is the hierarchical path to the signal or integer variable. Only one
signal or integer variable can be used to control window switching.
The syntax of the rtvs_config command supports the sel_val option that determines
the signal value or integer value that selects each RTVS configuration.
The syntax of the rtvs_config command is as follows:
rtvs_config -sel_val <value> [-icfile <icfile_name>] [-sim_opt
<file_name>] -control <control_file_name> -label "<config_label>";

Arguments
-sel_val <value>

Defines the signal value or integer value associated with the mixed-signal configuration
defined in the command. The signal can be from the Verilog netlist, or SPICE netlist that is

accessed through XMR. The signal can only be of logic type with value 1b'0, 1b'1, 1b'x, or
1b'z. Any integer value equal or bigger than 0 is acceptable.
-icfile <icfile_name>

(Optional) You should use this option with care because it affects all windows created by
the events. You can specify the initial values of the window using this option.
-sim_opt <file_name>

(Optional) You should use this option with care because it affects all windows created by
the events. You can change analog simulation settings using this option.
-control <control_file_name>

This local control file defines the new configuration for specific blocks using use_spice,
use_verilog. and related commands. This configuration also inherits the blocks that are
defined in the default configuration by the main control file. In case of conflicts, commands
in the local control file override the ones in the main control file.
-label "<config_label>"

Specifies a configuration label for the new configuration. The Verilog testbench uses this
label to identify and manage differences in circuit structures and cross-module references
between configurations. The use of this option for each rtvs_config command is
mandatory, and each label must be unique (not used in another rtvs_config command).

Example

simulation switches between two configurations.

The rtvs_option -sel_sig option identifies the logic signal top.ctrl in the Verilog

The RTVS Hierarchy Checker is a feature in Verdi that analyzes and compares the
hierarchical structure of digital and analog views in a mixed-signal design. This feature is
essential for ensuring accurate state transfer between digital and analog domains during
RTVS simulation. Structural mismatches between these views can cause simulation
failures, making it difficult to identify problematic cells manually. The Hierarchy Checker
automates this process, helping you to detect and resolve mismatches before running
RTVS simulations.

Licensing Requirements
To use hierarchy checking for RTVS qualification, you must have the Verdi Elite (verdi
-elite) or Verdi Apex (verdi -apex) license.

Accessing and Using the RTVS Hierarchy Checker
Accessing the Hierarchy Checker
To access the Hierarchy Checker:
1. In the Instance pane, select an analog node in the hierarchy tree.
2. Right-click the node and choose RTVS Hierarchy Checker.
Alternatively, you can access Hierarchy Checker from Tools > AMS > RTVS Hierarchy
Checker option.
The RTVS Hierarchy Checker menu is available only in RTVS flow.
The following figure shows the RTVS Hierarchy Checker form.
Figure 123

RTVS Hierarchy Checker Form

The find and filter functionality synchronizes with Preferences > General> Find/Filter >
Find/Filter Options. For more information, see the Find/Filter Page section in Preference
chapter of the Verdi(R) and Siloti(R) Command Reference Guide.

. You can modify the match case behavior flowing from the Preferences window by
selecting the Match Case option.

Configuring the Hierarchy Checker
To configure the Hierarchy Checker, perform the following steps:
1. Cells to Check: Enter the names of cells to check for mismatches, separated by
commas. Leave this field empty to check all RTVS switching cells in the design. A
placeholder Empty to Check All Cells indicates this option. You can also select cells
from the drop-down list. Wildcards are not supported.
2. Cells to Ignore: Enter the names of cells to skip during checking, separated by
commas. Wildcards are not supported.
3. Ports to Ignore: Specify ports to ignore in the format cell_name(port_name).
Separate multiple ports with commas, and also separate multiple
cell_name(port_name) pairs with commas.
4. Skip Encrypted Cells: Select this option to ignore encrypted cells during checking. By
default, this option is enabled.
5. Stop if Find First Mismatched Cell: Select this option to stop checking after the first
mismatch is found. By default, this option is enabled.
To run the mismatch analysis, click the Check button.

Reviewing Mismatch Results
The results of the mismatch analysis appear in the Cells and Detail panes as shown in
the following figure:
Figure 124

RTVS Hierarchy Checker Showing the Mismatch Results

* The Cells pane lists cells with mismatches, including descendant cells.
For descendant cells, the ancestor cell hierarchy appears in braces (for example,
cell21(cell0.cell11)).
Use the Cells Filter field to filter the list of cells displayed in the Cells pane.
* The Detail pane provides detailed information about each mismatch.
Click a cell node (for example, cell21) to display all mismatch details. Click a specific
mismatch type (for example, port mismatch) to filter and view only those details.
You can select multiple mismatch types (for example, port and node) for combined
details. However, multi-cell selection is not supported.
Select a port or signal to highlight its definition in the Source View pane.

Exporting Results
To save the mismatch results to a local file, click Export. If a filter is applied, only filtered
results are exported.

Using Drag and Drop
You can drag cells from the Cells pane or port/node/instance names from the Detail pane
and drop them into the Cells to Check or Cell to Ignore fields for quick configuration.

Comparison Rules
The comparison rules used to identify mismatches are as follows:
* Case Sensitivity: The checker applies case sensitivity based on the language (For
example, case-sensitive for Verilog/Spectre, case-insensitive for VHDL/SPICE).
* Bus Format Expansion: The checker accounts for bus signals that might be
expanded differently in digital and analog netlists.
For example,
Signal[0:7] signal[0] , signal[1],
Signal[0:7] signal_0, signal_1,

* Port Matching: The checker considers port mapping specified in use_spice or
use_verilog commands.
For example, if the command use_spice -cell cell21 port_map (A=>in1,
B=in2, Y=>out); is in Init file, then port mismatch should not be reported.

* X-prefix Resolution: An instance in the analog view includes an x prefix, whereas its
corresponding instance in the digital view does not have this prefix. The checker uses
the resolve_x_inst_prefix command to match analog instances with an x prefix to
their digital counterparts.
For example, an instance in analog view has the name top.dut.xi1, whereas its
digital counterpart is top.dut.i1.

When you use this command, the hierarchy checker first verifies whether the instance
names in the analog and digital views are the same. If the names match, no further
action is required. If they do not match, the hierarchy checker removes the x prefix
from the analog instance name and attempts to match the names again.
* XMR Differences: The checker reports cross-module reference (XMR) differences for
RTVS instances.

Tcl Command to Add RTVS Hierarchy Checker
To add the RTVS Hierarchy checker, use the following Tcl command:
rtvsHierChecker

The syntax of the rtvsHierChecker command is as follows:
rtvsHierChecker -open|close [ -ignoreCell cell1,cell2,] [ -checkCell
cell1,cell2,] [-ignorePort cell1(port1,port2), cell2(port3,port3),]
[-ignoreEncrypted on|off] [-stopIfFind -on|off] [ -startCompare]
[ -pattern string] [ -export text.txt ]

Arguments
-open|-close

Open or close RTVS Hierarchy Checker form.
-checkCell

Set cells to check in finding mismatches.
-ignoreCell

Set cells to ignore in finding mismatches.
-ignorePort

Set ports to ignore in finding mismatches.
-ignoreEncrypted

Set ignore encrypted cell in finding mismatches.
-stopIfFind

Set to stop if find first mismatch.
-startCompare

Start to find mismatches.

Donut Configuration Support in RTVS

-pattern

Apply filter on found results.
-export

Export found results to file.

Example
rtvsHierChecker -open
rtvsHierChecker -ignoreCell cell1,cell2 -ignorePort cell1(port1,port2),
cell2(port3,port3) -ignoreEncrypted on -stopIfFind off -startCompare
rtvsHierChecker -pattern "*A*"
rtvsHierChecker -export "mismatches.txt"

The following are the limitations of RTVS Hierarchy Checker:
* Parameters are not supported in the swapping modules.
* Structural, union, enum, and interface signals are not supported in the swapping
modules.
* Wildcards or bus mapping specified in the port_map option of xa.init file are not
supported.

Donut Configuration Support in RTVS
RTVS is a feature that enables you switch between analog and digital views of selected
circuit blocks during simulation. This helps you balance simulation performance and
accuracy by using high-accuracy analog simulation only when needed. RTVS supports
both Verilog-top and SPICE-top flows and works with donut and non-donut partitioning.

Licensing Requirements
For supporting donut configuration in RTVS, you must have the Verdi Elite (verdi
-elite) or Verdi Apex (verdi -apex) license. In addition to the license, you also need the
add-on key RTVS-Debug.

Setting Up RTVS Instances
RTVS technology uses RTVS instances to represent circuit blocks that can switch
between digital and analog views during simulation. Each RTVS instance shows both

Donut Configuration Support in RTVS

digital and analog views of a circuit block. However, only one view is active and simulated
at a time.
When you set up RTVS, Verdi reviews the circuit structure and:
* Creates an RTVS instance for each circuit block that might need to switch views. For
time-based RTVS, the tool sets view switching windows and switching happens for
those blocks. For event-based RTVS, switching depends on control signal events.
Even if switching does not happen, RTVS instances are still created to support possible
future switching.
* Does not create RTVS instances for circuit blocks that do not switch views.

Viewing the RTVS Status in Verdi

The AMS Profile View in Verdi provides a comprehensive dashboard for visualizing and
analyzing AMS profiling data. You can use this feature to find performance issues and
improve AMS flows. It shows the activity of design blocks and instances over set time
periods. With this dashboard, you can make better choices to boost performance and
efficiency in your AMS designs.

Licensing Requirements
To access the AMS Profile View feature, you must have the Verdi Elite (verdi -elite) or
Verdi Apex (verdi -apex) license.

Accessing AMS Profile View
You can access the AMS Profile View through the Verdi GUI.
To access AMS Profile View through Verdi GUI, choose Tools > AMS > AMS Profile.
This opens the singleton AMS Profile View window as shown in the following figure.

Figure 125

AMS Profile View Window

Opening the AMS Profile Directory
To open the AMS Profile Directory in Verdi, choose to File > Open and select the AMS
profile directory.
If the directory is invalid, the following warning message appears:
Failed to open AMS profile database at /path/to/profile_dir !

The directory must contain only two files with the suffix .profiler.fsdb in the selected
folder.
The two files must share the prefix and different suffixes: .inst.profiler.fsdb and
.subckt.profiler.fsdb

Configuring the Time Range
You can specify a time range for analyzing the AMS profile data. To set the start and end
time, perform the following steps:
1. Enter start time in the From textbox. The default time is 0.
2. Enter end time in the To textbox. The default time is the end of FSDB time range.
3. Adjust the Slider to select a time range. The slider synchronizes with the From and To
boxes.
The time unit matches the FSDB file dumped by the simulator.

Exploring the AMS Profile View Components
The components of the AMS Profile View are as follows:
* Instance Tree
* Top Active Instances/Subcircuits Table
* Top Active Instances/Subcircuits Line Chart

Instance Tree
This component displays a hierarchical view of instances with following columns:
* Instance: The name of the instance.
* Cumulative Sim Cost: The total simulation cost accumulated for each instance.
* Cumulative Sim Cost %: The percentage of the total accumulated simulation cost
relative to the overall performance.
By default, the first analog instance is selected and expanded two levels deep.
You can use the search pane or find bar to locate instances. Drag and drop is supported
for instance management. Sorting is not supported in the instance tree.
To accurately identify the top N instances, the traversal only extends downward to a
maximum of two levels in the hierarchy. As a result, the reported top N instances may not
truly reflect the highest instances. You can adjust the traversal level by configuring the
following environment variable:
setenv VERDI_AMS_PROFILER_TOP_N_TRAVERSE_LEVEL <level>

Top Active Instances/Subcircuits Table
This table provides insights into the most resource-intensive instances or subcircuits,
featuring the following columns:
* Instance/Subckt Name: The name of the instance or subcircuit.
* Cumulative Sim Cost: The total simulation cost for the instance/subcircuit.
* Cumulative Sim Cost %:The percentage of total simulation cost.
The Cumulative Sim Cost % column shows a value only for SPICE instances and
only within the selected instance. If you select a SPICE instance, this column displays
100%. If you select a non-SPICE instance, the column is empty. Instances outside the
selected instance also show empty values.

* Visible: A checkbox that determines whether the instance/subcircuit is displayed in the
corresponding line chart. By default, the checkbox is selected..
Single selection highlights the corresponding curve in the line chart.

Top Active Instances/Subcircuits Line Chart
This visual representation allows you to see the performance trends of the top active
instances or subcircuits over time.
The data for instances line chart depends on the instance tree selection and time range.
The data for subcircuits line chart does not depend on instance tree selection. However, it
depends on the time range.
The line chart provides the following information:
* Visualizes the top N expensive instances/subcircuits.
The default top N value is 3 and you can adjust the value up to 50. To increase the
limit, set the following environment variable.
setenv VERDI_AMS_PROFILER_TOP_N_THRESHOLD <desired_value>

* Supports display of accumulated or instantaneous values. From the Display Graphic
View With drop-down list, select the value type.
Accumulated value mode refers to the total or cumulative value of a measurement over
a specified period. It aggregates data points to provide a comprehensive view of the
total amount or sum of a particular variable.
Instantaneous value mode captures the delta in value between two points in time. It
provides a snapshot of the variable being measured, reflecting its current state without
any aggregation.

Designs
This chapter describes how to debug Verilog-A designs in the Interactive Debug mode.
Use the following capabilities for interactive simulation debug of Verilog-A mixed-signal
designs:

Compiling Mixed-Signal Design
Verdi only provides the Import Design from Library feature to load your mixed-signal
design into the Verdi platform. Therefore, you must compile your design using the Verdi
KDB with both digital and analog hierarchy/signals. The spicom utility allows you to
compile the analog modules.
The following section describes how to compile your Verilog-A design with the spicom
utility and how to load KDB into Verdi.

Compiling Verilog-A Blocks
To compile Verilog-A files with VCS, instantiate the Verilog-A module in a SPICE file.
Use this SPICE file to compile with the VCS and CustomSim simulator. For compiling the
SPICE designs, see Compiling and Importing a SPICE Design and Compiling With the
SPICE Unified Front-End Flow.
In a mixed-signal simulation, Verilog-A can be used as the analog view of a cell. Use
the .hdl command in the SPICE netlist to read Verilog-A files. In this flow, passing all

Verilog files, including Verilog-A to VCS at compile time is still possible although not
recommended. For more information about Verilog-A model instantiation, see the MixedSignal Simulation User Guide.
Limitation
With Verilog-A model instantiation, the KDB design hierarchy generates at compile time.
Verdi does not support analog simulator commands, such as set_va_view and .param
HSIMUSEVA=<module name>, to switch between SPICE and Verilog-A views during
simulation.

Performing Interactive Simulation Debug of Verilog-A
Mixed-Signal Design
After you compile your Verilog-A mixed-signal design, you can interactively debug it in
Verdi. Verilog-A Interactive Debug mode supports the following features for Verilog-A
designs:
* Provides various methods to dump the following Verilog-A signals:
Variables
Voltage and current of nodes (you can dump current if you use current in your
design).
Voltage and current of unnamed/named branches (you can dump current if you use
current in your design).
For more information about Verilog-A signal dumping, see Dumping Verilog-A Signals.
* Shows the following values in the annotation of Verilog-A signals in the interactive
debug mode:
Variable's value
Voltage of node and unnamed/named branch
* Shows Verilog-A signals in the interactive Watch tab.
* Saves/restores the simulation session/state.
* Waveform to save/restore a signal .rc file with Verilog-A signals in the form of V()
being dumped and restored.
The following sections describe the supported interactive simulation debug features:
* Getting Started
* Setting the Simulator Type in the Preference Page

* Using the Interactive Watch Tab
* Annotating Values
* Dumping Verilog-A Signals

Getting Started
Verdi supports the Verilog-A interactive debug mode with this enhancement. The user flow
is as follows:
1. Prepare the AMS design with Verilog-A.
2. Set the XA_HOME, VERDI_HOME, and VCS_HOME environment variables. Compile the
Verilog-A AMS design using VCS to generate a simulation executable with debug
capability. For more information, see the document of VCS/CustomSim/PLI.
3. Use Verdi to load the Verilog-A design with the cosim option, which you can specify
using the following methods:
Specify -msv when importing the design from the command line.
In nTrace, select File -> Import Design From library -> Options toggle on the
Cosim Debug command and load the Verilog-A design.
4. Select Simulation -> Invoke Simulator.
Verdi creates and opens a single FSDB to include the digital and analog signals dumped
by the FSDB dumper.
You can use AMS interactive debug with the Verilog-A design. The simulation runs
under VCS simulator control. When you run Verilog-A AMS interactive debug, VCS and
CustomSim impose some limitations.
* Does not support step or next into analog design.
* Breakpoints cannot be added into analog design.
* Rewind is blocked in the AMS interactive debug mode.
These limitations disable some menu commands and right-click menu options.
For more information on the Simulation and Interactive Debug commands, see the Verdi
Command Reference Guide.

Using the Interactive Watch Tab
The interactive Watch tab supports to show Verilog-A signals that include variable,
electrical nodes (electrical, voltage, and current), and branch at the current simulation
time. The Interactive Watch tab displays the variable's values and the voltage of electrical
nodes and branches at the current simulation time.

The Watch tab provides the following information about analog variables:

Unnamed branch, displayed in the (a,b) format.
* Value: Variable (Shown as variable's value) Node, unnamed/named branch, that is,
shows the voltage value at the current simulation time. For example, 3.30V.

You can turn on the source view annotation using the Source -> Active Annotation

voltage value is shown as 3.30V.

The variable, node, and branch values are displayed as shown in the following figure:
Figure 128

Active Annotation

* Changing the analog format and precision in annotation is not supported.

currently supported in simulator.

* Mathematic types such as 'real', 'integer', 'parameter' and 'genvar' cannot be added to

simulator does not dump signal, such as I(<a>) in FSDB, it dumps isub(a) or

Tracing Verilog-A Designs in the Temporal Flow View
To debug a design, you must understand the structure and the behavior of the design.
Visualizing the structure and behavior of the design helps you become familiar with the
design and simplifies the debugging process.
Temporal Flow View (TFV) provides flow views that are unique temporal views
and analysis tools that allow the visualization and analysis of the design's behavior
through time. TFV identifies the control and data paths that led to an error, including the
specific registers and signals involved. It traces these paths through multiple levels of
combinational logic across one or more register-to-register transfer stages.
TFV provides the following capabilities for the analysis of analog and digital signals and
are described in the following sections:
* Traces digital signals and analog signals on the tracing path using Trace This Value
(cycle based) / Trace Triggering Path (transition based).
* Displays Interface Elements (IEs) and Through Nets (TNs).
* Uses function blocks with specific labels to represent analog blocks on TFV. TFV does
not trace into the analog blocks. TFV only traces through analog blocks and uses a
specific label as analog blocks (the green symbol is an analog block symbol).

Tracing Verilog-A Designs in the Temporal Flow View

* Synchronize with nWave, nTrace, and nSchema, thereby showing the waveform,
source code, and circuit detail of digital and analog signals.
* Allows you to drag and drop signals to nWave, nTrace, and nSchema, showing the
waveform, source code, and circuit, respectively.
For more information about creating TFV, see Chapter Temporal Flow View Tutorial in the
Verdi User Guide and Tutorial and Chapter Flow Views in the Verdi and Siloti Command
Reference Manual.

Tracing Verilog-A Signals
The tracing rules of Verilog-A signals are the same as digital tracing rules. Both cyclebased and transition-based tracing are available for tracing analog blocks. The following
figure shows the process of tracing a digital signal, while a Verilog-A signal exists in the
tracing path.
Figure 142

Tracing a digital signal and reaching a Verilog-A signal with IE reports

The following figure shows TFV tracing without IE ports.
Figure 143

Tracing a digital signal and reaching a Verilog-A signal without IE reports

The snap time of Verilog-A blocks are same as their digital outputs. The detailed VerilogA circuits are not displayed in TFV. Alternatively, you can trace to analog circuits using
the schematic view in nSchema. You can later use the synchronization button in the TFV
toolbar (see Synchronization With nWave, nTrace, and nSchema).

Tracing Verilog-A Designs in the Temporal Flow View

If SPICE signals are in Verilog-A's modules, the symbols for the function blocks
is VA instead of SPICE.

Creating Verilog-A Signals in TFV
Creating TFV for Verilog-A signals is similar to creating TFV for a digital black box. TFV
uses function blocks with the specific word "VA" to represent Verilog-A signals. The analog
blocks are shown in green in TFV.
The following figure shows the initial window for generating TFV for a Verilog-A signal. If
an internal analog signal is selected for creating TFV, an output analog signal is mapped.
For example, if a signal in the analog block is not defined as an input or output, an output
pin within the same scope is automatically mapped. This allows the internal signal to be
displayed correctly during final viewing (see Figure: Verilog-A Block in TFV).
Figure 144

Verilog-A Block in TFV

to nWave, nTrace, and nSchema. The figure Synchronization from TFV shows the

You can drag and drop Verilog-A signals to nWave, nTrace, and nSchema. When you drag
Verilog-A signals from nWave, nTrace, and nSchema, TFV adds the dragged signals as
reference signals and shows the respective analog blocks.

Force debug for Verilog-A signals
TFV does not display any information about internal signals of analog modules, so the
force debug information of analog internal signals is not displayed in TFV.

Limitation
TFV cannot trace into analog instances. Also, tracing the internal signals of analog blocks
is not supported. If you create TFV for the internal signals, TFV is created with an outmost signal instead of the internal signals. Detail structures can be found by toggling up
the sync button of nSchema. That is, you can trace through analog blocks and see the
structural details if required.

Known Problems and Limitations
* For spicom
The spicom utility does not support inline subckt for Spectre format.
The spicom utility does not fully support global net. Trace connective feature is not
supported for global nets.
The spicom utility does not fully support global parameter, such as showing the
definition feature.
The port_map option for the use_verilog, use_spice, and use_vhdl commands
is not supported.
* For AMS virtual FSDB file
The digital FSDB file should be set as the master file which is the first FSDB file in
the virtual file.
Verdi only supports the virtual file that contains one digital FSDB file and one analog
FSDB file for AMS debugging.
If there are some scopes with the same name and different letter cases in the digital
FSDB file, the referenced scope in digital FSDB for merging the analog FSDB file is
randomly chosen.
* For nWave
Case Issue
For example, Signal A and v(a) are dumped in Verilog scope.
Drag-and-Drop and synchronize the selection may not work correctly for v(a) since
the signal name in the design is A.
* For nScehma
TFV related features are not supported for value types signals.
* For AMS debug
The Rebuild and Restart flow is not supported in Mixed Signal Verification flow.
* Support for editing the Interface Elements (IE) in Verilog-AMS

Chapter 5: Known Problems and Limitations

The runtime interface elements and inout interface elements are not supported.
* Support for Verilog-AMS in Verdi
You cannot add node current of the primitive device in Verilog-AMS instance.
For example, if the following statement is available in Verilog-AMS resistor
#(.r(10k)) R2 (b, gnd); then the annotation for b or gnd signals are not
displayed and are unable to add node current when drag-and-drop b or gnd signals
to waveform.
Since XA cannot dump voltage for unnamed branch, it is not recognized in nWave.
Unnamed branch does not support DND from nWave to design-based AP.
You cannot dump "single" port current if a Verilog-AMS instance is leaf instance.
You cannot dump voltage of unnamed branch.

Mapping the Port Configuration
In AMS support for leading trace, the following options are available These options help
ensure accurate pass-through between different design languages, such as Verilog,
VHDL, and Spice.
In AMS designs, each block in the design can have definitions in more than one view. For
example, a block can have both SPICE and Verilog definitions. To select a particular view
of a multiview cell, use the mixed-signal options use_spice or use_verilog.
By default, mixed-signal simulation assumes that a multiview cell (for example, a cell with
Verilog and SPICE views) has the same number of ports and port names in both views.
But, if the number of ports or the names of the ports differ between the two views then
compilation errors are issued.

Mapping the Port Configuration

To resolve the port inconsistency problem between different views the port_map option of
the use_spice, use_verilog, or use_vhdl options must be used.
Also, to handle discrepancy in the number of ports (for example, if one view has extra
ports), you can use the port_connect option.
The following table describes the mixed-signal commands and their descriptions:
Command

Description

use_spice

Used to explicitly instruct the tool to use the SPICEview
of a multiview cell for a child cell under a Verilog or
VHDL parent.

use_verilog

Used to explicitly instruct the tool to use the Verilog view
of a multiview cell for a child cell under a SPICE parent.

use_vhdl

Used to select the VHDL view of a multiview cell
instantiated in a SPICE block.

Modifying the Analog Configuration During Runtime (Using ace

Generally, it is required to re-compile, re-elaborate, and re-simulate after you modify
or adjust parameters or settings of a design. This change can happen frequently and
the process of simulating the design takes longer time. To reduce the simulation time,
CustomSim supports the interactive ucli command "ace reread". This enables you to
change the parameter or simulation settings during runtime with a SPICE design and
helps reduce the simulation time.
You can run the ace reread command in the Verdi Interactive Console to make
modifications to the analog configurations, such as simulation accuracy, temperature, or
limited aspects of a netlist during runtime (that is, during the simulation of a design).
For more information about the using the ace reread command in CustomSim, see the
Mixed-Signal Simulation User Guide.

The mixed-signal simulation supports multiple views for a cell, which may include both
digital and analog perspectives. At compile time, you can choose a single view for the cell.
This is called cell-based partitioning. You can also select specific instances of the cell. This
is known as instance-based partitioning. The selected view determines the master of the
respective instances when the design is elaborated. This selection cannot be changed
during the simulation, which is the limitation of the existing mixed-signal solution.
The Real-Time View Swapping (RTVS) feature addresses this limitation and lets you
switch between digital and analog views during simulation. You can select the analog
view for specific time windows to improve simulation accuracy. For other time periods, the
digital view runs, which helps maintain good overall simulation performance.
Using event-based RTVS configurations, you can use a control signal in the design to
choose various configurations at different time windows at runtime.

Licensing Requirements
To use an event-based RTVS configuration, you must have the Verdi Elite (verdi -elite)
or Verdi Apex (verdi -apex) license.

Use Model of Event-Based RTVS Configurations
In an even-based RTVS, switching views is selected by a logic signal or an integer
variable defined in the Verilog code. The signal or integer variable is identified by the
following command:
rtvs_option -sel_sig <signal_name>;

Where signal_name is the hierarchical path to the signal or integer variable. Only one
signal or integer variable can be used to control window switching.
The syntax of the rtvs_config command supports the sel_val option that determines
the signal value or integer value that selects each RTVS configuration.
The syntax of the rtvs_config command is as follows:
rtvs_config -sel_val <value> [-icfile <icfile_name>] [-sim_opt
<file_name>] -control <control_file_name> -label "<config_label>";

title: 3 Pins
text:
Defines the signal value or integer value associated with the mixed-signal configuration
defined in the command. The signal can be from the Verilog netlist, or SPICE netlist that is

accessed through XMR. The signal can only be of logic type with value 1b'0, 1b'1, 1b'x, or
1b'z. Any integer value equal or bigger than 0 is acceptable.
-icfile <icfile_name>

(Optional) You should use this option with care because it affects all windows created by
the events. You can specify the initial values of the window using this option.
-sim_opt <file_name>

(Optional) You should use this option with care because it affects all windows created by
the events. You can change analog simulation settings using this option.
-control <control_file_name>

This local control file defines the new configuration for specific blocks using use_spice,
use_verilog. and related commands. This configuration also inherits the blocks that are
defined in the default configuration by the main control file. In case of conflicts, commands
in the local control file override the ones in the main control file.
-label "<config_label>"

Specifies a configuration label for the new configuration. The Verilog testbench uses this
label to identify and manage differences in circuit structures and cross-module references
between configurations. The use of this option for each rtvs_config command is
mandatory, and each label must be unique (not used in another rtvs_config command).

The RTVS Hierarchy Checker is a feature in Verdi that analyzes and compares the
hierarchical structure of digital and analog views in a mixed-signal design. This feature is
essential for ensuring accurate state transfer between digital and analog domains during
RTVS simulation. Structural mismatches between these views can cause simulation
failures, making it difficult to identify problematic cells manually. The Hierarchy Checker
automates this process, helping you to detect and resolve mismatches before running
RTVS simulations.

Licensing Requirements
To use hierarchy checking for RTVS qualification, you must have the Verdi Elite (verdi
-elite) or Verdi Apex (verdi -apex) license.

Accessing and Using the RTVS Hierarchy Checker
Accessing the Hierarchy Checker
To access the Hierarchy Checker:
1. In the Instance pane, select an analog node in the hierarchy tree.
2. Right-click the node and choose RTVS Hierarchy Checker.
Alternatively, you can access Hierarchy Checker from Tools > AMS > RTVS Hierarchy
Checker option.
The RTVS Hierarchy Checker menu is available only in RTVS flow.
The following figure shows the RTVS Hierarchy Checker form.
Figure 123

RTVS Hierarchy Checker Form

The find and filter functionality synchronizes with Preferences > General> Find/Filter >
Find/Filter Options. For more information, see the Find/Filter Page section in Preference
chapter of the Verdi(R) and Siloti(R) Command Reference Guide.

. You can modify the match case behavior flowing from the Preferences window by
selecting the Match Case option.

Configuring the Hierarchy Checker
To configure the Hierarchy Checker, perform the following steps:
1. Cells to Check: Enter the names of cells to check for mismatches, separated by
commas. Leave this field empty to check all RTVS switching cells in the design. A
placeholder Empty to Check All Cells indicates this option. You can also select cells
from the drop-down list. Wildcards are not supported.
2. Cells to Ignore: Enter the names of cells to skip during checking, separated by
commas. Wildcards are not supported.
3. Ports to Ignore: Specify ports to ignore in the format cell_name(port_name).
Separate multiple ports with commas, and also separate multiple
cell_name(port_name) pairs with commas.
4. Skip Encrypted Cells: Select this option to ignore encrypted cells during checking. By
default, this option is enabled.
5. Stop if Find First Mismatched Cell: Select this option to stop checking after the first
mismatch is found. By default, this option is enabled.
To run the mismatch analysis, click the Check button.

* Port Matching: The checker considers port mapping specified in use_spice or
use_verilog commands.
For example, if the command use_spice -cell cell21 port_map (A=>in1,

title: 3 Pins
text:
* X-prefix Resolution: An instance in the analog view includes an x prefix, whereas its
corresponding instance in the digital view does not have this prefix. The checker uses
the resolve_x_inst_prefix command to match analog instances with an x prefix to
their digital counterparts.
For example, an instance in analog view has the name top.dut.xi1, whereas its
digital counterpart is top.dut.i1.

When you use this command, the hierarchy checker first verifies whether the instance
names in the analog and digital views are the same. If the names match, no further
action is required. If they do not match, the hierarchy checker removes the x prefix
from the analog instance name and attempts to match the names again.
* XMR Differences: The checker reports cross-module reference (XMR) differences for
RTVS instances.

Tcl Command to Add RTVS Hierarchy Checker
To add the RTVS Hierarchy checker, use the following Tcl command:
rtvsHierChecker

The syntax of the rtvsHierChecker command is as follows:
rtvsHierChecker -open|close [ -ignoreCell cell1,cell2,] [ -checkCell
cell1,cell2,] [-ignorePort cell1(port1,port2), cell2(port3,port3),]
[-ignoreEncrypted on|off] [-stopIfFind -on|off] [ -startCompare]
[ -pattern string] [ -export text.txt ]

Arguments
-open|-close

Open or close RTVS Hierarchy Checker form.
-checkCell

Set cells to check in finding mismatches.
-ignoreCell

Set cells to ignore in finding mismatches.
-ignorePort

Set ports to ignore in finding mismatches.
-ignoreEncrypted

Set ignore encrypted cell in finding mismatches.
-stopIfFind

Set to stop if find first mismatch.
-startCompare

Start to find mismatches.

Donut Configuration Support in RTVS

-pattern

Apply filter on found results.
-export

Export found results to file.

rtvsHierChecker -open
rtvsHierChecker -ignoreCell cell1,cell2 -ignorePort cell1(port1,port2),
cell2(port3,port3) -ignoreEncrypted on -stopIfFind off -startCompare
rtvsHierChecker -pattern "*A*"
rtvsHierChecker -export "mismatches.txt"

supported.

Donut Configuration Support in RTVS
RTVS is a feature that enables you switch between analog and digital views of selected
circuit blocks during simulation. This helps you balance simulation performance and
accuracy by using high-accuracy analog simulation only when needed. RTVS supports
both Verilog-top and SPICE-top flows and works with donut and non-donut partitioning.

Licensing Requirements
For supporting donut configuration in RTVS, you must have the Verdi Elite (verdi
-elite) or Verdi Apex (verdi -apex) license. In addition to the license, you also need the
add-on key RTVS-Debug.

Setting Up RTVS Instances
RTVS technology uses RTVS instances to represent circuit blocks that can switch
between digital and analog views during simulation. Each RTVS instance shows both

Donut Configuration Support in RTVS

digital and analog views of a circuit block. However, only one view is active and simulated
at a time.
When you set up RTVS, Verdi reviews the circuit structure and:
* Creates an RTVS instance for each circuit block that might need to switch views. For
time-based RTVS, the tool sets view switching windows and switching happens for
those blocks. For event-based RTVS, switching depends on control signal events.
Even if switching does not happen, RTVS instances are still created to support possible
future switching.
* Does not create RTVS instances for circuit blocks that do not switch views.

The AMS Profile View in Verdi provides a comprehensive dashboard for visualizing and
analyzing AMS profiling data. You can use this feature to find performance issues and
improve AMS flows. It shows the activity of design blocks and instances over set time
periods. With this dashboard, you can make better choices to boost performance and
efficiency in your AMS designs.

Licensing Requirements
To access the AMS Profile View feature, you must have the Verdi Elite (verdi -elite) or
Verdi Apex (verdi -apex) license.

Accessing AMS Profile View
You can access the AMS Profile View through the Verdi GUI.
To access AMS Profile View through Verdi GUI, choose Tools > AMS > AMS Profile.
This opens the singleton AMS Profile View window as shown in the following figure.

Figure 125

AMS Profile View Window

Opening the AMS Profile Directory
To open the AMS Profile Directory in Verdi, choose to File > Open and select the AMS
profile directory.
If the directory is invalid, the following warning message appears:
Failed to open AMS profile database at /path/to/profile_dir !

The directory must contain only two files with the suffix .profiler.fsdb in the selected
folder.
The two files must share the prefix and different suffixes: .inst.profiler.fsdb and
.subckt.profiler.fsdb

Configuring the Time Range
You can specify a time range for analyzing the AMS profile data. To set the start and end
time, perform the following steps:
1. Enter start time in the From textbox. The default time is 0.
2. Enter end time in the To textbox. The default time is the end of FSDB time range.
3. Adjust the Slider to select a time range. The slider synchronizes with the From and To
boxes.
The time unit matches the FSDB file dumped by the simulator.

Exploring the AMS Profile View Components
The components of the AMS Profile View are as follows:
* Instance Tree
* Top Active Instances/Subcircuits Table
* Top Active Instances/Subcircuits Line Chart

Instance Tree
This component displays a hierarchical view of instances with following columns:
* Instance: The name of the instance.
* Cumulative Sim Cost: The total simulation cost accumulated for each instance.
* Cumulative Sim Cost %: The percentage of the total accumulated simulation cost
relative to the overall performance.
By default, the first analog instance is selected and expanded two levels deep.
You can use the search pane or find bar to locate instances. Drag and drop is supported
for instance management. Sorting is not supported in the instance tree.
To accurately identify the top N instances, the traversal only extends downward to a
maximum of two levels in the hierarchy. As a result, the reported top N instances may not
truly reflect the highest instances. You can adjust the traversal level by configuring the
following environment variable:
setenv VERDI_AMS_PROFILER_TOP_N_TRAVERSE_LEVEL <level>

Top Active Instances/Subcircuits Table
This table provides insights into the most resource-intensive instances or subcircuits,
featuring the following columns:
* Instance/Subckt Name: The name of the instance or subcircuit.
* Cumulative Sim Cost: The total simulation cost for the instance/subcircuit.
* Cumulative Sim Cost %:The percentage of total simulation cost.
The Cumulative Sim Cost % column shows a value only for SPICE instances and
only within the selected instance. If you select a SPICE instance, this column displays
100%. If you select a non-SPICE instance, the column is empty. Instances outside the
selected instance also show empty values.

* Visible: A checkbox that determines whether the instance/subcircuit is displayed in the
corresponding line chart. By default, the checkbox is selected..
Single selection highlights the corresponding curve in the line chart.

Top Active Instances/Subcircuits Line Chart
This visual representation allows you to see the performance trends of the top active
instances or subcircuits over time.
The data for instances line chart depends on the instance tree selection and time range.
The data for subcircuits line chart does not depend on instance tree selection. However, it
depends on the time range.
The line chart provides the following information:
* Visualizes the top N expensive instances/subcircuits.
The default top N value is 3 and you can adjust the value up to 50. To increase the
limit, set the following environment variable.
setenv VERDI_AMS_PROFILER_TOP_N_THRESHOLD <desired_value>

* Supports display of accumulated or instantaneous values. From the Display Graphic
View With drop-down list, select the value type.
Accumulated value mode refers to the total or cumulative value of a measurement over
a specified period. It aggregates data points to provide a comprehensive view of the
total amount or sum of a particular variable.
Instantaneous value mode captures the delta in value between two points in time. It
provides a snapshot of the variable being measured, reflecting its current state without
any aggregation.

Interacting With the AMS Profile View
You can perform the following actions in the AMS Profile View window.

Enable or Disable Top N Widgets
* When you select a digital instance, top N widgets are disabled and cleared.
* When you select a SPICE instance, widgets are enabled.

Highlighting and Navigation
Select an instance in the instance tree or top N usage table of instances, right-click to
