* When you select a SPICE instance, widgets are enabled.

Highlighting and Navigation
Select an instance in the instance tree or top N usage table of instances, right-click to
navigate to the nTrace instance tree.

Tcl Commands Related to AMS Profile View
Tcl commands are provided for creating, closing, and manipulating the AMS profile view,
including commands for setting time ranges, and selecting instances.
The following are the Tcl commands:
* amsProfileViewOpenDb -path /global/verdi01/profile_dir: To open AMS
profile database directory.
* amsProfileViewCloseWindow: To close the AMS profile view window.
* amsProfileViewSetTopNCount -dataType inst/subckt -count n: To change the
number of top N items displayed in the AMS profile view for the specified data type.
* amsProfileViewSetTime -from from -to to: To set the time range for the AMS
profile view.
* amsProfileViewInstanceTreeSelect -inst instanceName: To select instance tree
item by instance name.
* amsProfileViewTableSelect -dataType inst/subckt -row n: Selects a row in
the top N table for the specified data type.
* amsProfileViewSetVisible -dataType inst/subckt -row n -visible on/off:
To select or deselect Visible column in top N table.
* amsProfileViewSetAllVisible -dataType inst/subckt -visible on/off: To
select and deselect All Visible check box in top N table.
* amsProfileViewSetValueType -dataType inst/subckt -valueType accum/
instant: To select a value type (accumulated or instantaneous) for the specified data
type.

The following are the limitations of AMS Profile View window:
* The dashboard does not support save/restore or reload functionality.
* If a very large N value is set, the graphic view may become cluttered and performance
may degrade.

text:
Compiling Verilog-A Blocks
To compile Verilog-A files with VCS, instantiate the Verilog-A module in a SPICE file.
Use this SPICE file to compile with the VCS and CustomSim simulator. For compiling the
SPICE designs, see Compiling and Importing a SPICE Design and Compiling With the
SPICE Unified Front-End Flow.
In a mixed-signal simulation, Verilog-A can be used as the analog view of a cell. Use
the .hdl command in the SPICE netlist to read Verilog-A files. In this flow, passing all

title: 3 Pins
text:
Verilog files, including Verilog-A to VCS at compile time is still possible although not
recommended. For more information about Verilog-A model instantiation, see the MixedSignal Simulation User Guide.
Limitation
With Verilog-A model instantiation, the KDB design hierarchy generates at compile time.
Verdi does not support analog simulator commands, such as set_va_view and .param
HSIMUSEVA=<module name>, to switch between SPICE and Verilog-A views during
simulation.

Performing Interactive Simulation Debug of Verilog-A
Mixed-Signal Design
After you compile your Verilog-A mixed-signal design, you can interactively debug it in
Verdi. Verilog-A Interactive Debug mode supports the following features for Verilog-A
designs:
* Provides various methods to dump the following Verilog-A signals:
Variables
Voltage and current of nodes (you can dump current if you use current in your
design).
Voltage and current of unnamed/named branches (you can dump current if you use
current in your design).
For more information about Verilog-A signal dumping, see Dumping Verilog-A Signals.
* Shows the following values in the annotation of Verilog-A signals in the interactive
debug mode:
Variable's value
Voltage of node and unnamed/named branch
* Shows Verilog-A signals in the interactive Watch tab.
* Saves/restores the simulation session/state.
* Waveform to save/restore a signal .rc file with Verilog-A signals in the form of V()
being dumped and restored.
The following sections describe the supported interactive simulation debug features:
* Getting Started
* Setting the Simulator Type in the Preference Page

* Using the Interactive Watch Tab
* Annotating Values
* Dumping Verilog-A Signals
* Saving or Restoring Simulation Session or State

title: 3 Pins
text:
Getting Started
Verdi supports the Verilog-A interactive debug mode with this enhancement. The user flow
is as follows:
1. Prepare the AMS design with Verilog-A.
2. Set the XA_HOME, VERDI_HOME, and VCS_HOME environment variables. Compile the
Verilog-A AMS design using VCS to generate a simulation executable with debug
capability. For more information, see the document of VCS/CustomSim/PLI.
3. Use Verdi to load the Verilog-A design with the cosim option, which you can specify
using the following methods:
Specify -msv when importing the design from the command line.
In nTrace, select File -> Import Design From library -> Options toggle on the
Cosim Debug command and load the Verilog-A design.
4. Select Simulation -> Invoke Simulator.
Verdi creates and opens a single FSDB to include the digital and analog signals dumped
by the FSDB dumper.
You can use AMS interactive debug with the Verilog-A design. The simulation runs
under VCS simulator control. When you run Verilog-A AMS interactive debug, VCS and
CustomSim impose some limitations.
* Does not support step or next into analog design.
* Breakpoints cannot be added into analog design.
* Rewind is blocked in the AMS interactive debug mode.
These limitations disable some menu commands and right-click menu options.
For more information on the Simulation and Interactive Debug commands, see the Verdi
Command Reference Guide.

Setting the Simulator Type in the Preference Page
You can set the VCS-AMS option from Tools -> Preference -> Simulation -> Simulator
menu. If you specify -msv in the command line, the simulator type in preference is
changed to VCS-AMS as illustrated in the following figure:
Figure 126

title: 3 Pins
text:
Simulator Type in Preference Form

When an error occurs, the following methods are available to resolve errors:
* Verdi supports -simType to indicate the simulator type when invoking Verdi. If you
specify both -msv and -simType, then Verdi displays a warning message and honors
-msv.
* Verdi provides a warning message when you invoke the simulation by different
simulator types when running Verilog-A AMS interactive debug. For example:
You can use the simulator type as VCS and run interactive mode with Verilog-A
AMS simv.
You can use the simulator type as VCS-AMS and run interactive mode with digital
only simv.

Using the Interactive Watch Tab
The interactive Watch tab supports to show Verilog-A signals that include variable,
electrical nodes (electrical, voltage, and current), and branch at the current simulation
time. The Interactive Watch tab displays the variable's values and the voltage of electrical
nodes and branches at the current simulation time.

You can add Verilog-A signals to the Watch tab using the drag and drop method or the
Add to Watch right-click menu option. Then, the selected signal is added to the Watch
tab, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 127

Signals Added to the Interactive Watch Tab

The Watch tab provides the following information about analog variables:
* Name: Variable, node, or named branch (this is displayed as specified in the design).
Unnamed branch, displayed in the (a,b) format.
* Value: Variable (Shown as variable's value) Node, unnamed/named branch, that is,
shows the voltage value at the current simulation time. For example, 3.30V.
* Type: Variable, node, unnamed branch, or named branch.
* Scope: Full hierarchical scope.
* Icon: Synchronize nTrace icon for Verilog-A signals.
You can summarize the effectiveness of each right-click menu option in the interactive
Watch tab in the analog design.
The following features are disabled with Verilog-A signals:
* Set Breakpoint
* Set Radix
* Add Object to Watch Tab
* Show Declaration, Show in Class Browser, View Object Reference
* Dump Object to FSDB file, Dump, Add Object to Waveform

The following are the limitations with the Watch tab:
* Mathematic types such as 'real', 'integer', 'parameter' and 'genvar' cannot be added to
the Watch tab (it is due to the limitation of CustomSim as mathematic types cannot get
value from the simulator).
* For internal nodes in a leaf Verilog-A scope, the value is not displayed (this is due to
the limitation of CustomSim).

Annotating Values
You can turn on the source view annotation using the Source -> Active Annotation
toggle menu (the hotkey is 'x').
If the cursor time is not equal to simulation time, you can get the annotation value from
FSDB. For more information, see section Verilog-A annotation in nTrace in the postsimulation mode.
If the cursor time equals simulation time, you can get the annotation value from IPI/
simulator (this is same as annotation of Verilog signals). Due to the known limitation of
CustomSim, only the voltage of electrical node and branch is displayed. For example, the
voltage value is shown as 3.30V.

The variable, node, and branch values are displayed as shown in the following figure:
Figure 128

Active Annotation

The following are the limitations with annotating Verilog-A signals:
* Changing the analog format and precision in annotation is not supported.
* No annotation for I(a,b) or I(mybranch) as it requests current value and it is not
currently supported in simulator.

* Mathematic types such as 'real', 'integer', 'parameter' and 'genvar' cannot be added to
the Watch tab (it is due to limitation of CustomSim, mathematic types cannot get value
from simulator).
* For internal nodes in leaf Verilog-A scope, the values are not displayed (it is due to
limitation of CustomSim).

Dumping Verilog-A Signals
Verdi allows you to dump variable, node, and branch values of Verilog-A signals. Dumping
a variable is similar to dumping a digital signal. The following sections discuss how to
dump nodes and branches.

Dumping Nodes
Similar to SPICE, the current of a node is annotated with different value according to their
position in the code. For example, if you drag and drop node a from the position of module
definition, then its port current I(<a>) is dumped.
However, naming a node might not be the same as naming a design. For example,
simulator does not dump signal, such as I(<a>) in FSDB, it dumps isub(a) or
in(va_inst). The following table summarizes the signals that Verdi triggers to dump
when you right-click or drag and drop to dump a.
Syntax

Signals Dumped

top.in(va), top.va.in(va)
top.va.isub(a)

fsdbDumpvars top.va +msv+vaI

Dumping Branches
You can dump two branch types in Verilog-A: unnamed branch and named branch. The
following table summarizes the signals dumped when you select "unnamed/named
branch".

Methods for Dumping Signals
Similar to interactive debug mode with digital design, you can dump Verilog-A signals in
the interactive debug mode using one of the following methods:
* In nTrace, right-click the signal/instance and select the Drag option. In nWave, rightclick the signal pane and select the Drag option.
* In nTrace, right-click the node/branch and select the Dump to FSDB File option.
* You can use the Dump dialog box, which is used to dump other HDL signals to dump
Verilog-A signal/scope as well. Select the Dump Voltage and Dump Current checkboxes to dump the signals. The selected signal/scope in source view is automatically

displayed in the Scope/Signal field (see Figure: Dumping Verilog-A Signals (Dump
Dialog Box).
Figure 129

Dumping Verilog-A Signals (Dump Dialog Box)

Saving or Restoring Simulation Session or State
Verdi already supports to save/restore the simulation session/state in the interactive mode
with the digital design. This feature provides the capability to save the currently debug
process or restore the point to continue the unfinished debug process. Verdi also supports
this feature in the Verilog-A interactive debug mode. Both the simulation states in digital
and analog are saved/restored.

title: 3 Pins
text:
The usage is as same as that of the digital design. You can use this feature with the
following commands:
* nTrace -> Simulation -> Save State
* nTrace -> File -> Save Session. Then, select the Save Simulation State option, as
shown in the following figure:
Figure 130

title: 3 Pins
text:
Save/Restore Session/State

After loading a mixed-signal design into Verdi, you can see the design hierarchy with both
analog and digital scopes in the Instance frame. You can also check the Verilog-A source
code in the source code window (see Figure: Showing Verilog-A Information).

Figure 131

Showing Verilog-A Information

If your design includes SPICE source code, the SPICE nodes are also shown in
the Instance frame.
The following table shows the nodes shown in the Instance frame:
Node Figure

Node Meaning
A Verilog-A mixed-signal module
A SPICE mixed-signal sub-circuit

Double-click a node in the Instance frame to jump to the corresponding definition source
code in the source code frame. The right-click menu commands are available for Verilog-A
signals.

Setting Preferences
The type of the attached value is the voltage value by default. You can use the following
steps to add or remove other types for the attached value:
1. Select the Tools -> Preferences menu to invoke the Preferences form.
2. Select the AMS Debug page and enable the types. You can select multiple signal
types.
Figure 132

Selecting Verilog-A Signal Value

3. Click the OK button to apply the setting.
Only V(signal) and I(signal) values are supported for the annotation of the
voltage and current types.

Active Annotation
After the virtual file containing digital and analog data files is loaded into the Verdi platform,
you can select the Source -> Active Annotation menu to see the node, branch, variable,
V(node), V(branch), I(node), and I(branch) values annotated in the source code (see
Figure: Active Annotation in Source Code). Verdi shows V(node) and V(branch) when
the Voltage option is toggled. Similarly, it shows I(node) and I(branch) when the Current
option is toggled.

Figure 133

Active Annotation in Source Code

The disciplines, such as electrical are not color-coded, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 134

Disciplines - electrical

The access function and its node/branch are shown as one word. Note that you cannot
select mybranch inside I(mybranch), as shown in the following figure:

The color-coding of I(node), I(branch), V(node), V(branch) are same as that of the
signal.

Dragging and Dropping Verilog-A Signals
You can drag the node, variable, branch, V(node), I(node), V(branch), I(branch) to the
other Verdi panes.
You can drop the node, variable, branch, V(node), I(node), V(named branch), I(named
branch) to the source window. The the source window shows the definition of node,
variable and named branch as default. However, you can change the drop action from the
Preferences setting.
Verdi does not support drag and drop of unnamed branch.

Viewing the Signal List
Use the View -> Signal List menu to see the Signal_List frame (see Figure: Verilog-A
Signals in Signal List).

Debugging Verilog-A Designs in the Waveform View

Figure 135

Verilog-A Signals in Signal List

Verdi also allows you to drag-and-drop signals from the Signal_List pane to the nWave
window.

The following are the limitations:
* Tracing a signal is not supported inside an analog block.
* Verdi does not support swapping of Verilog-A view with AMS setup.

Debugging Verilog-A Designs in the Waveform View
When you load a file with digital and analog data files into Verdi, you can add both signal
types into the nWave window that opens the file. You can also use the drag-and-drop and
synchronization features to add these signals.

Drag and Drop to nWave
You can drag one or more Verilog-A signals from the Source Code window and drop it
to the nWave window to add the selected signal, as shown in the following figure. Verdi
allows you to drag and drop variable, node, and branch.

Debugging Verilog-A Designs in the Waveform View

Figure 136

Add Signals by Dragging and Dropping

title: 3 Pins
text:
If the selected signal is not dumped into the FSDB file, the List of
Unrecognized Signal(s) dialog shows and lists the selected signal as an
unrecognized signal.
When you drag and drop a scope to nWave, it adds port signals to waveform. To add all
signals within the scope, set the preference using Tools -> Preferences -> Waveform ->
View Options -> Waveform Pane Miscellaneous.
In the nWave window, you can also choose the Signals -> Get Signals command to open
the Get Signals form. The Get Signals form enables you to select the dumped signals.
The Verilog-A signal is shown as

(see Figure: Get Signals Form).

Debugging Verilog-A Designs in the Waveform View

Figure 137

Get Signals Form

The following are the limitations with Verilog-A support in the waveform view:
Node:
* Adding node current of a primitive device in Verilog-A instance is not supported. For
example, consider the following statement in Verilog-A:
resistor #(.r(10k)) R2 (b, gnd);

Verdi does not show the node current annotation passing through b or gnd and it is
unable to add node current when you drag-and-drop b or gnd to waveform.
Branch:
* Dragging and dropping of unnamed branch from nWave to design-based AP is not
supported.

Drag and Drop From nWave
You can drag Verilog-A variable, node, or branch in the nWave window and drop it to
nTrace or nSchema to add the selected signal.
Limitation

Debugging Verilog-A Designs in the Schematic View

Branch:
Dragging and dropping unnamed branch from nWave to design-based AP is not
supported.

Dumping
If you use drag-and-drop or right-click to add Verilog-A signals to nWave, the tool dumps
those signals. However, if the Verilog-A instance is a leaf instance, the dumper cannot
dump only a specific port current. In this case, when you try to dump the port current,
nWave dumps all nodes and branches for that leaf Verilog-A instance.
The following are the limitations with the drag and drop feature:
* Does not dump single port current if a Verilog-A instance is a leaf instance due to
simulator and dumper.
* Dumping the voltage of an unnamed branch is not supported because the simulator
does not allow it. CustomSim cannot display voltage for unnamed branches. If you drag
and drop this signal into nWave, it appears as an unrecognized signal.

Batch Dumping
The Save/Restore signal rc file enables batch dumping for Verilog-A signals if restore
signals are not existing in FSDB.

Debugging Verilog-A Designs in the Schematic View
You can load and debug a Verilog-A scope in nSchema similar to nWave.
After the file containing digital and analog FSDB files is loaded into the Verdi platform, you
can also see the analog values in the nSchema window. To debug in the schematic view,
click
to invoke the nSchema window for the selected scope.

Verilog-A Scope

Color-Coding Signals in nSchema

* Analog, digital, or mixed signal signals
The analog blocks are displayed in green. When you open the nSchema window, all the
analog signals are displayed in the default color and you can change the default color of

You can also select non-default colors for analog, digital, and mixed-signals from the
menu, as shown in the following figure. However, there might be performance issues if

title: 3 Pins
text:
Tracing Verilog-A Designs in the Temporal Flow View
To debug a design, you must understand the structure and the behavior of the design.
Visualizing the structure and behavior of the design helps you become familiar with the
design and simplifies the debugging process.
Temporal Flow View (TFV) provides flow views that are unique temporal views
and analysis tools that allow the visualization and analysis of the design's behavior
through time. TFV identifies the control and data paths that led to an error, including the
specific registers and signals involved. It traces these paths through multiple levels of
combinational logic across one or more register-to-register transfer stages.
TFV provides the following capabilities for the analysis of analog and digital signals and
are described in the following sections:
* Traces digital signals and analog signals on the tracing path using Trace This Value
(cycle based) / Trace Triggering Path (transition based).
* Displays Interface Elements (IEs) and Through Nets (TNs).
* Uses function blocks with specific labels to represent analog blocks on TFV. TFV does
not trace into the analog blocks. TFV only traces through analog blocks and uses a
specific label as analog blocks (the green symbol is an analog block symbol).

title: 3 Pins
text: Tracing Verilog-A Designs in the Temporal Flow View

title: 3 Pins
text:
* Synchronize with nWave, nTrace, and nSchema, thereby showing the waveform,
source code, and circuit detail of digital and analog signals.
* Allows you to drag and drop signals to nWave, nTrace, and nSchema, showing the
waveform, source code, and circuit, respectively.
For more information about creating TFV, see Chapter Temporal Flow View Tutorial in the
Verdi User Guide and Tutorial and Chapter Flow Views in the Verdi and Siloti Command
Reference Manual.

title: 3 Pins
text:
Tracing Verilog-A Signals
The tracing rules of Verilog-A signals are the same as digital tracing rules. Both cyclebased and transition-based tracing are available for tracing analog blocks. The following
figure shows the process of tracing a digital signal, while a Verilog-A signal exists in the
tracing path.
Figure 142

Tracing a digital signal and reaching a Verilog-A signal with IE reports

The following figure shows TFV tracing without IE ports.
Figure 143

Tracing a digital signal and reaching a Verilog-A signal without IE reports

The snap time of Verilog-A blocks are same as their digital outputs. The detailed VerilogA circuits are not displayed in TFV. Alternatively, you can trace to analog circuits using
the schematic view in nSchema. You can later use the synchronization button in the TFV
toolbar (see Synchronization With nWave, nTrace, and nSchema).

Tracing Verilog-A Designs in the Temporal Flow View

If SPICE signals are in Verilog-A's modules, the symbols for the function blocks
is VA instead of SPICE.

Creating Verilog-A Signals in TFV
Creating TFV for Verilog-A signals is similar to creating TFV for a digital black box. TFV
uses function blocks with the specific word "VA" to represent Verilog-A signals. The analog
blocks are shown in green in TFV.
The following figure shows the initial window for generating TFV for a Verilog-A signal. If
an internal analog signal is selected for creating TFV, an output analog signal is mapped.
For example, if a signal in the analog block is not defined as an input or output, an output
pin within the same scope is automatically mapped. This allows the internal signal to be
displayed correctly during final viewing (see Figure: Verilog-A Block in TFV).
Figure 144

Verilog-A Block in TFV

Synchronization With nWave, nTrace, and nSchema
You can use the synchronization buttons in the TFV toolbar to synchronize analog signals
to nWave, nTrace, and nSchema. The figure Synchronization from TFV shows the
synchronization buttons in TFV.
Figure 145

Synchronization from TFV

The order from left to right is the sync button to nWave, nTrace, and nSchema.

Tracing Verilog-A Designs in the Temporal Flow View

Dragging and Dropping Signals
You can drag and drop Verilog-A signals to nWave, nTrace, and nSchema. When you drag
Verilog-A signals from nWave, nTrace, and nSchema, TFV adds the dragged signals as
reference signals and shows the respective analog blocks.

Force debug for Verilog-A signals
TFV does not display any information about internal signals of analog modules, so the
force debug information of analog internal signals is not displayed in TFV.

Limitation
TFV cannot trace into analog instances. Also, tracing the internal signals of analog blocks
is not supported. If you create TFV for the internal signals, TFV is created with an outmost signal instead of the internal signals. Detail structures can be found by toggling up
the sync button of nSchema. That is, you can trace through analog blocks and see the
structural details if required.

title: 3 Pins
text:
Known Problems and Limitations
* For spicom
The spicom utility does not support inline subckt for Spectre format.
The spicom utility does not fully support global net. Trace connective feature is not
supported for global nets.
The spicom utility does not fully support global parameter, such as showing the
definition feature.
The port_map option for the use_verilog, use_spice, and use_vhdl commands
is not supported.
* For AMS virtual FSDB file
The digital FSDB file should be set as the master file which is the first FSDB file in
the virtual file.
Verdi only supports the virtual file that contains one digital FSDB file and one analog
FSDB file for AMS debugging.
If there are some scopes with the same name and different letter cases in the digital
FSDB file, the referenced scope in digital FSDB for merging the analog FSDB file is
randomly chosen.
* For nWave
Case Issue
For example, Signal A and v(a) are dumped in Verilog scope.
Drag-and-Drop and synchronize the selection may not work correctly for v(a) since
the signal name in the design is A.
* For nScehma
TFV related features are not supported for value types signals.
* For AMS debug
The Rebuild and Restart flow is not supported in Mixed Signal Verification flow.
* Support for editing the Interface Elements (IE) in Verilog-AMS

title: 3 Pins
text:
Chapter 5: Known Problems and Limitations

The runtime interface elements and inout interface elements are not supported.
* Support for Verilog-AMS in Verdi
You cannot add node current of the primitive device in Verilog-AMS instance.
For example, if the following statement is available in Verilog-AMS resistor
#(.r(10k)) R2 (b, gnd); then the annotation for b or gnd signals are not
displayed and are unable to add node current when drag-and-drop b or gnd signals
to waveform.
Since XA cannot dump voltage for unnamed branch, it is not recognized in nWave.
Unnamed branch does not support DND from nWave to design-based AP.
You cannot dump "single" port current if a Verilog-AMS instance is leaf instance.
You cannot dump voltage of unnamed branch.

Introduction
The Verdi(R) Automated Debug Platform and the Siloti(R) Visibility Automation System
are advanced solutions for debugging digital designs. These solutions increase design
productivity with complex System-on-Chip (SoC), ASIC, and FPGA designs.
The Verdi platform provides powerful technology to help users to do the following:
* Comprehend complex and unfamiliar design behavior
* Automate difficult and tedious debug processes
* Unify diverse and complicated design environments
* Infer the dynamic behavior of a design over time.
The Siloti system speeds up simulation. It does so by eliminating the overhead associated
with recording signal values and by enabling full visibility of design activity based on a
relatively small amount of signal data. This data is captured during full-chip simulation,
regression simulation, and hardware emulation/acceleration. The Siloti system is fully
integrated with the Verdi platform so that users can leverage the benefits of full visibility for
gate or RTL debug.
Synopsys also provides the following two modules that complement the Verdi platform:
* The nAnalyzerTM Design Analysis module for debugging the implementation aspects of
a design. These aspects include clock trees and static timing failures.
* The nECOTM Automated Netlist Modification module for solving problems associated
with manual netlist changes.
Verdi and Siloti systems and the additional nAnalyzer and nECO modules enable
engineers. They can locate, isolate, understand, and resolve bugs in a fraction of the
time of traditional solutions. This maximizes the efficiency and productivity of expensive
engineering resources, significantly reduces costs, and dramatically accelerates the
process of getting silicon to market.
This chapter consists of the following sections:
* Product Overview
* User Interface Overview

Product Overview

Product Overview
This chapter provides information on the primary components in the Verdi platform. With
the exception of the nCompare module that has its own document, each component has
its own chapter in this manual.
Refer to the Utilities chapter for details on the Verdi command line options and other
provided utilities. Refer to the Preferences chapter for details on setting preferences for
the Verdi components.

nTrace
nTrace is a source code viewer and analyzer. It operates on the Knowledge Database
(KDB) to display a design hierarchy and source code (Verilog, VHDL, SystemVerilog,
mixed, and power languages like CPF/UPF) for selected design blocks. nTrace quickly
identifies the signal connectivity information (drivers and loads) without any simulation
overhead. With the FSDB, the simulation results can be back-annotated in the source
code and then nTrace can analyze and determine a signal's active driver at a particular
simulation time.
Refer to the nTrace chapter for details. Also refer to the Language Support and Compile/
Import Methods chapter for details on language support.

nWave is a state-of-the-art graphical waveform viewer and analyzer. It is fully integrated
with the Verdi platform's source code, schematic, and flow views. A waveform search
engine combined with backward and forward navigation allows users to search for signal
transitions, bus values, discrepancies, or user-defined events easily.
nWave also offers the following:
* Flexible signal group management
* User-customizable glitch detection
* Built-in logic analyzer
* Logical operations
* Events
* Display of delays back-annotated from SDF files
* Mixed analog/digital (A/D) display capabilities (including overlap, vertical zoom, delta x
and y, arithmetic operations, analog-to-digital signal conversion, and others)

Product Overview

* Transaction/message display

nSchema
nSchema is a schematic viewer and analyzer. It generates interactive debug-specific logic
diagrams showing the structure of selected portions of a design including the following:
* RTL diagrams show the interconnection of finite state machines, storage elements, and
multiplexers.
* Gate-level diagrams show the interconnection of semiconductor vendor cells.
* Special flattened diagrams cut through the design hierarchy to isolate connected
design elements.
nSchema dynamically generates partial schematics to focus on the circuits of interest
within a large design.
Basic editable schematic capabilities and support for power design intent are also
available.
Refer to nSchema and Editable Schematic chapters for details.

nState
nState is a finite state machine (FSM) viewer and analyzer. It generates bubble diagrams
for the visualization of state machines that are automatically recognized by the Verdi
platform when compiling the Verilog/VHDL source code modules. States and transitions
are annotated with logic conditions and animated with simulation results. nState analyzes
the simulation results to determine state and transition coverage.

Flow Views
The Flow Views are unique temporal views and analysis tools. They allow the visualization
and analysis of a design's behavior through time. The Temporal Flow View identifies and
displays causal control and data paths - the registers and signals that actually cause the
erroneous values to occur. It does it through multi-level combinational logic within one
or more register-to-register transfer stages. This type of intelligently filtered temporal
representation allows users to locate and identify problems in the most efficient manner
possible. The Temporal Flow View also supports power aware debug.
Refer to the Flow Views chapter for details.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Product Overview

The nCompare Waveform Comparison module compares simulation results stored in
FSDB dump files. It does so by using flexible, user-specified comparison criteria. The
nCompare module is optimized for extremely fast comparison of large data sets. It is fully
integrated with nWave to intuitively display any differences between runs.
FSDB

Refer to the nCompare chapter for details.
The Verdi platform also includes these secondary components. Each component has its
own chapter in this manual.

Assertion Debug
Assertion Debug support provides visualization and analysis capabilities for assertions and
assertion results.
Refer to the Assertion Debug chapter for details.

Testbench Debug
Testbench Debug provides visualization and comprehension capabilities for designs
including the SystemVerilog Testbench code.
Refer to the Testbench Debug and Interactive Simulation Debug chapters for details.

Power Aware Debug
Power Aware Debug provides visualization and analysis capabilities for designs including
power design intent source code (that is, CPF or UPF).
Refer to the Power Aware Debug chapter for details.

Transaction/Message Analyzer
The Transaction/Message Analyzer window provides visualization and analysis
capabilities for transactions and message data.
transactions

Refer to the Transaction/Message Analyzer chapter for details.

nMemory
The nMemory window allows multi-dimensional memory arrays (including twodimensional) to be viewed in a tabular format. The display of word size and radix can be
modified. The array can be searched for a specific value.
Refer to the Memory/MDA Pane chapter for details.

Product Overview

nRegister
The nRegister window provides a graphical window for viewing simulation results. Lines,
rectangles, arrows, and text can be added and the objects aligned to create a unique
representation of the results.
Refer to the Register Window chapter for details.

nEditor
nEditor is a complete text editor. The text is color-coded by language syntax.
Refer to the nEditor chapter for details.

Siloti
The Siloti system provides the Visibility Analysis engine. It determines the minimum set
of signals for full visibility of the design. The system also provides the Data Expansion
engine to compute the remaining signal values 'on-demand'. In addition, the optional
Abstraction Correlation module maps gate-level signal data to the RTL for easier debug
and understanding.
Refer to the Visibility chapter for details.

Additional Modules
The following modules can be purchased and used in conjunction with the Verdi platform.

nAnalyzer
The nAnalyzer module provides the ability to do the following:
* Analyze clock and reset trees (including crossing paths)
* Qualify Clock Tree Synthesis (CTS)
* Annotate standard delay format (SDF) files and CTS results
* Load and display timing results from standard timing analysis tools
* Perform switching analysis on a design
These functions build on top of the functional debug aspects of the Verdi platform.
Search for nAnalyzer in this document to locate related commands. Refer to the Clock
Analyzer chapter and the nAnalyzer User Guide and Tutorial for other details.

nECO
The nECO module provides the ability to perform gate-level engineering change orders
(ECOs) in the Verdi platform's flexible schematic views. The nECO module takes full
advantage of the Verdi platform's sophisticated capabilities to propagate changes
throughout the design hierarchy and automatically creates new nets and ports.
Search for nECO in this document to locate related commands. Refer to the nECO
chapter for Eco Window related commands and to the Preferences chapter for details on
setting preferences for nECO. Further, refer to the nECO User Guide and Tutorial for other

Framework and Customization
The User Interface consists of a central framework where all components are docked.
Each component (window or widget) has a default pane location. You can change
((undock) the default pane locations. To do so, drag (press and hold the middle mouse
button) the component and drop (release the middle mouse button) it at another location
(dock). If the default/new pane location is on top of an existing pane, a new tab is added.
All components can be undocked (become standalone panes). Some components (such
as, nSchema, nWave, Flow Views, and nState) may also become fully-functional separate
windows. When a widget is undocked, it always remains in the foreground.
When multiple panes are undocked as standalone windows, window titles of these active
windows are listed under the Window command. For the top window, the undocked

window titles are listed based on the window creation order. For a standalone window,
except for the top window, the top window title is listed first, followed by the remaining
undocked window titles based on their creation order. Select the window title of interest to
switch to the target window.
Figure 5

Windows Titles Listed on Top Window

Figure 6

Windows Titles Listed on Standalone Window

In addition, menu commands, bind keys, and toolbar icons can all be customized (such as,
names, locations, and symbols). Refer to the Tools > Customize Menu/Toolbar command
in the nTrace chapter for details.

Definitions
* Component: A window or widget that is either a part of the main window by default or
can be added by invoking a command.
* Pane: An area in the main window that is occupied by one or more components.
* Widget: A component that is a subsidiary pane of the main window. A widget does
not have its own toolbar or menu commands. A widget cannot be maximized to a full
screen size.
* Window: A component that has its own toolbar and menu commands. A window
can be docked in the main window as a pane or a tab or it may be undocked as a
standalone window. A window can be maximized to full screen size.

File -> Import Design

The File > Import Design command opens the Import Design form.
Even if the symbol library is specified in the Schematics folder > Symbol
Library page of the Preferences form (invoked with the Tools > Preferences
command). When importing the design with the HDL code and symbol library
at the same time, VHDL and Verilog treats the design as a user-defined module
in nTrace, instead of a symbol library cell. The module is treated as a symbol
library cell when -v or -y is specified.
The Import Design form includes the From Library tab and the From File tab. After
selecting the required design and top modules on either tab, click OK to close the form
and import the design with the specified options.

From Library Tab
A Verilog or VHDL design can be imported from a pre-compiled library. The Verilog and
VHDL source can be incrementally compiled into the defined libraries using these batch
mode compilers.
Figure 10

Import Design Form - From Library Tab

The Import Design form includes the following fields, sections, and buttons on the From
Library tab:
* From: Select if the Verdi Knowledge Database (KDB) is generated by Verdi Compile
or VC/VCS Native Compile. When Verdi Compile is selected, Verdi loads the Verdi
Knowledge Database generated by the vericom or vhdlcom utilities and the library
mapping from the novas.rc resource file is used. When VC/VCS Native Compile is
selected, Verdi loads the KDB generated by VCS and the library mapping from the
synopsys_sim.setup setup file is used.
* Virtual Top: This field can be used to import only a portion of the design. Refer to the
Virtual Top Example section for details.
Configuration File: Toggle the Virtual Top field to select Configuration File and
import part of the design into the Verdi platform to enhance performance. Refer to the
verdi section in Utilities chapter for details.
* Working Directory: Specify the working directory for the library in this text field.
* Library: This section lists the available libraries in the current working directory. Library
names in the Library section are listed by library type first (standard libraries have

higher priority than user-defined libraries), then by letter case (uppercase has higher
priority than lowercase), and the remaining are sorted by alphabetical order.
* Design Unit: This section lists all top objects from the selected pre-compiled library.

Virtual Top Example
To maintain the consistency of the design hierarchy, the correct hierarchical paths of the
top sub-hierarchy modules must be specified. The definitions are stored in a .map file and
the syntax is as follows:
module_name = hierarchical_instance_name

The Verdi platform generates a virtual top automatically according to the definitions in the
.map file and imports only a subset of the design.
The hierarchical instance name in the virtual top (.map) file accepts
environment variables to specify the complete hierarchical path.
Assume there is a VHDL design with a top module, system, which contains two instances:
cpu and pram and that cpu contains an instance alub. Assume only alub and pram should
be loaded into the Verdi platform instead of loading the entire system hierarchy. First,
specify the design files associated with cpu, pram, and their sub-instances in a file called
vtop.f. Then there are two methods for defining the virtual top file.
Method 1. Define the contents of a virtual top file, vtop.map, as follows:
alub = system.i_cpu.i_alub
pram = system.i_pram

Method 2. Alternatively, specify environment variables in UNIX as follows:
setenv vtop1 system
setenv vtop2 i_cpu

Then, define the contents of a virtual top file, vtop.map, as follows:
alub = $vtop1.$vtop2.i_alub
pram = $vtop1.i_pram

After the virtual top file and design source list file are created, this subset of the design can
be imported with the virtual tops system and i_cpu using either one of the following two
methods:

text:
The virtual top is effective both when importing a design from a library and
when importing a design from source (or from files). However, when importing
from source, the -vtop option does not have an effect if the specified top is
included in the imported source. For example, assume that a design has the
following design hierarchy:
system ----> (system.v)
- i_cpu (CPU) ----> (CPU.v)
- i_ALUB (ALUB) ----> (ALUB.v)
- i_CCU (CCU) ----> (CCU.v)
- i_PCU (PCU) ----> (PCU.v)
Assume a run_all.f design file list contains:
system.v
ALUB.v
CCU.v
CPU.v
Assume a run_cpu.f design file list contains:
ALUB.v
CCU.v
CPU.v

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Assume a vtop.map map file contains:
CPU=system.i_cpu
The following two commands have the same imported design hierarchy and the
same contents in the system module (the same as system.v):
verdi -vtop vtop.map -f run_all.f
verdi -f run_all.f
The following two commands have the same imported design hierarchy, but
different contents in the system module:
verdi -vtop vtop.map -f run_cpu.f
====> The system module is built virtually.
verdi -f run_all.f
The following two commands have a different imported design hierarchy:
verdi -vtop vtop.map -f run_cpu.f
verdi -f run_cpu.f

For more details on importing a verilog design into Verdi, click the following video link.
This video focuses on importing Verilog and VHDL designs into the Verdi
platform from a file, from a library, and by using the graphical user interface
(GUI). Verilog source files are specified in a run file through the command
line and Verdi is invoked with a particular command. Importing from a library
requires the Verilog design to be precompiled into a Verdi library using the
Vericom utility. Using the GUI involves invoking the Verdi GUI, selecting the
'Import Design' option from the nTrace menu, and opting to import from a file or
a compiled library.

Reload Design

File > Reload Design

Shift+L

This command reloads the design files and simulation results. The Verdi platform
maintains the current debugging environment with the latest source and simulation results
but the trace results from previous operations in each window are removed. When the
design is imported from source files and one or more source files are modified with the
Source > Edit Source File command, the Reload Design command can be invoked to
recompile the design and all opened windows are updated with the new design.
When the design is imported from a pre-compiled library and one or more
source files are modified, the design must be recompiled outside the Verdi
platform using the vericom/vhdlcom utilities first and then reloaded with the
updated library using the Reload Design command.

View Import Log

File > View Import Log

This command opens the Text Viewer frame to view the compile log file.
Figure 15

Text Viewer Frame - Compile Log

Refer to the Text Viewer Frame for details.

Compile Design

File -> Compile Design

This command compiles a Verilog or VHDL design from a pre-compiled library that is
already created by using the utilities vericom or vhdlcom.
vericom

Select a design with the browser or the command line window then click OK.
Verilog and VHDL source can be incrementally compiled into the defined libraries using
the batch mode compilers vericom and vhdlcom respectively. For details, refer to the
vericom, vhdlcom, and verdi sections in the Utilities chapter.
vericom

Figure 16

Compile Design Form

Language: Select the design language to be compiled using the Language options:
Verilog, Verilog-2001, SystemVerilog, SystemVerilog-2009, SystemVerilog-2012,
VHDL-87, VHDL-93, VHDL-2000, or VHDL-2008.
Library Name: Specify the library names and their library paths. Click the Mapping button
on the right side.
Working Directory: Input the working directory of the library in the Working Directory
text field.

Design Files: Displays the Verilog files to be compiled into the Verdi platform. Add or
delete files in the Design Files list by selecting the file and clicking Add or Delete.
Filter: This is the file format filter for the File List. Additional filters can be added in this
selection field using a semicolon (;) as the separator.
Options: Clicking the Options button opens the Compile Design Options form.
Compile Design with Verilog Options
If Verilog is selected in the Language option of the Compile Design form, the following
options are displayed and serve as command line options when design files are compiled
into the Verdi platform.
Figure 17

Compile Design Options Form (Verilog)

Compile Method: Choose to either incrementally add the compiled Verilog modules
into the library (Increment (-inc)) or remove the previously saved Verilog modules
(Replacement (-rep)).
Library Directories (-y): Specify the library directory, which appends on the command line
option -y. Type in the directory path text field. Alternatively, click the Browse button to view
the directory structure and specify a library path.
Do Not Tag -y Library as Library Cell (-ssy): When this option is turned on, library
modules in the library directory (-y) is not automatically tagged as library cells.
Library Files (-v): This text field is used to specify the library file, which appends on the
command line option -v. Either type in the library file text field or click the Browse button
to view the directory structure and specify a library file.
Do Not Tag -v Library as Library Cell (-ssv): When this option is turned on, library
modules in the library file (-v) is not automatically tagged as library cells.

Ignore 'celldefine Compiler Directive (-ssz): When this option is turned on, 'celldefine
compiler directives is ignored.
Other Options: See the supported Verilog reference manual for available options. For
these options, invoke the Verdi platform with the command option -h.
More: Click this button for more compile options as follows:
* Run as Mentor (-mentor): This option works with the Mentor simulator.
* Compile as NC Library Format (-nclib): This option uses the NC binding scheme.
With this option, vericom looks for libMap, workLibrary, viewMap, and defaultView as
specified in the [NC_Sim] section of the novas.rc resource file for compiling Verilog
source files into the Verdi Knowledge Database (KDB).
If the Compile as NC Library Format (-nclib) option is turned on, the NC Library
Name (-work) and NC View Name (-view) options is turned on.
NC Library Name (-work): Specify the NC library name (valid if -nclib is specified).
This option provides the same function as ncvlog -work library_name to use the

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
turned on, the NC Library
Name (-work) and NC View Name (-view) options is turned on.
NC Library Name (-work): Specify the NC library name (valid if -nclib is specified).
This option provides the same function as ncvlog -work library_name to use the
specified library name for the design units in the input Verilog source files. For
vericom -nclib -work novas -view novas -f ../src/novas.f

All design units in the file ../src/novas.f are compiled into the library novas and have a
view name novas.
Using the command line option, -work, overrides the workLibrary and libMap
variables in novas.rc.
* NC View Name (-view): Specify the NC view name (valid if -nclib is specified).
This option provides the same function as ncvlog -view view_name to use the specified
view name for the design units in the input Verilog source files. For example:
vericom -nclib -view novas ../src/novas.v

All design units in ../src/novas.v have a view name novas.
Using the command line option, -view, overrides the defaultView and viewMap
variables in novas.rc.
* Extract RTL (-extractRTL): This option automatically recognizes RTL storage
elements. The extracted storage elements are saved into the library.
* Specify novas.rc (-rcFile): Specify the resource file - novas.rc.

Set as Default: Click this button to save all the settings as default compile options. You
can then click the Compile button right away to compile the design with the default options
just set.
Compile Design with VHDL Options
If VHDL is selected in the Language option of the Compile Design form, the following
options is displayed and serve as command line options when design files are compiled
into the Verdi platform.
Figure 18

Compile Design Options Form (VHDL)

Stop Design Compile when Error Occurs (-onerrorstop): This option stops compiling
the design if an error occurs.
Specify Run File (-fv): If many VHDL files are to be compiled, pack them sequentially into
a pack file and pass this file to vhdlcom. For example, if you have three source files called
v1.vhd, v2.vhd and v3.vhd, you can create a file called run.f or whatever name you wish to
use. Create its contents as follows:
Each file name must occupy its own line
v1.vhd
v2.vhd
v3.vhd

Skip Compile (-skip): You can specify the compiler to skip. You can skip Entity,
Architecture, Package, Package Body, or Configuration structures.
Just Compile (-just): You can specify the compiler to compile. You can just compile
Entity, Architecture, Package, Package Body, or Configuration structures.
Other Options: See the supported VHDL reference manual for available options. For
these options, you can invoke the Verdi platform with the command option -h.

More: Click this button to get more compile options as follows:
* Compile All Entities (architecture) as Symlib (-libcell): Compiles all entities
(architectures) the same as the symbol library.
* Verbose Messages (-verbosemsg): Verbose mode. Displays status messages to the
screen.
* Preload Basic Library (-prelib): If Yes is specified, vhdlcom loads two standard
packages (standard and textio) before parsing the design (the default value is Yes).
* Extract RTL (-extractRTL): This option automatically recognizes RTL storage
elements. The extracted storage elements are saved into the library.
* Specify novas.rc (-rcFile): Specifies the resource file - novas.rc.
1. To save both Verilog/VHDL options, click Save as Default twice for both
language types.
2. After compiling, you might see the following message:
"You may have to reload design after compilation if library
is the same."

This message notifies you that reloading the design may be necessary.
if you compile something into the same library which might cause bad
behavior in the Verdi platform. If a design is not currently imported into
the Verdi platform, the message is not shown. You can turned off this
message in the menu as follows: Tools > Preferences > General page.
3. If the Verdi platform exits, the compile language type (Verilog,
Verilog-2001, VHDL-87, VHDL-93, and VHDL-2000) is saved to novas.rc
as the default language for compiling the design for the next time the
Verdi platform runs.

text:
If loaded successfully, the simulation results automatically apply to the nWave window
when invoking the Tools -> New Waveform command. The Load Simulation Results form
performs the same function as the File -> Open command in the nWave window. This
automatically shows G1 in the nWave signal pane.
The Verdi time unit is determined in the following priority order:
1. The setting of the Waveform -> Waveform Time -> Set Window Time Unit command
icon when a waveform frame is opened.
or the
2. The setting of windowTimeUnit in the novas.rc resource file if the waveform is not
opened or the opened waveform does not include the time unit setting.
3. The time unit of the FSDB file specified in the Open Waveform File command.
For more information on how to generate a simulation result file (*.fsdb)
using Novas object files for FSDB dumping, refer to the Linking Novas Files
with Simulators and Enabling FSDB Dumping document.
The Load Simulation Results form includes the following options and field:
* Extract Equivalent Nets: When this option is turned on, the equivalent signals
of every signal stored in the FSDB file are found and added to the signal list.
For example, if a signal system.clock is in the FSDB file, the equivalent signals
system.i_cpu.clock, system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.clock, system.i_cpu.i_CCU.clock, and
system.i_pram.clock is included. The waveforms associated with these signals are now
available, since they are the same as system.clock. If this option is turned off and only
system.clock was stored in the FSDB file, the waveforms associated with the other
signals are not available.
* Filter: This is the file format filter for the file list in the right pane. The default file
extensions in the Filter field are * and *.fsdb; *.fsdb.gz; *.fsdb.bz2;*.ff; *.dump.
Additional filters can be added in this selection field using a semicolon (;) as the
separator.
* Open File by Time Range: When this option is turned on, a Time Range of Opened
File form opens. Here,the time range of interest can be specified in the From Time and
To Time text fields. This option speeds up the loading process when you want to load a
partial FSDB file.

Load Aux Annotation Waveform File

File -> Load Aux Annotation Waveform File

This command appends one more waveform file in the Verdi platform so you can see
active annotation and perform active trace. If a signal's value is not found in the primary
waveform file, the Verdi platform automatically looks in the auxiliary waveform file for
the value. After the second simulation file (waveform file format only) is specified in the
form, clicking OK appends the waveform file as the secondary result. The Message
frame shows Auxiliary file <file_name> for annotation is loaded, where the
<file_name> is the full path file name of the secondary waveform file name.
Figure 21

Append Simulation Result Form

Close Waveform File

File -> Close Waveform File

This command closes the simulation results so that they are not loaded when you open a
new nWave window.

Load Behavior Database

File -> Load Behavior Database

This command is available when the design is loaded from a pre-compiled
library.
This command opens the Load Behavior Database form where a previously created
behavior database can be loaded. A behavior database is created using the bacom utility.
Figure 22

Load Behavior Database Form

The following fields and option are available:
* File Name: Enter the file name directly or click the Browse button to open the Load
BDB File form and view the directory structure to load a Behavior Database (*.bdb) file.
* Enable Incremental Mode: When this option is turned on, the Behavior Database is
loaded incrementally. When this option is turned off, the entire Behavior Database is
loaded. The default value of this option is off.
When the -bdb_incr option is specified on the command line of the verdi utility, this
option is turned on automatically.
* Apply to Specified Scope: When this option is turned on, the behavior database
is only applied to the specified scope. When this option is turned off, the behavior
database applies to the entire design. The default value of this option is off.
After turning the option on, specify the path to load the top module of the Behavior
Database (BDB) file. Either type in the text field or click the Browse button to open the
Instance Manager form where the design hierarchy can be browsed and one scope
can be selected at a time. Alternatively, drag a scope from the nTrace design browser
frame and drop it to the Apply to Specified Scope text field.

Import CPF/UPF Files

File -> Import CPF/UPF Files

This command is available when CPF/UPF files have already been loaded from
the command line.
This command loads a CPF/UPF file. Refer to the Import CPF/UPF Files command
description in the Power Aware Debug chapter for details.

Reload CPF/UPF Files

File -> Reload CPF/UPF Files

Shift+R

This command is available when CPF/UPF files have already been loaded from
the command line.
This command reloads the current CPF/UPF files. Refer to the Reload CPF/UPF Files
command description in the Power Aware Debug chapter for details.

SDF
The following are the sub-commands of the SDF command.

Load SDF Files - nAnalyzer

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
This command opens the Import SDF form where an SDF (Standard Delay Format) file
(*.sdf) can be imported.
The following mnemonic keys are introduced:
* Design Name: alt + d
* SDF File: alt + s
* Filter: alt + f
* Report Undefined Paths: alt + r

Verdi closes the loaded SDF file when a design is imported or reloaded.
Figure
* 23

Import SDF Form

An SDF library file is created by running the sdfin utility, a batch mode compiler for SDF
files. The sdfin utility parses and saves the SDF file into a *.sdb file. The usage of sdfin is
as follows:
> sdfin [-vhdl] sdfFile [sdfFile2]

Refer to the sdfin section in the Utilities chapter in this manual and the nAnalyzer User's
Guide and Tutorial for details.
The Import SDF form includes the following fields and option:
* File: Displays the selected file name.
* Filter: Allows you to select the file types to display.
* Design Name: This text field identifies the region or scope of the design for the cell
entry that contains timing data. The design name does not need to be specified if the
timing data is for the top module. If the timing data is only for a lower-level design,
to view the SDF annotation (when the Schematic -> SDF Annotation option is
turned on) for the instance in nSchema, the full hierarchical instance name must be
in this text field. For example, if the cell entry starts from the system.i_cpu.i_alub,
system.i_cpu.i_alub should be specified in the Design Name text field.

To map the SDF file correctly to the design, the following two methods are available:
1. Loading the design from the system level testbench. Use the SDF virtual top and
specify the complete hierarchical instance name in the Design Name text field.
In an SDF file with the following design hierarchy in the header:
(DELAYFILE
(SDFVERSION "sdf 3.0")
(DESIGN "system.i_cpu")

Enter system.i_cpu in the Design Name text field.
2. Loading the design from a sub-module of the CPU (that is, the ALUB module with
instance i_ALUB). Use the design virtual top.
In an SDF file with the following design hierarchy in the header:
(DELAYFILE
(SDFVERSION "sdf 3.0")
(DESIGN "system.i_cpu")

Create a map file (that is, map.dat) that includes ALUB = system.i_cpu.i_ALUB in the
Design Name text field. Then, load the map file with the design.
* Report Undefined Paths: When this option is turned on, any cell/path delays exist in
an SDF file that does not match the current design is reported. The default value of this

Import Path Data Files - nAnalyzer

File -> Import Path Data File

This command opens the Import Report File form where a timing report file (*.xml
extension) can be imported.
More than 20 different types of reports can be generated from Primetime timing
analysis. For example: report_annotated_delay, report_cell, report_timing,
report_constraint, report_delay_calculation, and so on. The Verdi platform
with the nAnalyzer module only accepts the reports that were created with
report_timing and report_constraint from Primetime.
The Verdi platform does not extract all of the information from a Primetime
report. The following list of information is extracted:
* Start point & End point
* Incremental Delay & Accumulated delay
* Rising & Falling
* Data Arrival Time & Data Require time
* Clock network delay
* Clock uncertainty delay
* Library setup time
* Slack
The following list of information is ignored:
* Capacitance
* Transition time
* Fan In/Out number
* Any item that we does not list in "Extract"
The timing report file can be imported directly from the original report file or from the
converted XML file which can be created from tool outputs by using the conversion

utilities. That is, pt2Xml.pl, AMBIT.pl, astrol2Xml.pl, DC.pl, EinsTimer.pl, HAL2Xml.pl,
magma.pl, pearl.pl, RTLC2Xml.pl, and SE2Xml.pl). Refer to the Timing section in the
Utilities chapter for details.
Figure 24

Import Report File Form

The Import Report File form includes the following fields and options:
* Design Name: Specify the design name in this field and the root path of the design
name is concatenated to each element in the timing report.
* Select File: Select an import file type. The default value of this option is Prime Time
Report.
* Filter: Use this dynamic selection field for the file format filter of the file list. The default
file extensions are *.xml and *.rpt. The desired filter can be added by using a semicolon
(;) as the separator.
* Filter:After the Prime Time Report option is selected, the Filter option can be turned
on. Clicking the Filter button opens the Filter form where viewing of the display area in
the Timing Report form can be configured. Refer to the Filter Form for details.
* Directory for Converting XML: When this option is turned on, the Set the Directory to
Converting XML File form is opened so the directory for the converted XML file can be
set.
After the timing report output file is read, the path information is displayed in the Timing
Report Form where the path to trace can be selected.
The Prime Time Report (PTR) file (*.rpt extension) can be loaded directly. The PTR file is
automatically translated to an XML timing report with the pt2Xml.pl utility. A sample PTR
file is shown below:

Timing Report Form
After clicking the OK button in the Import Report File form, the Timing Report form opens.

Figure 25

Timing Report Form

The main display area in the Timing Report form shows the paths from static timing
analysis (STA) reports. If a path has a timing violation, the path is highlighted in red.
Five default columns are available in the main display area. The width of each column
can be adjusted by placing the cursor over the vertical bar in the heading row and then
pressing and holding the left mouse button. The column headings are summarized as
* Start Point: Indicates the point where the timing path starts.
* End Point: Indicates the point where the timing path ends.
* Arrival Time: Indicates the time when the path arrives at the end point.
* Required Time: Indicates the expected time from the start point to the end point of a
path.
* Slack: Indicates the difference between the analyzed time and the require time.

The following two column headings can be optionally added with the Attach Extracted
Clock Domain Results option:
* Clock Source of Start Point: Indicates the point where the clock source starts.
* Clock Source of End Point: Indicates the point where the clock source ends.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
n headings can be optionally added with the Attach Extracted
Clock Domain Results option:
* Clock Source of Start Point: Indicates the point where the clock source starts.
* Clock Source of End Point: Indicates the point where the clock source ends.
If an SDF file is already loaded, the following three column headings is displayed in the
Timing Report table. Click the Configure Columns button to view them.
* Insertion Delay of Start Point: Indicates the insertion delay of the specified path's
start point.
* Insertion Delay of End Point: Indicates the insertion delay of the specified path's end
point.
* Clock Skew: Indicates the difference between the insertion delay of the end point and
the insertion delay of start point.
The Timing Report form includes the following options:
* Configure Columns: Click this button to customize the display in the main display
area of the Timing Report form. Refer to the Configure Columns Form section for
* Attach Extracted Clock Domain Results: After clock domains in the nTrace or
nSchema windows are extracted and this option is turned on, the Clock Source of
Start Point and Clock Source of End Point information is available for viewing on the
main display area of the Timing Report form. Click the Configure Columns button to
view the Clock Source of Start Point and Clock Source of End Point columns. If
clock domains are not extracted before enabling the Attach Extracted Clock Domain
Results option, a message prompting to extract clock domains is issued.
* Delay Precision: Select a preferred time precision from 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001.
The default value of this option is 0.01.
* Enable Sorting: When this option is turned on, paths can be sorted by ascending
slack time or descending slack time. By default, the paths are sorted by Ascending
slack time.
* Enable Grouping: When this option is turned on, paths can be sorted by group. The
paths can be grouped by Start Point, Clock Domain of Start Point, or Clock Domain
of End Point. Only one option can be selected at a time. If the Enable Sorting option
is also turned on, the sorting order is by group first and then the paths is sorted by
slack time within the group.

* Filter: Click this button to open the Filter form where viewing of the main display area
in the Timing Report form can be customized. Refer to the Filter Form section for
* Information: This section displays the original timing report information.
The Show On section has the following options. Select one or more timing paths (either
drag-left or ctrl-left-click for multiple selections) in the main display area of the Timing
Report form. Click the Show button to view the path(s) in either text (File Viewer option)
or schematic (nSchema option) format. Path(s) can also be shown by dragging the path(s)
in the Timing Report form and dropping the path(s) to the nSchema window.
* File Viewer: Select this option to view the selected path(s) in the Text Viewer frame.
Path Report: When this option is turned on, click the Show button to view the total
delay, delay, type, arrival time, require time and slack for the selected path(s) in the
Text Viewer frame.
Skew Summary Report: When this option is turned on and an SDF file is imported,
click the Show button to view the skew summary report for the selected path(s) in
the Text Viewer frame.
Delimiter: Specify the delimiter separating the hierarchy names. The default is the
forward slash (/) character.
* nSchema: Select this option to view the timing report in the nSchema window.
* Set False Path: Click this button to open the Set False Path form where the selected
path(s) in the Timing Report form can be added as false path to the Set False Path
form. False path(s) can also be added by dragging the path(s) highlighted in the Timing
Report form and dropping the path(s) to the Set False Path form.
Figure
* 26

Set False Path Form

The Type column shows the false path type as InstPin (instant pin). The From and To
columns refer to the start point and end point of the false path respectively.
Refer to the Tools -> Set False Path command in the Crossing Paths window for details
about options in the Set False Path form.
* Show: After selecting a viewing option, click this button to display the results in the
specified format.
* Compare with SDF: Click this button to open the Compare with SDF form where the

Analyze Simulation Loop Data

File -> Analyze Simulation Loop Data

If a loop occurs during a simulation, the simulation time does not advance. This causes
signals in the loop to have abnormal glitch count and the simulation to freeze. If this data
is captured using FSDB, Verdi can find these abnormal glitch signals from the FSDB.
Further, it can identify the loop path through Verdi TFV and the nSchema tracing engine.
Verdi reads the FSDB file and fetches the signals that have an abnormal glitch number
(>1000). Verdi detects critical paths from this signal list and reports them in the GUI. To do
so, Verdi uses the -loopdbg option.
Prerequisites
For Verdi to display the loop path, the VCS simulation must have been executed using the
-loopdbg option. This option enables capturing the FSDB with loop debug data.
Use Model
verdi -dbdir simv.daidir -loopdbg_dir loop-work-dir

loop-work-dir is the directory in which the user ran simv with the -loopdbg option or the
directory the user specified in simv with the -loopdbg_dir option.

The loop-work-dir includes the FSDB and loop report data dumped by simv.
To analyze the simulation loop data, perform the following steps:
Choose the work directory through File > Analyze Simulation Loop Data

Viewing Paths Related to the Freeze Issue
The Critical Paths table lists all the paths that are related to the freeze issue. This table
comprises the following columns:
* Loop column
The values of the Loop column are "Full" or "Partial".
The `Full' path means the path is closed in a loop. Typically this requires breaking the
loop in the design to fix the freeze issue.
The `Partial' path means the path is not closed in a loop. However, the signals in
the path still have abnormal glitch counts. This is usually caused by the simulator
generating a loop calculation by mistake and resulting in a freeze problem.
* Start Point and End Point columns: These two columns values are signal names.
These columns specify the start and end signals of the path.

Sorting
Each column in the Signal List pane can be sorted by clicking the Signal heading column.
After sorting, the Signal List can be sorted as follows:
* Ascending: Sort signal names alphabetically by the ascending order.
* Descending: Sort signal names alphabetically by the descending order.
* Declaration: Sort signals by the definition order.
The Value column cannot be sorted.
The Signal column can be sorted in ascending, descending, and declaration
order.
All other columns in the Signal List can be sorted in ascending and
descending order.

Clicking the Filtering icon
to open the Signal Type Filter menu where signal type(s)
can be selected for display in the Signal List pane. The available types include:
* Input: Displays input ports.
* Output: Displays output ports.
* Inout: Displays inout ports.
* Wire/Signal: Displays wire type signals.
* Register: Displays register data type signals.
* Parameter: Displays parameter signals.
* Constant: Displays constant signals.
* Assertion: Displays the assertion signals.
* Buffer: Displays the buffer signals.
* Linkage: Displays the linkage signals.
* $unit: Displays all the global signals supported in the Signal list.
* Interface/Modport: Displays the Interface/Modport signals.
* Event: Displays the event signals.

* Isolation: Displays Isolation signals in power designs. This type is available when a
CPF/UPF file is loaded.
* Retention: Displays Retention signals in power designs. This type is available when a
CPF/UPF file is loaded.
* Level Shifter: Displays Level-shifted signals in power designs. This type is available
when a CPF/UPF file is loaded.
* SRSN/SPA: Displays SRSN/SPA signals in power designs. This type is available when
a UPF file is loaded.
* Repeater:Displays the repeater signals. This type is available when a UPF file is
* CSN: Displays the CSN signals. This type is available when a UPF file is loaded.
* ACK: Displays the ACK signals. This type is available when a UPF file is loaded.
* Simulation Only: Displays simulation information in power designs. This type is
available when a UPF file is loaded.
* UPF Inserted: Displays UPF inserted signals in the HDL design. This type is available
when a UPF file is loaded. The icon of UPF inserted signal is shown with a red dot
.
* Other: Displays other signal types.
* All: Displays all signal types.

Identify False Logic

View -> Identify False Logic

This toggle command turns the display of false logic in the source code frame on and off.
When this command is turned on, false logic is displayed in gray in the source code frame
after calculating expression values in the control logic. When the design is loaded again
or the cursor time is changed, expression values is calculated again and new false logic
is displayed in gray. When an FSDB file is loaded, nTrace calculates expression values,
signals, function calls, and constants, and then display false logic in gray; otherwise, only

constants and constant expressions are included. When this command is turned off, false
logic is not highlighted in gray in the source code frame. The default value of this option is
Identify false logic feature is not supported for VHDL and Verilog generate
block.

View -> Source Code Folder -> Collapse All in Design

When this command is invoked, all statement, comment, and port list folders in the whole
design as well as line numbers are folded, and the folded line number is marked in red.
1. Alternatively, click the plus (+) or minus (-) symbols to expand or collect the
source code folders.
2. The folding column width is adjusted based on the maximum folding
width of the current file. For example, the folding column must contain 4
folding marks if the current file has an always block that includes 3 level of
statements (3+1 = 4).
3. When the start or end point of the folder cannot be seen in the present value
window, a left-click on the black straight line scrolls to the out-of-sight start
or end point. If both the start and end points of the folder cannot be seen,
nTrace scrolls to start point only.
4. The folded line number color can be specified in the Preference -> Source
Code -> Color page.

Find Scope

Source -> Find Scope

Shift+S

This command opens the Find Scope form where all imported files can be viewed by type.
The files can be viewed by sorting alphabetically or by call level.
The section below Scope Type lists the results matching the specified type and sort
method. After selecting a result in the Scope Type section (only one Scope Type option
can be selected at a time), the section below Instance List shows the instance (when the
selection in the Scope Type is File) or hierarchical path (when the selection in the Scope
Type is Function, Module, or Task). If multiple scopes are selected in the Scope Type

section, instances of the selected modules are listed scope by scope in the Instance List
Figure 54

Find Scope Form

Find/Filter > Find/Filter Options. For more information, refer to the Find/Filter Page. You
the Match Case option.
For Verilog designs, the Scope Type section includes the following options. The default
type is Module.
* File: List by Verilog/VHDL file name including full directory path.
* Module: List by Verilog module name.
* Task: List by Verilog task name.
* Function: List by Verilog/VHDL function name.

For VHDL designs, the Scope Type section includes the following options. The default
type is Entity (Architecture).
* Entity (Architecture): List by VHDL entity (architecture) name.
* File: List by Verilog/VHDL file name including full directory path.
* Function: List by Verilog/VHDL function name.
* Package: List by VHDL package name.
* Procedure: List by VHDL procedure name.
For mixed Verilog/VHDL designs, all scope types are available.
The Sort by section includes the following sorting methods. Only one sorting method can
be selected at a time. The default value of this option is Alphabet.
* Alphabet: List the selected type alphabetically.
* Call Level: List the selected type by the call level as displayed in the design browser.
When the Match Case option is turned on, the search with the string set in the Filter text
field is case-sensitive. The default value of this option is on.
In the Filter text field, enter a string to search for source types matching the string.
Wildcard characters are supported.
Click the Save button to open the Save Result form where you can view the directory
structure and specify a file name to save the search results to. The saved file is in ASCII
format.
Click the Go To button to highlight the selected item in the right column of the nTrace
source code frame. You can also double-click the result in the Instance List section.
Click the Close button to close the Find Scope form without making any changes.
When you first enter the Find Scope dialog box, no module item is selected by default. As
a result, the instance list is not immediately populated. This prevents the dialog box from
becoming busy or unresponsive, even if the first module in the list contains a large number
of instances.

Figure 55

Find Scope- Searching in Background

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
When you select a module name that has many instances, the system shows a busy bar
at the top right of the main window. You can continue to work on other tasks while the
system processes your request. The busy bar lets you stop or restart the task if needed.
While the task is running, you cannot use the following features until the task finishes or
you stop it:
* ScopeType ComboBox
* Filter
* Any selected item under Module-Name list
Dialog Box UI Behavior During Background Search:
* When the background task is running, the instances list is empty. No items are
displayed until the search completes.
* At the bottom of the dialog box, the text searching in background is displayed instead
of a numeric value.
Limitation
The following is the limitation of the Non-blocking mode:
* The non-blocking mode in the full_load flow only supports module or architecture
types. However, the smart_load flow supports all types in non-blocking mode.

Find Signal/Instance/Instport

Source -> Find Signal/Instance/Instport

Shift+A

This command finds a signal, instance or instance port (Instport) in the source code by the
signal, instance or instance port's hierarchical name.
Figure 56

Find Signals Form

The Find Signal form includes the following options and fields:
* Find: Select Signal, Instance or Instport from the Find selection field. In the table
below the Find selection field, enter the hierarchical name of desired the signal,
instance or instance port. Then click the Find button.

Select Ctrl+A key to select all the signals in the Find Form. Select Ctrl+W key to add
all the selected signals at once in the Find Signal form. The signals are then added
to the nWave window. The minimum signals which can be added is 1000 which is the
default value. The default value for the signals which can be added in the Find Signal

form can be changed using the Get Signals -> Options form -> Others tab -> Ask if

The Find Signal/Instance/Instport text field supports the following regular
expressions:

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Expression

? (question
mark)

Any character Matches any one character.

* (asterisk)

Zero or more

Finds zero or more occurrences of the
preceding expression.

| (pipe)

OR

Matches the expression before or after
the pipe sign "|". Mostly used within a
group. For example, "[sponge]|[mud] bath"
matches "sponge bath" and "mud bath".

One or more

Matches at least one occurrence of the
